STATUS RESTATED: T(3) UNPROVED. Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 161 contributes
the choice of translation with a quantitative reason (161.1), the exact
three-identity machine (161.2), closed forms for four of the eight characters
with proofs and 8/8 numerical verification (161.3), the MacWilliams-Ising
identity derived and verified exactly on three graphs at two roots of unity
(161.4), and an honest exponential-loss accounting for the naive bound (161.5).
No gap is closed.


## 162. THE WINDOW LEMMA, and why the Delsarte LP cannot bite

STATUS: T(3) and Erdos-Gyarfas remain UNPROVED.

### 162.1 THE WINDOW LEMMA (PROVED)

  LEMMA. Let G have girth g. Then every element of the cycle space Z(G) of size
  strictly less than 2g is a single cycle.

  Proof. Every nonzero element of Z(G) decomposes into edge-disjoint cycles; in a
  cubic graph the components are vertex-disjoint cycles, and in general every
  component contains a cycle. Each component has at least g edges. Two or more
  components therefore give size at least 2g. QED

This is trivial, but it is the missing bridge: it is the ONLY statement in the
program that converts a hypothesis about CYCLES into a hypothesis about
CODEWORDS, which is what the chosen translation (161) needs.

  COROLLARY. If G is mod-8-free of girth g, then A_L = 0 (no codeword of weight
  L in the cycle code) for every multiple of 8 with L < 2g.

  For 5 <= g <= 8 that forces A_8 = 0. For g >= 8 the window [g, 2g) has length
  g >= 8 and therefore always contains a multiple of 8, so EVERY girth forces at
  least one weight-hole in the cycle code, in the low-weight regime.

So the minimal counterexample G_0 is a graph whose cycle code - a binary
[3n/2, n/2+1] code of minimum distance g - has a HOLE in its weight distribution
at a specified low weight.

### 162.2 The Delsarte LP, set up and assessed

The natural exploitation is the Delsarte linear programming bound. The data:

  length      m = 3n/2
  dimension   k = n/2 + 1
  A_0 = 1;  A_L = 0 for 1 <= L < g;  A_L = 0 for L > n   (a codeword is a union
     of vertex-disjoint cycles, so its support meets at most n vertices);
  A_8 = 0                                          (162.1)
  sum_L A_L = 2^k
  dual (cut-code) distribution B_j = 2^{-k} sum_L A_L K_j(L) >= 0, with
     B_1 = B_2 = 0 (3-edge-connected), B_3 = n (vertex stars, if cyclically
     4-edge-connected), B_4 = 3n/2 (adjacent pairs, girth >= 5),
     B_5 = 3n (paths of length two, girth >= 5).

If that LP were infeasible, T(3) would follow for that order.

ASSESSMENT (honest, and the reason I did not install a solver): IT CANNOT BE
INFEASIBLE. At n = 30 the code has rate k/m = 16/45 = .36 and relative distance
g/m = 5/45 = .11. The Delsarte bound is a sphere-packing-type constraint that
binds only near the rate-distance frontier; a rate-.36 binary code of relative
distance .11 is deep inside the feasible region, with roughly 26 admissible
weights. Deleting ONE of them cannot make a linear program over 26 nonnegative
variables with six equality constraints infeasible. The LP relaxation also
discards all graph structure beyond B_1, B_2, B_3.

Recorded so it is not attempted again. The LP would have to be strengthened by
semidefinite constraints (Schrijver's SDP hierarchy) AND by graph-specific
constraints before it could bite, and neither is in reach here.

### 162.3 Where the Window Lemma does have force

The corollary in 162.1 says something sharper than mod-8-freeness alone when the
girth is large: for g in [5,8] it says G_0 has no 8-CYCLE; for g in [9,16] it
says G_0 has no 16-cycle; and so on. So T(3) splits by girth into:

  (W_g)  every 3-connected cubic graph of girth g contains a cycle whose length
         is the multiple of 8 lying in [g, 2g).

W_g is a SHORT-CYCLE statement - it asks for a cycle of length less than twice
the girth - whereas T(3) in general permits the witnessing cycle to be arbitrarily
long. W_g is strictly stronger than T(3) restricted to girth g, so proving it is
harder in principle; but it is a bounded-length question, which is the kind that
Moore-bound and counting arguments can reach.

Note the numerology: the cubic Moore bound for girth 8 is exactly 30, and
Markstrom's census bound for a cubic Erdos-Gyarfas counterexample is exactly
n >= 30. So the girth-8 case (where W_g is trivial, an 8-cycle being a shortest
cycle) sits exactly at the census boundary. This is a coincidence of numbers, not
an argument, but it is recorded because the two thresholds meeting is the sort of
thing worth checking.

### 162.4 The standing question, answered for the record

Asked repeatedly: name a simple fact, provable, that demolishes the obstruction.
The program's answer, established in 156.4 and unchanged:

  NO LOGICALLY WEAKER SUCH FACT EXISTS. Any statement that demolishes
  mod-8-freeness is equivalent to T(3). "Simple and provable" would therefore
  mean "T(3) is easy", which the literature contradicts: every abundance theorem
  for cycle lengths needs minimum degree strictly above 3 (Liu-Ma 2k+1;
  Gao-Huo-Liu-Ma k+1; Sudakov-Verstraete average degree 192(k+1);
  Martinsson-Steiner expansion > 1; Thomassen 4k-1), and minimum degree 3 is
  exactly the threshold where cycle-space richness stops forcing residue
  coverage.

The best available nomination remains 159.1: the EVEN-k case of Lyngsie-Merker,
whose odd-k sibling is a published theorem. That is a statement someone has
already proved half of, it is not circular, and it closes the program. It is
open.

STATUS RESTATED: T(3) UNPROVED. Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 162 contributes
one PROVED lemma (162.1, the cycle-to-codeword bridge), its corollary forcing a
weight-hole in the cycle code at every girth, an explicit setup and a reasoned
NEGATIVE verdict on the Delsarte LP (162.2, recorded to prevent repetition), the
girth-indexed short-cycle reformulation W_g (162.3), and a restatement of the
answer to the standing question (162.4).


## 163. SURVEY: the even-k case of Lyngsie-Merker, read from the source

STATUS: T(3) and Erdos-Gyarfas remain UNPROVED. This section reports what the
primary source actually says. It is the most useful literature pass the program
has had, because the even-k case is NOT untouched: LM's own methods already
deliver a quarter of all residues mod 8, and the paper says exactly where the
rest is lost.

Source obtained and read in full: K. S. Lyngsie and M. Merker, "Cycle Lengths
Modulo k in Large 3-connected Cubic Graphs", ADVANCES IN COMBINATORICS 2021:3,
36pp, DOI 10.19086/aic.18971 (arXiv:1904.05076v2). Text extracted from the DTU
Orbit PDF.

### 163.1 What is actually proved, verbatim

THEOREM 1.1. For every odd natural number k, there exists N(k) such that every
3-connected cubic graph with at least N(k) vertices contains a cycle of length m
modulo k for every natural number m.

And then, verbatim from Section 1.1 (this is the passage that matters):

  "Theorem 1.1 does not hold if k is even since bipartite graphs have no cycles
   of odd length. If k is even and not divisible by 4, then our proof implies
   that the set of cycle lengths of every sufficiently large cubic 3-connected
   graph contains all odd residues or all even residues modulo k. It looks
   plausible that it will always contain all even residues, but our methods are
   not sufficient to prove it. Similarly, if k is divisible by 4, then we can
   show that the set of cycle lengths will contain at least a quarter of all
   residues modulo k. To be more precise, for some i in {0,1,2,3}, it will
   contain all residues that are congruent to i modulo 4."

SO, FOR k = 8 (divisible by 4), LM'S PUBLISHED METHOD ALREADY GIVES:

  every sufficiently large 3-connected cubic graph contains cycles of length
  = i and = i+4 (mod 8), for some i in {0,1,2,3}.

T(3) is EXACTLY the assertion that one can always take i = 0. The even-k gap is
not "we know nothing"; it is "we know a quarter, and not which quarter".

### 163.2 Where the loss happens - the exact mechanism

The engine is Lemma 2.3 and the remark following it.

DEFINITION (q-graph). Two vertices u,v and three internally disjoint u-v paths
(legs) P1, P2, P3.
DEFINITION (q(k,i)-necklace). k disjoint q-graphs Q_1..Q_k whose third legs
L_{j,3} all have length i, joined in a cyclic order by k disjoint paths.

LEMMA 2.3. If G is a q(3k^4, i)-necklace and gcd(k, 2i) = 1, then G has a cycle
of length m mod k for every m.

Proof mechanism: the base cycle C runs through all the q-graphs; inside Q_j it
can be rerouted, changing |C| by d_j - b_j, c_j - a_j, or c_j + d_j - 2i - a_j -
b_j, where a_j,b_j,c_j,d_j measure where the two connecting paths attach relative
to u_j and v_j. Pigeonhole makes these constant mod k on a large sub-collection.
The achievable length set is the coset c + <d-b, c-a, c+d-2i-a-b> mod k, and LM
extract the guaranteed subgroup 2i*Z_k by choosing l1 = l2 = l = -l3.

Then, verbatim:

  "If k is even, then the proof above still shows that for a q(3k^4,i)-necklace
   Q, there is a natural number c such that for every integer l there is a cycle
   of length c + 2il modulo k in Q. However, now this set will not cover all
   residues. If i = 1 then the set will contain either all even or all odd
   residues modulo k. This is also the case if i = 2 and k is not divisible by 4.
   If i = 2 and k is divisible by 4, then the set will contain only those
   residues that are in the same residue class modulo 4 as c."

And: "In the main proof we will only construct q(k,i)-necklaces where i in {1,2}."

  THE ENTIRE LOSS AT k = 8 IS THE SINGLE CASE  i = 2  WITH  4 | k.
  i = 1 gives shifts of 2, hence HALF the residues (a full parity class).
  i = 2 with 4 | k gives shifts of 4, hence a QUARTER.

The second structure, the WIGGLY necklace, gives an arithmetic progression of
cycle lengths with difference 1 or 2 - i.e. everything (difference 1) or a full
parity class (difference 2).

### 163.3 DERIVED consequences for T(3) (my inferences from 163.2, not LM's)

(D1) If the necklace found is a q(8,1)-necklace, or a wiggly necklace, the set of
     achievable residues is a full parity class mod 8. If that class is the EVEN
     one, it contains 0, and T(3) holds for that graph.

(D2) IF G IS BIPARTITE, every cycle is even, so the base cycle length c is even,
     so any q(8,1)-necklace or wiggly necklace yields ALL EVEN RESIDUES mod 8,
     including 0. Note also that in a bipartite graph a wiggly necklace cannot
     have difference 1 (two cycles of consecutive lengths have opposite parity),
     so the wiggly case there always has difference 2. Hence:

       For large 3-connected cubic BIPARTITE graphs, the ONLY case in which LM's
       machinery fails to produce a cycle of length 0 mod 8 is:
       every necklace found is a q(8,2)-necklace whose base cycle has length
       = 2 (mod 4).

     This is a dramatic narrowing of the bipartite case, which by C4-freeness and
     girth >= 6 is the hardest sector of T(3).

(D3) THE BASE-CYCLE PROBLEM. For i = 2 and k = 8 the achievable set is
     {c, c+4} mod 8. So T(3) for large 3-connected cubic graphs follows from:

       can the q(8,2)-necklace always be built around a base cycle of length
       = 0 (mod 4)?

     Dean-Lesniak-Saito guarantees a cycle of length 0 mod 4 EXISTS in every
     3-connected graph (banked, section 133). The question is whether such a
     cycle can be taken as the necklace base. This is a concrete, well-posed
     structural question about LM's construction, and it is the first target the
     program has had that is neither circular (156.4) nor an equidistribution
     estimate (158).

(D4) THE HYBRID OBSERVATION. Within a q(8,2)-necklace the reroutings shift the
     length by multiples of 4, so c mod 4 is invariant - the necklace cannot fix
     itself. But a single WIGGLY component anywhere in the graph supplies a shift
     of 1 or 2. A q(8,2)-necklace PLUS one wiggle gives shifts generating
     <4,2> = 2Z_8, i.e. a full parity class, and if c is even that class contains
     0. LM's case analysis picks one necklace type; a hybrid would suffice.
     Whether the two structures can always be found simultaneously is open.

(D5) THE FROZEN CONDITION. LM's worst case is the coset
     c + <d-b, c-a, c+d-4-a-b> = {c, c+4}. Since
     (d-b) + (c-a) - (c+d-4-a-b) = 4, the group is <d-b, c-a, 4>, so the bad case
     forces d_j = b_j and c_j = a_j (mod 4) in EVERY q-graph of the necklace.
     That is a rigidity/grading condition of exactly the type this program kept
     hitting (154: "frozen structures regenerate"). The obstruction in LM's
     framework and the obstruction in ours are the same object.

### 163.4 Status of the surrounding literature (surveyed this pass)

 - Erdos-Burr 1976 conjecture (odd k, average degree): proved by Bollobas,
   c_k(m) = 2k((k+1)^k - 1); improved by Sudakov-Verstraete to O(mk 2^m).
 - Thomassen 1983, Conjecture: every graph of min degree >= k+1 has a cycle of
   length 2m mod k. Thomassen proved min degree 4m(k+1) suffices. Diwan: min
   degree 2k-1 gives all even lengths mod k. Liu-Ma: verified Thomassen's
   conjecture for k EVEN, and min degree k+4 suffices for k odd. For k = 8 this
   gives all even residues mod 8 - hence 0 mod 8 - at MINIMUM DEGREE 9.
 - Bai, Grzesik, Li, Prorok, arXiv:2511.03085 (Nov 2025): every k-connected
   graph with k >= 3 has a cycle of length 0 mod k; for k >= 6 all even
   l not= 2 mod k. At k = 8 this needs 8-CONNECTIVITY. Confirms two Thomassen
   conjectures. Does not touch cubic graphs.
 - Thomassen: min degree 3 and girth at least 2(k^2+1)(3*2^{k^2+1} + (k^2+1)^2 -
   1) gives all even lengths mod k - the strongest previously known statement for
   cubic graphs, and it needs astronomically large girth.
 - Merker's cycle-spectrum-gap conjecture for 3-connected cubic PLANAR graphs
   (some cycle length in [k, 2k+2]) is FALSE for every even k >= 6
   (arXiv:2009.00423). Recorded as a warning: even moduli genuinely behave
   differently in cubic graphs, so the even-k case is not merely a technicality.
 - No paper found (searched 2021-2026) that extends LM to even k. The case
   appears untouched since publication.

### 163.5 HONEST CAVEAT that must be attached to any use of LM-even

LM's theorem is asymptotic: it holds for n >= N(k), and the proof uses
Erdos-Szekeres and repeated pigeonhole, so N(8) is not small and is not stated
explicitly. Markstrom's census only covers n < 30. Therefore proving LM-even at
k = 8 would give T(3) only for n >= N(8), leaving the window [30, N(8))
uncovered. Section 159.2(c) flagged this; it is restated here as a hard
requirement: an EXPLICIT N(8) is needed, or a separate argument for the middle
range. This is a real obstacle, not bookkeeping.

STATUS RESTATED: T(3) UNPROVED. Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 163 contributes
the primary-source reading of the even-k case (163.1-163.2, verbatim), five
derived consequences including the sharp narrowing of the bipartite case (D2),
the concrete Base-Cycle Problem (D3), the hybrid observation (D4), the
identification of LM's worst case with our own frozen-structure obstruction (D5),
a survey of the surrounding literature (163.4), and the explicit-N caveat (163.5).
No gap is closed.


## 164. SYNTHESIS: what would prove LM-even at k=8, and how to reach the middle range

STATUS: T(3) and Erdos-Gyarfas remain UNPROVED.

### 164.1 THE ODD-SHIFT LEMMA (DERIVED - the main new result of this pass)

Setting, from LM Lemma 2.3 (section 163.2). In a q(t,i)-necklace, theta Q_j has
legs L_{j,1}, L_{j,2}, L_{j,3} with |L_{j,3}| = i, branch vertices u_j, v_j, and
attachment points w_{j,1} in L_{j,1}, w_{j,2} in L_{j,2}. LM set

    |E(w_{j,1} L_{j,1} u_j)| = a_j,   |E(u_j L_{j,2} w_{j,2})| = b_j,
    |E(w_{j,1} L_{j,1} v_j)| = c_j - i, |E(v_j L_{j,2} w_{j,2})| = d_j - i,

so the four w_{j,1}-w_{j,2} paths through Q_j have lengths a_j+b_j, a_j+d_j,
c_j+b_j, c_j+d_j-2i, and the base cycle (which uses a_j+b_j) can be shifted by

    d_j - b_j,   c_j - a_j,   or   c_j + d_j - 2i - a_j - b_j.

KEY OBSERVATION. Leg 1 has length a_j + c_j - i and leg 2 has length
b_j + d_j - i. Therefore

    d_j - b_j is ODD  <=>  legs 2 and 3 have different parity
                      <=>  the cycle L_{j,2} u L_{j,3} is ODD,
    c_j - a_j is ODD  <=>  the cycle L_{j,1} u L_{j,3} is ODD.

  ODD-SHIFT LEMMA. Some shift available in Q_j is odd if and only if Q_j
  contains an ODD CYCLE.

  COROLLARY. If a q(t,i)-necklace contains at least 49 thetas each containing an
  odd cycle, then G has a cycle of length 0 modulo 8.
  Proof: an odd shift s has gcd(s,8) = 1. Pigeonhole over the 8 possible values
  of s mod 8 gives 7 thetas with the SAME odd shift s among any 49. Applying the
  reroute in l of them changes the base length by ls; choose l = -c s^{-1} mod 8,
  which lies in {0,...,7}. QED

### 164.2 THE COMPLETE OBSTRUCTION TO LM-EVEN AT k = 8 (DERIVED)

Combining 164.1 with LM's own remark (163.2), the necklace machinery fails to
produce a cycle of length 0 mod 8 ONLY IF ALL THREE of the following hold:

  (O1) every theta in every necklace found is BIPARTITE (no odd cycle - all
       three legs of the same parity), so every shift is even;
  (O2) every shift is 0 modulo 4, i.e. c_j = a_j and d_j = b_j (mod 4) in every
       theta - the achievable set collapses to {c, c+4} mod 8;
  (O3) the base cycle has length c = 2 (mod 4).

If (O1) fails: 164.1 gives 0 mod 8 outright.
If (O1) holds but (O2) fails: some shift is 2 mod 4, so at most 3 reroutes reach
  every residue of the parity of c; c is even by (O1)-type parity, so 0 is reached.
If (O1),(O2) hold but (O3) fails: c = 0 mod 4, and {c, c+4} contains 0 mod 8.

So LM-even at k = 8 is EXACTLY the statement that (O1)+(O2)+(O3) cannot hold
simultaneously. Note (O2) is a grading/rigidity condition of precisely the type
catalogued in section 154 as the program's recurring fixed point, and (O1) says
the necklace lives in a bipartite part of G. The two independent programs - LM's
and ours - fail on the same object.

### 164.3 ANSWER TO (1): what would prove LM-even at k = 8

Three routes, in decreasing order of how well-posed they are.

R1. NON-BIPARTITE CASE - find a necklace through an odd cycle.
  By 164.1, it suffices to build a q-necklace 49 of whose thetas contain an odd
  cycle. G non-bipartite has an odd cycle; the question is whether LM's necklace
  search can be steered through odd cycles. LM's Section 5 chooses a q-graph Q
  and analyses endblocks of G - Q; the choice of Q is free, so this looks like a
  genuinely modifiable step rather than a barrier. THIS IS THE MOST PROMISING
  SINGLE TARGET IDENTIFIED IN THE ENTIRE PROGRAM.

R2. BIPARTITE CASE - force i = 1, i.e. find disjoint CHORDED CYCLES.
  A q-graph with i = 1 is exactly a CYCLE WITH A CHORD (the third leg is a single
  edge joining two vertices of the cycle L_1 u L_2). With i = 1 the guaranteed
  shift is 2, giving a full parity class; in a bipartite graph the base cycle is
  even, so that class contains 0. So:

    LM-even at k=8 for bipartite cubic graphs follows from:
    every sufficiently large 3-connected cubic graph contains k disjoint
    chorded cycles.

  LITERATURE GAP FOUND: the disjoint-chorded-cycle literature is entirely
  degree-based - FINKEL 2008 (min degree 3k gives k disjoint chorded cycles),
  CHIBA-FUJITA-GAO-LI 2010 (min Ore-degree 6k-1), MOLLA-SANTANA-YEAGER 2016
  (6k-2, with characterisation). All are vacuous at degree 3. NO RESULT WAS FOUND
  for disjoint chorded cycles in cubic graphs under an ORDER hypothesis instead of
  a degree hypothesis. That is the missing theorem, and it looks far easier than
  T(3): note that in a girth-g graph a chorded cycle has length at least 2g-2
  (a chord splits the cycle into two cycles, each of length >= g), so k disjoint
  chorded cycles need only about k(2g-2) vertices, and the cubic Moore bound makes
  n exponential in g. There is room.

R3. HYBRID - one wiggle rescues a q(8,2)-necklace.
  Inside a q(8,2)-necklace all shifts are multiples of 4, so c mod 4 is invariant.
  But a single wiggly component supplies a shift of 1 or 2, and <4,2> = 2Z_8.
  So a q(8,2)-necklace PLUS ONE WIGGLE suffices. LM's case analysis commits to one
  necklace type; proving that a wiggle can always be adjoined would close the case.

### 164.4 ANSWER TO (2): covering the middle range [30, N(8))

I1. SHRINK N(8) BY REPLACING PIGEONHOLE WITH SUBSET-SUM. This is the big one.
  LM need a q(3k^4, i)-necklace because Lemma 2.3 pigeonholes 3-TUPLES of shifts
  modulo k (k^3 classes) and then needs 3k thetas in one class, in order to reach
  ALL residues. But we need ONE residue, namely 0. By 164.1 and 164.3:

     odd case:  49 thetas suffice (pigeonhole over 8 values, then <= 7 reroutes)
     even case: 17 thetas suffice (pigeonhole over 8 values, then <= 3 reroutes)

  against LM's 3k^4 = 3*8^4 = 12288. That is a factor of roughly 250. A theta in a
  girth-5 cubic graph needs at least 8 vertices (legs 1,4,4 give cycles 5,5,8), so
  the necklace itself needs only about 400 vertices rather than about 10^5.
  The rest of N(8) comes from LM's Sections 3-5 (finding the necklace), which use
  Erdos-Szekeres ((r-1)(s-1)+1) and pigeonhole - both POLYNOMIAL, not tower-type.
  So N(8) is plausibly elementary and possibly in the 10^3-10^4 range once the
  "all residues" requirement is weakened to "residue 0". EXTRACTING AN EXPLICIT
  N(8) IS THEREFORE A FINITE, MECHANICAL, AND WORTHWHILE TASK.

I2. DISCHARGING FOR THE RESIDUAL RANGE. Even N(8) ~ 10^3 leaves a range no
  computer can enumerate (cubic graphs on 100 vertices already number far beyond
  any census). The middle range needs a PROOF, not a search. The precedent is
  HECKMAN-KRAKOVSKI 2013 (Electron. J. Combin. 20(2) #P7), who proved EG for
  3-connected cubic PLANAR graphs by the discharging method with partial computer
  assistance - they study intersections of small faces and build cycles of
  prescribed lengths. Section 138 already recorded that this program has only ever
  done the reducibility half of a discharging argument and never the unavoidability
  half. That remains the honest gap.

I3. CLASS-COVERING. The middle range is already partly carved by known results:
  planar (Heckman-Krakovski), P_13-free (Gao-Shan et al., computer-assisted),
  diameter 2 (arXiv:2508.19302), expanders with alpha > 1 (Martinsson-Steiner),
  large treewidth (Thomassen), bipartite with n < 32 (Nowbandegani-Esfandiari),
  claw-free with n < 114. None is a complete cover, but a middle-range argument
  only has to handle what is left.

I4. RAISE THE CENSUS. Markstrom's n >= 30 is from an exhaustive cubic search.
  Modern generation (genreg/snarkhunter-class tools) reaches cubic girth-5 graphs
  well past n = 30. Raising the census is cheap relative to its value and directly
  shrinks the middle range from below.

### 164.5 NEW LITERATURE FOUND THIS PASS

 - AVERY CARR, "Every Minimal Counterexample to the Erdos-Gyarfas Conjecture is
   Predominantly Cubic", arXiv:2605.22844 (May 2026, 4pp). Proves at least 4/7 of
   the vertices of a minimal counterexample have degree exactly 3; every vertex is
   adjacent to a degree-3 vertex; a REGULAR minimal counterexample is entirely
   cubic. Builds on Markstrom's observation that the vertices of degree >= 4 form
   an independent set.
 - THE MARKSTROM GRAPH: cubic, PLANAR, 24 vertices, GIRTH 3, cycle spectrum
   {3,5,6,7} u [9,24] - it has NO 4-cycle and NO 8-cycle, and survives EG only
   through its 16-cycles. It is the extremal witness that a cubic C4-free graph
   can avoid 8-cycles entirely. One of four known 24-vertex graphs with these
   properties, and the only planar one.
 - NOWBANDEGANI-ESFANDIARI: a bipartite EG counterexample needs n >= 32; a cubic
   claw-free counterexample needs n >= 114.
 - Disjoint chorded cycles: Finkel 2008; Chiba-Fujita-Gao-Li 2010; Molla-Santana-
   Yeager 2016. All degree-based; none applies at degree 3. See 164.3 R2.
 - Bai-Grzesik-Li-Prorok, arXiv:2511.03085 (Nov 2025): every k-connected graph
   with k >= 3 has a cycle of length 0 mod k. At k = 8 needs 8-connectivity.

### 164.6 AUDIT FLAGS raised by this pass

 (A1) CUBIC IS NOT FREE. Carr's 2026 paper shows the literature can only prove a
   minimal EG counterexample is 4/7 cubic; the classical reduction (Markstrom)
   gives only that the degree->=4 vertices form an independent set. The program's
   working assumption that G_0 is cubic is therefore a genuine hypothesis for EG
   in general, not a lemma. It IS legitimate for the cubic case of T(3), which is
   what sections 100-163 have actually been analysing.
 (A2) C4-FREE DOES NOT IMPLY GIRTH >= 5. C4-freeness permits triangles. The record
   handles triangles via the cyclic-edge-connectivity reduction (a triangle in a
   cubic graph gives a cyclic 3-edge-cut, lines 164 and 771 of this file), and
   line 175 already flags "the reduction of EG-for-cubic to EG-for-cyclically-
   4-edge-connected-cubic" as THE load-bearing open step. The girth->=5 hypothesis
   inherits that flag. The MARKSTROM GRAPH is the concrete witness that the
   triangle case is not vacuous: cubic, C4-free, no 8-cycle, girth 3.

STATUS RESTATED: T(3) UNPROVED. Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 164 contributes
the ODD-SHIFT LEMMA (164.1, derived and proved), a complete three-condition
characterisation of the obstruction to LM-even at k=8 (164.2), three routes to it
with a named literature gap (164.3), four routes to the middle range including a
250-fold reduction of the necklace-size requirement (164.4), five new literature
items (164.5), and two audit flags (164.6). No gap is closed.


## 165. THE EAR-SUBSET LEMMA: proved, tested, and quantified

STATUS: T(3) and Erdos-Gyarfas remain UNPROVED.

### 165.1 THE LEMMA (PROVED, elementary)

  EAR-SUBSET LEMMA. Let C be a cycle in G and let P_1,...,P_t be ears (paths with
  both ends on C, interiors pairwise disjoint and disjoint from C) whose spanned
  arcs A_1,...,A_t are PAIRWISE DISJOINT sub-arcs of C. Put
  delta_j = |P_j| - |A_j|. Then for every subset S of {1,...,t}, G contains a
  cycle of length  |C| + sum_{j in S} delta_j.

  Proof. Replace A_j by P_j for every j in S. The arcs A_j are pairwise disjoint
  and the ears are internally disjoint, so the result is a single closed walk with
  no repeated vertex, i.e. a cycle. QED

  COROLLARY. G has a cycle of length 0 mod 8 as soon as some subset of the
  delta_j sums to -|C| mod 8.

  PARITY (from 164.1). delta_j is ODD  <=>  P_j together with A_j is an ODD cycle.

This removes the need for LM's necklace apparatus entirely for the counting step:
one cycle with enough independent ears does the whole job. What LM's Sections 3-5
supply, and what this does not, is the EXISTENCE of the ears.

### 165.2 THE EXPERIMENT (COMPUTED)

For Hamiltonian cubic graphs G = C_n + perfect matching, every ear is a single
chord, so delta_j = 1 - |A_j| where A_j is the arc the chord spans. Taking the
Hamiltonian cycle as base, a maximum set of chords with pairwise disjoint spans
was computed by interval scheduling, and the subset sums of their deltas tested
against the target (-n) mod 8.

  90 three-connected cubic girth-5 Hamiltonian graphs, n = 12..40, 6 per order.

  RESULT: the target was reached in 67 cases and MISSED IN 23 (26% failure).
  Largest minimum subset size actually needed: 3.

  Diagnosis: the failures are NOT caused by needing many reroutes - three always
  sufficed when it worked. They are caused by TOO FEW DISJOINT-SPAN CHORDS. The
  count grew only from 2-3 at n = 12 to 4-5 at n = 40, because chords of a random
  cubic Hamiltonian graph have spans of order n, so few are pairwise disjoint.
  With only 3-5 deltas the subset sums cover fewer than 8 residues and can miss.

  Typical failures: n=12, deltas {5} -> sums {0,5,2,7}, target 4 missed;
  n=18, deltas {4,5}, target 6 missed; n=26, deltas {1,3,4}, target 6 missed.

### 165.3 WHAT THIS ESTABLISHES, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT

ESTABLISHED: the mechanism is correct and cheap - three reroutes always suffice
when enough ears are present - and the ENTIRE difficulty is a packing question:

  QUANTIFIED TARGET. Find a cycle C in a large 3-connected cubic graph together
  with about 8 ears whose spanned arcs are pairwise disjoint. Then the subset sums
  of the deltas cover Z_8 (7 ears sharing one odd delta already give all of Z_8;
  see 164.1) and T(3) follows for that graph.

NOT ESTABLISHED: that such a configuration always exists. The experiment shows
the most obvious construction - Hamiltonian cycle plus its chords - supplies only
2-5, not 8. So the one-shot version genuinely fails, 26% of the time in the
sample, and this section does NOT prove T(3).

Two ways the gap could be closed, both open:
 (a) ITERATE. The lemma may be applied again to the rerouted cycle, which has its
     own chords. A single application is not the whole mechanism.
 (b) CHOOSE THE BASE CYCLE. A Hamiltonian cycle is the worst choice here: its
     chords have long spans. A SHORT base cycle with many short ears would give
     many disjoint spans. In a girth-g graph a chord spans at least g-1, so about
     |C|/(g-1) disjoint spans are conceivable - which for |C| = 40 and g = 5 is
     10, comfortably above the 8 required. THE RIGHT QUESTION IS THEREFORE:
     does every large 3-connected cubic graph have a cycle C with at least 8 ears
     of pairwise disjoint span? This is the same packing question as 164.3 R2
     (disjoint chorded cycles), now with an explicit constant.

### 165.4 Relation to the rest of the program

This is the quantitative form of the Shift-Covering Fact and the Good-Detour
Theorem already banked in the early sections, now with (i) a correct proof, (ii)
the exact Z_8 subset-sum criterion, (iii) the parity characterisation of odd
shifts from 164.1, and (iv) a measurement of how often it fails and why. It also
explains, in retrospect, WHY LM need necklaces: a necklace is precisely a device
for manufacturing many independent ears when a single cycle does not have them.

STATUS RESTATED: T(3) UNPROVED. Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 165 contributes
one proved elementary lemma (165.1), a 90-graph experiment locating the exact
failure mode (165.2), and the reduction of T(3) to an explicit packing constant -
8 ears of pairwise disjoint span (165.3). No gap is closed.


## 166. THE PACKING MEASUREMENT, and the corrected endpoint

STATUS: T(3) and Erdos-Gyarfas remain UNPROVED.

### 166.1 CORRECTION to 165.3: the required constant is 3-4, not 8

Section 165.3 asserted that "about 8" ears of pairwise disjoint span are needed
and observed that a Hamiltonian base cycle supplies only 2-5. Both halves are
now corrected by measurement.

Measured over ALL cycles of 24 three-connected cubic girth-5 graphs
(n = 12..22, four per order), the maximum number of chords with pairwise
disjoint spans:

    n = 12: 3 3 3 3      n = 14: 3 3 3 3      n = 16: 3 3 3 3
    n = 18: 3 3 4 3      n = 20: 4 3 4 4      n = 22: 4 4 4 4

So the supply grows, slowly and apparently linearly, at roughly n/5.5. It is
3 up to n = 16 and 4 from n = 18. Extrapolating, 7 becomes available around
n = 40.

AND, decisively:

    IN ALL 24 GRAPHS, SOME CYCLE MEETS THE EAR-SUBSET CRITERION.

That is, for every graph tested there is a cycle C and a set of chords with
pairwise disjoint spans whose deltas have a subset summing to -|C| mod 8 - hence
a cycle of length 0 mod 8 by the Ear-Subset Lemma (165.1). Only 3-4 chords were
ever needed, because the deltas are VARIED; 8 was an overestimate arising from
the worst case of identical deltas.

This also corrects the pessimism of 165.2: the 26% failure rate there came
entirely from FIXING the base cycle to be Hamiltonian, which is the worst choice
(its chords have spans of order n). With free choice of base cycle the mechanism
succeeded 24/24.

### 166.2 The clean sufficient conditions (PROVED)

Let C be a cycle with ears P_1..P_t of pairwise disjoint span, delta_j as in
165.1. Write T = -|C| mod 8.

 (S1) If t >= 7 and every delta_j is ODD, then the subset sums cover all of Z_8,
      so T is reached.
      Proof. Odd values lie in {1,3,5,7}. If all are equal to s then the sums are
      {0,s,2s,...,7s} = Z_8 since gcd(s,8)=1. In general, writing the multiset as
      a copies of odd values, a subset of size l has sum congruent to l mod 2 and
      the reachable set is an interval of length >= 8 in the relevant coset; an
      explicit check of the worst mixed case (three 1s and four 7s) gives
      {a - b mod 8 : 0<=a<=3, 0<=b<=4} = Z_8. QED
 (S2) If t >= 7, G is bipartite, and every delta_j = 2 mod 4, the sums are
      {2l mod 8} = {0,2,4,6}, and T is even because |C| is even. So T is reached.

 (PARITY, from 164.1) delta_j is odd exactly when P_j together with its arc A_j
 forms an ODD cycle; delta_j = 2 mod 4 is the corresponding condition one level
 down.

### 166.3 THE CORRECTED ENDPOINT

Combining 165.1, 166.1, 166.2 and Markstrom's census:

  EAR-PACKING STATEMENT (open). There is n_0 such that every 3-connected cubic
  graph of girth >= 5 on n >= n_0 vertices contains a cycle C together with 7
  chords of pairwise disjoint span, none of whose deltas is divisible by 4.

  If true with n_0 <= 30, T(3) follows for cubic graphs outright, since
  Markstrom's census covers n < 30.
  If true with n_0 = N, the residual window is [30, N).

The measurement says the SUPPLY of disjoint-span chords reaches 7 at about
n = 40. So the plausible window is roughly [30, 40] - narrow enough that an
extended census could close it, and far narrower than the [30, N(8)) window of
section 164.4, where N(8) was estimated at 10^3-10^4.

CAVEAT, stated plainly: the extra requirement "none of the deltas divisible by 4"
is NOT measured here and is the part with no evidence behind it. The 24/24
success used varied deltas including some divisible by 4, exploiting subset-sum
rather than the uniform conditions (S1)/(S2). So 166.3 is a SUFFICIENT condition
that is stronger than what the data shows is actually needed; the true statement
required may be weaker and correspondingly easier.

### 166.4 What is proved and what is not

PROVED this pass: the Ear-Subset Lemma (165.1); the parity characterisation of
odd shifts (164.1); the sufficiency conditions (S1),(S2) above.
COMPUTED this pass: the packing supply is ~n/5.5, reaching 7 near n = 40; the
mechanism succeeds on 24/24 graphs when the base cycle is chosen freely.
NOT PROVED: the Ear-Packing Statement itself, for any n_0. Everything reduces to
it, and it is an unproved packing assertion about cubic graphs.

STATUS RESTATED: T(3) UNPROVED. Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 166 contributes
a CORRECTION to 165.3 (the constant is 3-4, not 8; free choice of base cycle
raises the success rate from 74% to 24/24), two proved sufficiency conditions
(166.2), and a corrected endpoint whose residual window is plausibly [30,40]
rather than [30,10^4] (166.3). No gap is closed.


## 167. THE 2-ADIC EAR CRITERION: three chords suffice

STATUS: T(3) and Erdos-Gyarfas remain UNPROVED.

### 167.1 CORRECTION (18th) to 166.3: the growth rate was over-estimated

Section 166.3 extrapolated "supply ~ n/5.5, reaching 7 near n = 40" from the two
observed values 3 and 4. Two data points cannot establish a growth rate. Measured
further (3 graphs per order, maximised over ALL cycles):

    n = 12,14,16 : 3 3 3       n = 18 : 3 3 4      n = 20,22 : 4
    n = 24 : 4 4 4             n = 26 : 4 4 4      n = 28 : 5 5 5
    n = 30 : 5 5 5             n = 32 : 5 5 5

The value increases by 1 at n ~ 18 and again at n ~ 28 - roughly +1 per TEN
vertices, and the thresholds are widening (12 -> 18 -> 28). A linear fit gives
k = 3 + (n-12)/10, so 7 disjoint-span chords need n ~ 52; a geometric fit
(thresholds in ratio ~1.55) gives n ~ 66.

So the residual window claimed in 166.3 as [30,40] is wrong. It is [30, ~52-70]
for that sufficient condition. Corrected.

### 167.2 But the count was never the obstacle - the 2-ADIC CRITERION

Section 166.1 already showed the criterion is met with only 3-4 chords, because
the deltas are VARIED. The uniform conditions (S1),(S2) of 166.2 needing seven
chords were far stronger than what is actually used. Here is the sharp condition.

  (S3) 2-ADIC EAR CRITERION (PROVED). Let C be a cycle with three ears of
  pairwise disjoint span whose deltas satisfy

        v_2(delta_1) = 0,   v_2(delta_2) = 1,   v_2(delta_3) = 2,

  i.e. delta_1 odd, delta_2 = 2 mod 4, delta_3 = 4 mod 8. Then the eight subset
  sums are exactly Z_8, so every target is reached and G has a cycle of length
  0 mod 8.

  Proof. Write a = delta_1 (odd), b = delta_2 in {2,6}, c = delta_3 = 4.
  The four even subset sums are 0, b, 4, b+4, which is {0,2,4,6} whether b = 2 or
  b = 6. The four odd subset sums are a + {0, b, 4, b+4} = a + {0,2,4,6}, which is
  all four odd residues. Union = Z_8. QED

  THREE ears suffice - and three disjoint-span chords are available already at
  n = 12 by 167.1. THE PACKING COUNT IS NOT THE OBSTACLE.

### 167.3 Translation into cycle lengths

For a chord (ear of length 1) spanning an arc A, delta = 1 - |A| and the cycle it
forms with its arc has length 1 + |A| = 2 - delta (mod 8). So:

    v_2(delta) = 0   <=>  the chord-cycle is ODD
    v_2(delta) = 1   <=>  the chord-cycle is 0 or 4 mod 8, i.e. = 0 mod 4
    v_2(delta) = 2   <=>  the chord-cycle is 6 mod 8

  THREE-RESIDUE EAR STATEMENT (open). Every sufficiently large 3-connected cubic
  graph of girth >= 5 contains a cycle C and three chords of C with pairwise
  disjoint spans such that the three cycles they form with their arcs have
  lengths that are respectively ODD, = 0 (mod 4), and = 6 (mod 8).

  This implies T(3) by (S3).

BIPARTITE CASE - only TWO ears are needed. In a bipartite graph there are no odd
cycles, so v_2 = 0 is unavailable; but the target -|C| is even, and the four
subset sums of {delta_2, delta_3} with v_2 = 1 and 2 are 0, b, 4, b+4 = {0,2,4,6},
which contains every even target. So:

  BIPARTITE ENDPOINT (open). Every sufficiently large 3-connected cubic bipartite
  graph of girth >= 6 contains a cycle C and TWO chords of disjoint span whose
  chord-cycles have lengths = 0 (mod 4) and = 6 (mod 8) respectively.

Two chords. This is by a wide margin the weakest statement the program has ever
reduced T(3) to on the hardest sector.

### 167.4 Why this connects to what is already proved

 - DEAN-LESNIAK-SAITO (banked, 133) gives a cycle of length 0 mod 4 in every
   3-connected graph. That is exactly the v_2 = 1 ingredient - it exists; what is
   missing is that it can be realised as a CHORD-CYCLE of a common cycle C.
 - The UNIFORM-CLASS THEOREM (banked; via Dirac's K_4-subdivision theorem) says
   no graph of minimum degree 3 has all circuits congruent mod 4. That is exactly
   the statement that the residues needed in 167.3 do not all collapse - again,
   globally rather than locally at one cycle C.
 - So both ingredients of the Three-Residue Ear Statement are known to exist
   SOMEWHERE in the graph. The entire remaining content is LOCALISATION: bringing
   them onto one cycle as chords with disjoint spans.

That is the sharpest formulation of the residual gap that this program has
produced, and it is the first one in which every ingredient is already a theorem
and only their co-location is missing.

### 167.5 Honest status

PROVED this pass: the 2-adic criterion (S3), with proof.
COMPUTED this pass: the supply of disjoint-span chords is 3 (n<=16), 4 (n=18-26),
5 (n=28-32) - correcting 166.3.
NOT PROVED: the Three-Residue Ear Statement, or its two-chord bipartite form.
Localisation is the gap, and it is not closed.

STATUS RESTATED: T(3) UNPROVED. Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 167 contributes
a CORRECTION to 166.3 (growth +1 per ten vertices, not n/5.5), one proved
sufficiency criterion needing only THREE ears (167.2), its translation into three
cycle residues and a TWO-ear bipartite form (167.3), and the observation that both
ingredients are already theorems so that only localisation remains (167.4).
No gap is closed.


## 168. DIRECT TEST of the Three-Residue Ear Statement: 27/28

STATUS: T(3) and Erdos-Gyarfas remain UNPROVED.

### 168.1 Refinement to the arc-selection counts of 165-167

Sections 165.2, 166.1 and 167.1 selected arcs by interval scheduling on the
SHORTER arc of each chord. That is not the full freedom: NESTED chords can also be
combined, by taking the OUTER arc of the outer chord and the inner arc of the
inner one. However, arcs chosen for a disjoint family are disjoint arcs of a
circle, so AT MOST ONE of them can exceed a semicircle. Hence at most one chord in
any disjoint family uses its longer arc, and the shorter-arc greedy undercounts by
AT MOST 1. The counts in 167.1 stand to within 1. Recorded so the point is not
re-litigated.

### 168.2 The test

For every cycle C of each test graph, every chord of C was listed with BOTH of its
arcs; for arc A the shift is delta = 1 - |A| and its 2-adic valuation
v_2(delta) in {0,1,2,3} was computed (3 meaning delta = 0 mod 8). The question
asked was exactly the criterion of 167.2/167.3:

  is there a cycle C carrying chords with PAIRWISE DISJOINT arcs whose valuations
  are {0,1,2}  (general case),  or {1,2}  (bipartite case)?

28 three-connected cubic girth-5 graphs, n = 12..24, four per order.

  RESULT: 27 of 28 satisfy the statement. ONE FAILURE, at n = 14.

Witness cycles were typically not the longest cycle - lengths 12,15,16,17,19,
20,21,22 appear as witnesses in graphs of order 16 to 24 - confirming 166.1's
point that the Hamiltonian cycle is a poor base.

### 168.3 Honest reading of the result

THE STATEMENT AS WRITTEN IN 167.3 IS NOT UNIVERSALLY TRUE. It fails for at least
one 3-connected cubic girth-5 graph on 14 vertices. Two things soften this, and
neither is a rescue:

 (a) n = 14 is far below Markstrom's census bound n >= 30, so the failure does not
     touch the program: T(3) only needs the statement for n >= 30, and no failure
     was seen at n >= 16 in this sample.
 (b) The test used CHORDS ONLY. The Ear-Subset Lemma (165.1) applies to arbitrary
     ears - paths through the rest of the graph - which are far more numerous than
     chords. The failing graph may well satisfy the ear version.

So the corrected target is:

  THREE-RESIDUE EAR STATEMENT (corrected, open). There is n_0 such that every
  3-connected cubic graph of girth >= 5 on n >= n_0 vertices contains a cycle C
  and three EARS with pairwise disjoint arcs whose shifts have 2-adic valuations
  0, 1 and 2. (Bipartite: two ears, valuations 1 and 2.)

with the data supporting n_0 <= 16 for the chord-only version on this sample, and
one explicit counterexample at n = 14 fixing n_0 > 14.

### 168.4 Where the whole program now stands

  PROVED and banked: the Ear-Subset Lemma (165.1); the odd-shift parity
  characterisation (164.1); the 2-adic criterion (167.2, three ears suffice);
  the Window Lemma (162.1); the degree filtration and the mod-4 Gauss-sum formula
  (155.2, 155.3, verified 8/8 in 161.3); the MacWilliams-Ising identity (161.4,
  verified exactly).
  IMPORTED: Dean-Lesniak-Saito (a cycle 0 mod 4 in every 3-connected graph);
  Lyngsie-Merker for odd k, with their even-k remark read from source (163);
  Markstrom's census n >= 30.
  MEASURED: the ear mechanism succeeds on 27/28 graphs; the supply of
  disjoint-arc chords is 3 (n<=16), 4 (n=18-26), 5 (n=28-32).
  OPEN, and the single remaining gap: the corrected Three-Residue Ear Statement
  of 168.3 - a LOCALISATION statement, since Dean-Lesniak-Saito already supplies
  the v_2 = 1 residue and the Uniform-Class Theorem already supplies
  non-collapse mod 4 somewhere in the graph.

STATUS RESTATED: T(3) UNPROVED. Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 168 contributes a
refinement bounding the arc-selection undercount by 1 (168.1), a direct 28-graph
test of 167.3 giving 27/28 with an explicit failure at n = 14 (168.2), the
corrected statement (168.3), and a consolidated statement of what is proved,
imported, measured and open (168.4). No gap is closed.


## 169. IS THE TOWER THE RIGHT LADDER? A strategic audit

STATUS: T(3) and Erdos-Gyarfas remain UNPROVED.

### 169.1 AUDIT FLAG (serious): does T(3) actually deliver EG?

T(3) as used throughout sections 100-168 says: every C4-free graph of minimum
degree 3 contains a cycle of length DIVISIBLE BY 8. But a length divisible by 8
need not be a power of two - 24, 40, 48, 56 are all 0 mod 8 and none is a power
of two. So T(3) as stated does NOT by itself yield a power-of-two cycle.

The early record (line 11) states the target as a WINDOW statement - "every cubic
graph has a cycle of length in B = {3,4} u [6,8] u [11,16] u [22,32] u ..." - which
is a different object from a residue statement. Somewhere between that and the
modular formulation there must be a pinning step converting "0 mod 2^k" into
"exactly 2^k", or the tower must be a window tower rather than a residue tower.

THIS SHOULD BE RE-VERIFIED BEFORE ANY FURTHER WORK ON T(3). If the pinning step
does not exist, then sections 100-168 have been sharpening a statement that is
necessary-looking but not sufficient, and the correct target is the window form.
I flag it rather than assert an error, because the derivation predates the
material I can currently see.

### 169.2 Why the modular tower is the WORST-shaped ladder

Section 155.2 proved: LENGTH MOD 2^k IS A POLYNOMIAL OF DEGREE k-1 ON THE CYCLE
SPACE. Hence:

    rung 2 (mod 4)  = quadratic  = Dean-Lesniak-Saito 1993, proved
    rung 3 (mod 8)  = cubic      = T(3), open
    rung 4 (mod 16) = quartic    = strictly harder again
    rung k          = degree k-1

Each rung is a genuinely higher-degree problem, and quadratic forms over F_2 have
a complete classical theory (Arf/Brown) while cubic forms do not. So this ladder
gets harder by a precise and unavoidable mechanism. It is the wrong ladder to be
on, and section 155.2 already contained the proof of that without my noticing the
strategic consequence.

Worse, the conversion itself is lossy: going from "cycle of length 2^k" to "cycle
of length 0 mod 2^k" WEAKENS the conclusion (24 is not a power of two) while
STRENGTHENING the required proof (degree k-1). That is the wrong trade in both
directions.

### 169.3 Ladders considered and rejected

 (a) WINDOW / INTERVAL LADDER ("a cycle of length in [k, 2k+2]"). MERKER's
     conjecture of exactly this shape for 3-connected cubic PLANAR graphs is FALSE
     for every even k >= 6 (arXiv:2009.00423, found in section 164.5). Known
     counterexamples. Rejected.
 (b) CONSECUTIVE-LENGTHS LADDER. To catch a power of two in [2^{k-1}, 2^k] one
     needs about 2^{k-1} consecutive cycle lengths. Bondy-Vince gives TWO cycles
     differing by 1 or 2 at minimum degree 3, and every stronger result needs
     degree above 3 (section 154). Exponentially short of what is needed. Rejected.
 (c) MINOR / DENSITY LADDERS. EG is not minor-closed, and every density theorem
     (Bondy-Simonovits, Sudakov-Verstraete) is vacuous at cubic density. Rejected.

### 169.4 THE LADDER THAT LOOKS RIGHT: stratify by GIRTH

Observe the two ends are already theorems, and they point at each other:

  HIGH GIRTH IS DONE. Thomassen: minimum degree 3 and girth at least
  2(k^2+1)(3*2^{k^2+1} + (k^2+1)^2 - 1) gives cycles of all even lengths modulo k.
  Astronomical but finite, and it is the strongest known statement for cubic
  graphs (quoted in Lyngsie-Merker, section 163.4).

  LOW GIRTH FEEDS THE PROVED MECHANISM. A chord of a cycle in a girth-g graph
  spans at least g-1 (section 164.3), so SMALL GIRTH MEANS SHORT SPANS MEANS MANY
  PAIRWISE DISJOINT ARCS - which is exactly the resource the proved Ear-Subset
  Lemma (165.1) and 2-adic criterion (167.2) consume. The measured supply
  (3 at n<=16, 4 at n=18-26, 5 at n=28-32; section 167.1) was taken at girth 5,
  the smallest girth in the C4-free regime, i.e. the most favourable case.

So girth is the one parameter on which the two available tools move in OPPOSITE
directions and therefore meet:

  GIRTH LADDER. For each g, prove EG for minimum-degree-3 graphs of girth exactly
  g. Large g by Thomassen; small g by ear-packing, whose resource grows as g
  shrinks. Only the crossover region is open, and the crossover is a QUANTITATIVE
  question, not a new qualitative phenomenon.

Advantages over the modular tower:
 - no degree escalation: one never needs mod 16 or mod 32;
 - no lossy conversion: one targets the exact power of two directly;
 - both endpoints are already theorems;
 - the open middle is a single crossover estimate rather than an infinite family
   of increasingly hard rungs.

Honest cost: Thomassen's girth threshold is astronomical, so the crossover region
is enormous. The ladder is better SHAPED, not obviously easier. Closing it would
require improving Thomassen's girth bound substantially, which is itself a known
open problem.

### 169.5 The native ladder, for comparison

The forbidden-powers ladder is EG's own form: G has a C_4, or G is C4-free and has
a C_8, or G is {C_4,C_8}-free and has a C_16, and so on. Every rung is
non-vacuous - the MARKSTROM GRAPH (cubic, planar, 24 vertices, girth 3) is
{C_4, C_8}-free and survives only through its 16-cycles (section 164.5) - and
rung k concerns graphs whose girth exceeds roughly 2^{k-1}, i.e. it AUTOMATICALLY
feeds into the high-girth end of 169.4. So the native ladder and the girth ladder
are the same ladder viewed from the two ends. That is a reason to prefer them
jointly over the modular tower.

STATUS RESTATED: T(3) UNPROVED. Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 169 contributes
one serious AUDIT FLAG (169.1: divisibility by 8 is not a power of two, so the
tower needs a pinning step that must be re-verified), the strategic reading of
155.2 showing the modular tower gets harder by a proved mechanism (169.2), three
rejected ladders with reasons (169.3), and the girth-stratified ladder with its
honest cost (169.4-169.5). No gap is closed.


## 170. THE BINARY EAR BASIS: an exact, inductive route to EG with no tower

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section replaces the modular tower
by an EXACT construction. It removes the pinning-step problem flagged in 169.1
entirely, because it produces a cycle of length exactly 2^k rather than a residue.

### 170.1 BINARY EAR BASIS LEMMA (PROVED)

  LEMMA. Let delta_1,...,delta_k be integers with v_2(delta_j) = j-1 for each j
  (i.e. delta_1 odd, delta_2 = 2 mod 4, delta_3 = 4 mod 8, ...). Then the map

        {0,1}^k  ->  Z_{2^k},     S  |->  sum_{j in S} delta_j  mod 2^k

  is a BIJECTION.

  Proof. Write delta_j = 2^{j-1} u_j with u_j odd. Suppose two subsets S =/= T give
  the same value mod 2^k. Let m be the least index in which they differ. Then
  their difference is  +- delta_m + sum_{j>m} eps_j delta_j  with eps_j in {0,+-1},
  which equals 2^{m-1}( +- u_m + 2*(integer) ). Its 2-adic valuation is exactly
  m-1 <= k-1 < k, so it is not 0 mod 2^k. Contradiction. The map is injective
  between sets of equal size 2^k, hence bijective. QED

This is the k-fold generalisation of the 2-adic criterion of 167.2 (which is the
case k = 3).

### 170.2 POWER-WINDOW CRITERION (PROVED) - exact powers of two

Combine 170.1 with the Ear-Subset Lemma (165.1).

  CRITERION. Let C be a cycle in G and let P_1,...,P_k be ears with PAIRWISE
  DISJOINT arcs A_1,...,A_k, and put delta_j = |P_j| - |A_j|. Suppose

     (i)  v_2(delta_j) = j-1  for j = 1,...,k,   and
     (ii) |C| + sum over {j : delta_j > 0} of delta_j  <  2^{k+1}.

  Then G contains a cycle of length EXACTLY 2^k.

  Proof. By 165.1 the numbers |C| + sum_{j in S} delta_j are cycle lengths, for all
  2^k subsets S. By 170.1 they realise every residue mod 2^k exactly once, so
  exactly one of them, say L, satisfies L = 0 mod 2^k. Every one of them is a cycle
  length, so L >= 3; and by (ii) L < 2^{k+1}. The only multiple of 2^k in
  [3, 2^{k+1}) is 2^k itself. Hence L = 2^k. QED

NO MODULI, NO TOWER, NO PINNING STEP. The output is the power of two itself.

### 170.3 The cleanest instance, and an exponential efficiency gain

Take delta_j = 2^{j-1} exactly. Then the 2^k cycle lengths are

        |C|, |C|+1, |C|+2, ..., |C| + 2^k - 1,

i.e. 2^k CONSECUTIVE cycle lengths, and condition (ii) reads |C| <= 2^k.

  COROLLARY. A cycle C with k ears of pairwise disjoint arcs and shifts exactly
  1, 2, 4, ..., 2^{k-1} yields 2^k consecutive cycle lengths; if |C| <= 2^k, one of
  them is 2^k.

Compare the literature on consecutive cycle lengths (surveyed in 163.4): FAN needs
minimum degree 3k-2 to get k cycles in arithmetic progression with difference 2;
LIU-MA need k+1 for floor(k/2) consecutive even lengths; SUDAKOV-VERSTRAETE need
average degree 8k. All are ADDITIVE - k structures give O(k) lengths. The binary
ear basis is MULTIPLICATIVE: k ears give 2^k lengths, because the shifts combine as
a binary basis rather than by repetition. That is an exponential efficiency gain,
and it is the reason this route can work at minimum degree 3 where all the others
need degree growing with k.

BIPARTITE VARIANT. In a bipartite graph every ear-cycle is even, so every delta is
even and v_2 = 0 is unavailable. Use v_2(delta_j) = j for j = 1..k-1: the 2^{k-1}
sums realise every EVEN residue mod 2^k exactly once, and |C| is even, so the same
argument gives a cycle of length exactly 2^k from only k-1 ears.

### 170.4 The induction the user asked for

  BUILD THE BASIS ONE BIT AT A TIME. Given a cycle C carrying ears with shifts of
  2-adic valuations 0,1,...,j-1 on pairwise disjoint arcs, adjoin one more ear,
  with arc disjoint from those already used, whose shift has valuation exactly j.
  Stop when 2^k >= |C|.

  BASE CASE (j = 0, a shift of odd valuation): by 164.1 a shift is odd exactly when
  the ear together with its arc is an ODD CYCLE. So the base case asks for an odd
  cycle attached to C as an ear - available in any non-bipartite graph, and not
  needed at all in the bipartite case by 170.3.

  BUDGET. Termination needs k = ceil(log_2 |C|) ears, hence at most
  ceil(log_2 n) ears with pairwise disjoint arcs.

### 170.5 THE BUDGET MATCHES THE MEASURED SUPPLY

Section 167.1 measured the maximum number of chords of a cycle with pairwise
disjoint arcs, over all cycles, in 3-connected cubic girth-5 graphs:

        n = 12..16 : 3        n = 18 : 3-4       n = 20-26 : 4
        n = 28-32 : 5

and log_2 n over the same range is 3.58, 4.17, 4.32-4.70, 4.81-5.00.

  THE MEASURED SUPPLY IS ESSENTIALLY floor(log_2 n) - EXACTLY THE BUDGET THAT
  170.4 REQUIRES.

That is the first time in this program that a measured resource and a required
resource have matched. It is also why the earlier target of "7 ears" (166.3) felt
out of reach while this one does not: 7 ears is what a LINEAR scheme would need;
log_2 n ears is what the BINARY scheme needs, and log_2 n is what exists.

### 170.6 Honest statement of the gap

PROVED here: 170.1 (binary ear basis), 170.2 (power-window criterion), 170.3
(consecutive-length corollary and bipartite variant). These are unconditional and
elementary.

NOT PROVED: that the required ears exist. Specifically, the open statement is now

  BINARY EAR CONJECTURE. Every graph of minimum degree 3 contains a cycle C and
  ears P_1,...,P_k with pairwise disjoint arcs such that v_2(|P_j| - |A_j|) = j-1
  for each j and |C| + sum_{delta_j > 0} delta_j < 2^{k+1}.

The measurement of 170.5 says the COUNT is available. What is not established is
that the ears can simultaneously be given the prescribed 2-adic valuations and
kept within the window - the same localisation difficulty as 168.4, but now with a
budget that matches the supply instead of exceeding it.

Also unresolved: 169.1's audit flag on the old tower. This section does not repair
that route; it bypasses it.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 170 contributes three proved
elementary results (170.1-170.3), an exact route to powers of two that needs no
modular tower and no pinning step, an explicit induction (170.4), and the first
match in the program between a required and a measured resource (170.5). No gap
is closed.


## 171. THE BINARY EAR CONJECTURE IS FALSE (goal: prove or disprove -- DISPROVED)

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. The Binary Ear Conjecture of 170.6 is
DISPROVED, in two independent ways, one of them a defect in how I stated it and
one of them genuine.

### 171.1 FAILURE MODE A: the statement of 170.6 was mis-specified

170.6 required v_2(delta_j) = j-1, so delta_1 must be ODD. By 164.1 a shift is odd
exactly when the ear together with its arc is an ODD CYCLE. Hence:

  THE CONJECTURE AS WRITTEN IN 170.6 IS FALSE FOR EVERY BIPARTITE GRAPH,
  trivially, since a bipartite graph has no odd cycle at all.

170.3 had already recorded the bipartite variant (valuations 1..k-1) and 170.6
dropped it. My error. The repair is to allow a VALUATION SHIFT c >= 0.

### 171.2 The corrected criterion (PROVED)

  SHIFTED POWER-WINDOW CRITERION. Let C be a cycle and P_1..P_k DISTINCT ears with
  pairwise edge-disjoint arcs A_j and pairwise disjoint interiors; put
  delta_j = |P_j| - |A_j|. Suppose for some integer c >= 0:
     (i)   v_2(delta_j) = c + j - 1   for j = 1..k;
     (ii)  2^c divides |C|;
     (iii) |C| + sum over {delta_j > 0} delta_j  <  2^{c+k+1};
     (iv)  |C| + sum over {delta_j < 0} delta_j  >=  3.
  Then G contains a cycle of length exactly 2^{c+k}.

  Proof. Write delta_j = 2^c eps_j with v_2(eps_j) = j-1. By the Binary Ear Basis
  Lemma (170.1) the subset sums of the eps_j form a complete residue system mod
  2^k, so the subset sums of the delta_j realise every multiple of 2^c modulo
  2^{c+k}. By (ii), |C| = 0 mod 2^c, so exactly one subset S gives
  L = |C| + sum_{j in S} delta_j = 0 mod 2^{c+k}. By the Ear-Subset Lemma (165.1)
  L is a cycle length; (iv) gives L >= 3 and (iii) gives L < 2^{c+k+1}; the only
  multiple of 2^{c+k} in [3, 2^{c+k+1}) is 2^{c+k}. QED

Conditions (iv) and "DISTINCT ears" are new relative to 170.2 and are NECESSARY -
see 171.3.

### 171.3 A BUG IN MY OWN CHECKER, and what it changed

The first exhaustive run allowed a single chord to be used TWICE, once with each
of its two arcs. Since a chord has empty interior and its two arcs are
edge-disjoint, this passed every test - but replacing both arcs of the same chord
leaves the chord traversed twice, a degenerate "2-cycle", not a cycle. The run
also omitted condition (iv), so subsets whose total shift drove the length below 3
were counted.

Both are now fixed. The effect was real: Q3 (the cube) was reported SATISFIED by
the buggy checker and is NOT satisfied by the fixed one. Any conclusion drawn from
the first run is withdrawn.

### 171.4 FAILURE MODE B: genuine counterexamples

Exhaustive search over ALL cycles, ALL ears, both arc choices, all shifts
c <= 3 and all k <= 4, with the fixed checker:

    K_4          (n=4)   NO binary ear basis
    K_{3,3}      (n=6)   NO binary ear basis
    Q_3 (cube)   (n=8)   NO binary ear basis
    PETERSEN     (n=10)  NO binary ear basis

    Heawood      (n=14)  SATISFIED  target 8, c=1, k=2, |C|=6, deltas [2,4]
    GP(7,2)      (n=14)  SATISFIED  target 8, c=1, k=2, |C|=6, deltas [2,4]

So the conjecture is FALSE even in its corrected form. Note all four
counterexamples contain a power-of-two cycle outright (K_4, K_{3,3}, Q_3 have a
C_4; Q_3 and Petersen have a C_8), so EG is untouched: what fails is the
CRITERION, not the conjecture it was meant to prove.

Worked example of the failure, Q_3 on its Hamiltonian cycle 0,1,2,3,7,6,5,4:
the four chords all have arcs of length 3 or 5, giving delta in {-2,-4}, so
valuations 1 and 2 are both available and (i),(ii) can be met - but every such
pair has |C| + (-2) + (-4) = 8 - 6 = 2 < 3, so (iv) fails. The cube is blocked by
the length floor, not by the arithmetic.

### 171.5 MAJOR CORRECTION to 170.5: the budget is 2, not log_2 n

170.5 claimed the induction needs about log_2 n ears and celebrated that the
measured supply of disjoint-arc ears is about log_2 n. THAT WAS THE WRONG BUDGET.
Every successful witness found here uses k = 2 - two ears - with the valuation
shift c absorbing all the low-order bits. For target 2^m one needs
c + k = m with k >= 2, so k = 2 and c = m-2 always suffices arithmetically.

The correct budget is therefore TWO EARS plus a cycle length divisible by 2^{m-2},
not log_2 n ears. This is a correction in the FAVOURABLE direction: the resource
requirement is far smaller than 170.5 claimed. It also re-derives 167.3's
two-chord bipartite condition as the special case (c,k) = (1,2), now producing the
exact length 8 rather than a residue.

### 171.6 The repaired conjecture and its status

  REPAIRED BINARY EAR CONJECTURE. There is n_0 such that every graph of minimum
  degree 3 on at least n_0 vertices satisfies the hypotheses of 171.2 for some
  c, k.

DATA: false for n = 4, 6, 8, 10 (the four graphs above); true for every graph
tested with n >= 14. So n_0 >= 11 if it is true at all. This is now the live
question, and it is much better posed than 170.6 because the budget is two ears.

HONEST LIMIT: the repaired statement is still at least as strong as EG, so proving
it is proving EG. Its value is that the required configuration is now small and
explicit - a cycle of even length with two ears of consecutive 2-adic valuation -
rather than an unbounded binary basis.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 171 achieves the stated goal: the
Binary Ear Conjecture of 170.6 is DISPROVED, both by mis-specification (171.1) and
by four exhaustively verified counterexamples to its corrected form (171.4). It
also contributes the corrected criterion with proof (171.2), the disclosure and
repair of a bug in my own checker (171.3), and a major correction to the resource
estimate of 170.5 (171.5).


## 172. THE INDUCTION, REVISED: Hensel descent on the 2-adic distance

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section replaces the induction of
170.4, which 171 showed to be inducting on the wrong parameter.

### 172.1 What was wrong with the old induction

170.4 inducted on the NUMBER OF EARS k, building a binary basis one bit at a time.
171.5 showed that k = 2 always suffices arithmetically: for target 2^m one takes
the valuation shift c = m-2 and k = 2. So the ladder in k HAS NO RUNGS - there was
nothing to induct on.

Worse, the real cost of the old scheme was SIMULTANEITY. The Ear-Subset Lemma
(165.1) requires the ears to have pairwise edge-disjoint arcs AND pairwise disjoint
interiors AT THE SAME TIME. That single requirement is what produced all four
counterexamples of 171.4 (K_4, K_{3,3}, Q_3, Petersen): each of those graphs has
ears with the right 2-adic valuations, but never two that can be used together.

### 172.2 THE REVISION: one ear at a time, inducting on v_2(|C| - 2^m)

  HENSEL DESCENT LEMMA (PROVED). Let C be a cycle, P an ear spanning arc A, and
  C' = (C \ A) u P the rerouted cycle, so |C'| = |C| + delta with
  delta = |P| - |A|. Fix a target T. If

        v_2(|C| - T) = v_2(delta) = t,

  then v_2(|C'| - T) > t.

  Proof. |C'| - T = (|C| - T) + delta. Both summands equal 2^t times an odd
  number, so their sum is 2^t times an even number. QED

  DESCENT CRITERION. Suppose there is a cycle C_0 with 3 <= |C_0| < 2^{m+1} from
  which one can repeatedly choose an ear whose shift satisfies
  v_2(delta) = v_2(|C| - 2^m) while keeping the length in [3, 2^{m+1}). Then G has
  a cycle of length EXACTLY 2^m.

  Proof. Each move strictly increases v_2(|C| - 2^m). While |C| =/= 2^m and both
  |C| and 2^m lie in [3, 2^{m+1}), we have 0 < ||C| - 2^m| < 2^{m+1}, so
  v_2(|C| - 2^m) <= m. The valuation therefore cannot increase more than m+1
  times, and the only way the process can continue is by reaching |C| = 2^m. QED

THE KEY GAIN: successive moves act on DIFFERENT cycles, so NO DISJOINTNESS IS
REQUIRED between the ears used at different steps. The simultaneity that killed
171.4 is gone. The induction is now on the 2-adic distance to the target, which
really does have rungs (one per bit), and the descent has length at most m+1.

### 172.3 The hypothesis must be EXISTENTIAL, not universal (COMPUTED)

Two forms were tested exhaustively on ten graphs.

 UNIVERSAL H_m: every cycle in the window admits a valuation-matching ear.
   FALSE. Petersen fails at 2^2 (from a 6-cycle); Heawood fails at 2^2 and 2^3
   (from a 14-cycle); Mobius-Kantor fails at 2^2, 2^3 and 2^4. Yet Heawood and
   Mobius-Kantor both contain 8-cycles, so H_m is sufficient but far from
   necessary.

 EXISTENTIAL H'_m: SOME cycle in the window descends to 2^m.
   TRUE on all ten graphs tested, with explicit descent paths:

     K_4            3 -> 4
     K_{3,3}        4
     Q_3 (cube)     4 -> 8
     PETERSEN       5 -> 6 -> 8
     Heawood        6 -> 8
     GP(7,2)        6 -> 12 -> 8
     Mobius-Kantor  8            and  16
     Pappus         6 -> 12 -> 8 and  6 -> 12 -> 8 -> 16
     Desargues      8            and  8 -> 16
     Dodecahedron   5 -> 8       and  5 -> 8 -> 16

  ALL FOUR COUNTEREXAMPLES OF 171.4 ARE RESOLVED. Petersen, which admits no binary
  ear basis whatsoever, descends 5 -> 6 -> 8: from |C| = 5, v_2(5-8) = 0 so an odd
  shift is needed and delta = +1 gives 6; then v_2(6-8) = 1 so a shift = 2 mod 4 is
  needed and delta = +2 gives 8.

### 172.4 The revised open statement

  HENSEL DESCENT CONJECTURE. Every graph of minimum degree 3 admits, for some m, a
  cycle C_0 with 3 <= |C_0| < 2^{m+1} and a sequence of at most m+1 single-ear
  reroutes, each with v_2(delta) equal to the current v_2(|C| - 2^m) and each
  staying inside [3, 2^{m+1}), ending at a cycle of length exactly 2^m.

Relative to 171.6 this is a strictly better-shaped target:
 - no simultaneity and no disjointness anywhere;
 - the object sought is a PATH of length <= m+1 = O(log n) in the cycle space,
   not a single rigid configuration;
 - it has genuine inductive structure - one rung per bit of the 2-adic distance;
 - it verified 10/10 including every graph that refuted the previous formulation.

It remains at least as strong as EG, so proving it is proving EG. What is now
needed at each rung is a purely local existence statement:

  RUNG LEMMA (open). Given a cycle C in a graph of minimum degree 3 with
  3 <= |C| < 2^{m+1} and |C| =/= 2^m, and t = v_2(|C| - 2^m), there is an ear on C
  (or on some cycle reachable so far) with v_2(delta) = t and |C| + delta still in
  [3, 2^{m+1}).

By 164.1 the t = 0 case asks for an ear whose ear-cycle is ODD, and 172.3 shows
the universal form of the Rung Lemma is false - so the eventual proof must carry
along the freedom to change the base cycle, which is exactly what the existential
formulation provides.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 172 contributes the diagnosis
that the old induction had no rungs (172.1), the Hensel Descent Lemma and Criterion
with proofs (172.2), the computational finding that the universal hypothesis is
false and the existential one holds 10/10 with explicit paths (172.3), and the
revised open statement with its local Rung Lemma (172.4). No gap is closed.


## 173. THE RUNG LEMMA: Hensel descent reduced to a divisibility statement

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section proves the rungs of the
172 induction and reduces the whole conjecture to one clean structural statement.

### 173.1 The move set is exactly the theta-neighbours (PROVED)

Let C be a cycle and P an ear spanning the two arcs A, A' of C. Then C, P u A and
P u A' are the three cycles of a THETA with branch lengths

        a = |A|,   b = |A'|,   c = |P|,   |C| = a+b.

Rerouting C through P replacing A gives the cycle P u A' of length b+c; replacing
A' gives P u A of length a+c. So:

  ONE EAR-MOVE FROM C GOES TO ONE OF THE OTHER TWO CYCLES OF A THETA THROUGH C,
  and every such cycle is reachable. Equivalently C -> C' is a move iff C ^ C' is
  a single path.

### 173.2 Theta parity dichotomy (PROVED)

(a+b) + (a+c) + (b+c) = 2(a+b+c) is even, so among the three cycles of a theta
EITHER ALL THREE ARE EVEN OR EXACTLY ONE IS. Consequently:

 - from an ODD cycle, the two other cycles of any theta are one odd and one even;
 - a move that increases v_2(|C| - 2^m) beyond 0 requires an ALL-EVEN theta.

### 173.3 THE RUNG LEMMA (PROVED - the main result of this section)

  RUNG LEMMA. Let T = 2^m, let C be a cycle with t = v_2(|C| - T) and t < m.
  Suppose C has an ear P such that 2^t divides |P| and 2^t divides |A| (hence
  also |A'|, since |A|+|A'| = |C|). Then at least one of the two moves through P
  is ADMISSIBLE: it produces a cycle C' with v_2(|C'| - T) > t.

  Proof. Since t < m we have 2^{t+1} | T, and v_2(|C| - T) = t forces
  v_2(|C|) = t exactly. Write a = 2^t alpha, b = 2^t beta, c = 2^t gamma. Then
  |C| = 2^t(alpha+beta) with v_2(|C|) = t, so alpha+beta is ODD; exactly one of
  alpha, beta is odd, say alpha odd and beta even.
    If gamma is ODD  then alpha+gamma is even, so 2^{t+1} | (a+c);
    if gamma is EVEN then beta+gamma is even, so 2^{t+1} | (b+c).
  In either case the corresponding new length L' satisfies 2^{t+1} | L', and since
  2^{t+1} | T we get v_2(L' - T) >= t+1 > t. QED

  COROLLARY (rung t = 0 is unconditional). For t = 0 the divisibility hypothesis
  is vacuous, so EVERY ear of C yields an admissible move. Moreover every cycle in
  a 2-connected graph of minimum degree 3 has an ear: each vertex of C carries a
  third edge, which is either a chord or leads into a component of G - V(C) that,
  by 2-connectivity, attaches to C again. Hence rung 0 always fires (subject only
  to the window).

  Note the corollary recovers 172.3's observation that the t = 0 move lands on the
  even one of the two ear-cycles: with |C| odd, a and b have opposite parity, so
  exactly one of a+c, b+c is even.

### 173.4 THE REDUCTION

Combining 172.2 (Descent Criterion) with 173.3:

  HENSEL DESCENT CONJECTURE  follows from  the

  DIVISIBLE THETA CONJECTURE. For every cycle C in a graph of minimum degree 3 and
  every t >= 0 with 2^t | |C|, the cycle C has an ear P with
        2^t | |P|   and   2^t | |A|
  for one of the two arcs A -- and, for the descent, with the resulting length
  kept in [3, 2^{m+1}).

Equivalently: C admits a theta all three of whose branch lengths are divisible by
2^t. For t = 0 this is trivial; for t = 1 it asks for an ear of even length
attaching at even distance along C.

This is a substantial simplification of the target:
 - it is a statement about ONE cycle and ONE ear, not about a descent;
 - it involves no window arithmetic except at the last step;
 - it is monotone in t, and the descent uses each t at most once;
 - the parity dichotomy 173.2 shows exactly which thetas can serve.

### 173.5 Computational status (COMPUTED)

The greedy search of 172.3 was replaced by a proper bounded-depth backtracking
search over the move set of 173.1. Results, 26 graphs, ZERO failures:

  K4 [3,4]           K3,3 [4]            Q3 [4]            Petersen [5,6,8]
  Heawood [6,8]      GP(7,2) [6,12,8]    Mobius-Kantor [8] Pappus [6,12,8]
  Desargues [8]      Dodecahedron [5,8]  McGee [7,8]
  and 15 random 3-connected cubic girth-5 graphs, n = 12..20, e.g.
  [10,8], [5,6,8], [11,8], [9,6,12,8], [14,8], [12,8], [10,12,8].

Every descent found is SHORT - at most three moves - although the criterion
permits m+1. All targets found were 2^2 or 2^3.

### 173.6 What remains

PROVED in 172-173: the Hensel Descent Lemma and Criterion; the identification of
the move set with theta-neighbours; the theta parity dichotomy; the Rung Lemma;
the unconditional firing of rung 0.

OPEN: the Divisible Theta Conjecture of 173.4, and the window bookkeeping.
It remains at least as strong as EG. Its value over every earlier formulation in
this program is that it is a SINGLE-CYCLE, SINGLE-EAR divisibility statement with
no simultaneity, no disjointness, and no residue menus.

The first genuinely open case is t = 1: does every cycle of even length in a
graph of minimum degree 3 have an ear of even length attaching at even distance?
By 173.2 this is exactly the question of whether every even cycle lies in an
ALL-EVEN theta. In a bipartite graph every theta is all-even, so the question is
purely about the non-bipartite case - where, however, rung 0 has already been used
to arrive at an even cycle, so the relevant even cycles are those reachable from
odd ones by a single ear-move.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 173 contributes the theta
description of the move set (173.1), the parity dichotomy (173.2), the RUNG LEMMA
with proof and the unconditional rung 0 (173.3), the reduction of the whole
conjecture to the Divisible Theta Conjecture (173.4), and a corrected
backtracking search giving 26/26 (173.5). No gap is closed.


## 174. BASE CASE CLOSED; THE t = 1 INDUCTION STEP PROVED

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section closes the base case of the
172-173 induction and proves the first induction step under an explicit and often
automatic hypothesis.

### 174.1 THE BASE CASE IS COVERED (PROVED)

Three ingredients, all now established.

 (B1) A STARTING CYCLE IN THE WINDOW ALWAYS EXISTS. Let g be the girth and take a
      shortest cycle C_0, |C_0| = g. Choose m = ceil(log_2 g). Then 2^m >= g and
      2^{m+1} >= 2g > g, so 3 <= |C_0| < 2^{m+1}. QED

 (B2) RUNG 0 FIRES UNCONDITIONALLY (173.3 Corollary). If v_2(|C| - 2^m) = 0 the
      divisibility hypothesis of the Rung Lemma is vacuous, so EVERY ear works;
      and every cycle of a 2-connected graph of minimum degree 3 has an ear.

 (B3) THE DESCENT IS FINITE: t <= m-1 always. Indeed 0 < ||C| - 2^m| < 2^{m+1}
      forces v_2(|C| - 2^m) <= m, and v_2 = m would give |C| - 2^m = +-2^m, i.e.
      |C| = 0 or |C| = 2^{m+1}, both excluded. So there are at most m rungs.

So the induction has a base and a bounded ladder. Everything now rests on the
induction step: the Divisible Theta Conjecture at level t (173.4).

### 174.2 THE PARITY-VECTOR ARGUMENT (PROVED) - the t = 1 step

Fix a cycle C with |C| even, and let B be a bridge of C WITH INTERNAL VERTICES,
with attachments x_1,...,x_r on C. Fix a spanning tree of the component of
G - V(C) inside B, together with the attaching edges, and let

     l_i = distance from x_i to a fixed root in that tree,
     p_i = position of x_i along C.

For any i,j the tree gives an ear P_ij with |P_ij| = l_i + l_j - 2*(overlap), so

     |P_ij| = l_i + l_j   (mod 2),      |A_ij| = p_i - p_j   (mod 2),

the second because |C| is even, so both arcs between x_i and x_j have the same
parity. Assign to each attachment the PARITY VECTOR

     v_i = ( l_i mod 2 , p_i mod 2 )  in  F_2^2.

If v_i = v_j for some i =/= j then the ear P_ij has EVEN length and EVEN arcs, so
by the Rung Lemma (173.3 with t = 1) one of its two moves is admissible. Hence:

  LEMMA. If some bridge of C with internal vertices has at least 5 attachments,
  the t = 1 rung fires.
  Proof. Five vectors in the 4-element set F_2^2 must repeat. QED

  COROLLARY 1. If C has exactly one bridge and C is not Hamiltonian, the t = 1
  rung fires. Proof: in a cubic graph every vertex of C sends exactly one edge off
  C, so the attachment counts satisfy sum_k r_k = |C|; with one bridge r = |C| >=
  girth >= 5. QED

  COROLLARY 2 (BIPARTITE: three attachments suffice). If G is bipartite then
  l_i mod 2 and p_i mod 2 both record the bipartition class of x_i (the first
  relative to the root, the second relative to x_1), so l_i + p_i is CONSTANT over
  i. The parity vectors therefore lie on a line in F_2^2 - only two possible
  values - and any THREE attachments already repeat. Since in a 3-connected graph
  every bridge with internal vertices has at least 3 attachments:

     BIPARTITE t = 1 RUNG (PROVED). If G is 3-connected and bipartite and C is a
     NON-HAMILTONIAN cycle with |C| = 2 (mod 4), then the t = 1 move exists.

### 174.3 The residual cases at t = 1, and why they are small

By 174.2 the t = 1 step can only fail when EVERY bridge of C with internal
vertices has at most 4 attachments AND (in the bipartite case) C is Hamiltonian.

 (R1) BIPARTITE, C HAMILTONIAN. Then every ear is a chord, of odd length 1, and
      both its arcs are odd. The Rung Lemma's t = 1 hypothesis fails, but the
      all-odd branch case of 173.2 is still available: with a = |A| and c = 1, the
      move is admissible iff 1 = -a (mod 4), i.e. iff some chord has both arcs
      = 3 (mod 4). (Both arcs are automatically congruent mod 4, since
      |C| = 2 mod 4.) So the failure requires EVERY chord to have arcs = 1 mod 4.
      Since the descent is existential we may instead move to any non-Hamiltonian
      cycle of length = 2 mod 4 and apply Corollary 2. So (R1) needs the graph to
      have NO non-Hamiltonian cycle of length 2 mod 4 in the window, on top of the
      chord condition.

 (R2) NON-BIPARTITE, ALL BRIDGES WITH <= 4 ATTACHMENTS. Then, since
      sum_k r_k = |C|, there are at least |C|/4 bridges, and each must have its
      3 or 4 parity vectors PAIRWISE DISTINCT in F_2^2 - a "rainbow" condition on
      every bridge simultaneously. Chords (2 attachments, no internal vertices)
      contribute only odd ears and are governed by the all-odd case as in (R1).

Both residual cases are rigidity conditions of exactly the kind catalogued in 154:
they demand that a parity invariant be constant or rainbow everywhere at once.

### 174.4 Why t >= 2 does not follow from the same argument, stated honestly

The parity-vector argument works because |P_ij| = l_i + l_j is exact MOD 2 even
when the Steiner tree is not a star. Modulo 4 that fails: |P_ij| = l_i + l_j -
2*(overlap), and the overlap term is not controlled. The argument therefore does
NOT lift to t >= 2 as it stands. Two possible repairs, both open:
  - restrict to bridges whose Steiner tree is a STAR, where
    |P_ij| = l_i + l_j exactly and the pigeonhole becomes a zero-sum problem
    (find i,j with l_i + l_j = 0 and p_i = p_j mod 2^t) - an
    Erdos-Ginzburg-Ziv-type question in Z_{2^t} x Z_{2^t};
  - or use the freedom to change the base cycle so that only t <= 1 ever occurs,
    which by 173.5 is what the computed descents actually do: every descent found
    in 26 graphs used at most three moves and never needed t >= 2 more than once.

### 174.5 Status

PROVED here: (B1)-(B3), so the base case is closed; the parity-vector lemma; the
