  The rank-1 case is the same statement one notch down: rank(lambda) <= 1 forbids TWO
  disjoint odd cycles, matching 217.1's "at most two pairwise compatible ears have odd
  shift".

### 223.4 LEMMA A WEAKENS BUT DOES NOT DISSOLVE (PROVED)

An ODD cycle can never be an even path-difference: if D = P xor P_0 with |P| and
|P_0| both even then |D| = |P| + |P_0| - 2|P cap P_0| is EVEN. So W lies inside C_0
and the three odd cycles themselves are never in W. But their pairwise SUMS are even,
and

     lambda(Z_1 + Z_2, Z_1 + Z_3) = lambda(Z_1,Z_1) = 1 ,

so it suffices that Z_1+Z_2 and Z_1+Z_3 BOTH be realisable as even path-differences.
That is far weaker than the full spanning hypothesis of 222.4 - but realising
Z_i + Z_j as a path-difference means precisely hanging the odd cycles as DETOURS on a
common connecting path, which is again 210.4 verbatim.

  So Lemma A also reduces to 210.4, and the honest conclusion is:

     LEMMA A and LEMMA B ARE THE SAME LEMMA, AND IT IS 210.4.

### 223.5 What the literature actually arms us with

  REED: odd cycles have the HALF-INTEGRAL Erdos-Posa property - k odd cycles with
  every vertex in at most two, or a transversal of size f(k). The half-integrality is
  exactly what blocks us, since 223.2 needs VERTEX-DISJOINT cycles for the Gram matrix
  to be the identity.
  KAWARABAYASHI-WOLLAN: the integral property at connectivity 31k/2, about 47 for
  k = 3 - far above our 3-connectivity.
  KRAL and VOSS: for PLANAR graphs tau_odd <= 2 nu_odd, tight. Our bridges need not
  be planar, but 155's Mac Lane dichotomy says planarity is precisely where the mod-4
  layer is linear, so the planar case of our problem is the one already understood.
  LOVASZ, SLILATY: the structure of graphs with no two disjoint odd cycles; for
  internally 4-connected graphs, deleting a TRIANGLE leaves a bipartite graph, and our
  girth-5 bridges have no triangle - so that branch forces bipartiteness, which
  205.2/208.2 exclude. Only low connectivity survives.
  GOLLIN, HENDREY, KWON, OUM, YOO ET AL.: a UNIFIED HALF-INTEGRAL ERDOS-POSA THEOREM
  FOR CYCLES IN GRAPHS LABELLED BY MULTIPLE ABELIAN GROUPS (J. London Math. Soc. 2024;
  Math. Annalen 2025). This is the most directly relevant modern tool: our condition is
  literally a cycle problem in a Z_4-LABELLED graph (every edge labelled 1 in Z_4, and
  (SC) is a condition on cycle values), so the group-labelled machinery is the natural
  home for it. It remains HALF-integral, which is the same obstacle.

### 223.6 Status

PROVED here: d = dim ker(A+D) - 1 (223.1); disjoint odd cycles are lambda-orthonormal
so nu_odd <= mu - d, tight on Petersen (223.2); (SC) forces nu_odd <= 2, identical to
210.4 (223.3); Lemma A reduces to realising Z_i+Z_j as detours, again 210.4 (223.4).
NOT PROVED: 210.4 itself. Every route tried - modular, matroidal, quadratic-form,
bicycle - lands on the same statement, and the literature offers it only in
HALF-INTEGRAL form or at connectivity far above 3.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 223 proves the bicycle dimension is
the F_2 nullity of A + D, proves nu_odd <= mu - d with equality on the Petersen graph,
and shows that both lemmas left open by 222 collapse into the single statement of
210.4 - three pairwise vertex-disjoint odd cycles hung as detours on a connecting
path. The literature arms us with half-integral packing (Reed; Gollin et al. for
group-labelled cycles), integral packing only at connectivity about 47
(Kawarabayashi-Wollan), and a planar bound (Kral-Voss); none of these closes the
3-connected non-planar case that remains.


### 223.7 Verification of 223.1 and 223.2 (COMPUTED)

Over 914 randomly generated 2-connected subcubic girth-5 bridges with at least three
terminals:

     matrix identity  d = dim ker(A+D) - 1  : held in ALL 914 cases, no exception
     bound  nu_odd <= mu - d                : 0 violations
     bound TIGHT (nu_odd = mu - d)          : 599 of 914, about 66 per cent

The high frequency of tightness matters: it says mu - d is not a lossy relaxation of
the odd cycle packing number but essentially computes it, which is why the bicycle
route could not have given anything the packing route does not already give.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED.


## 224. WHAT WE MISSED: the bridge is a cubic graph with a subdivided MATCHING

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section combines two facts the program
has had for a long time but never put side by side. The combination collapses the
structure of the surviving bridge almost completely - and it VOIDS part of 218-221,
which is recorded as a correction.

### 224.1 The two facts

  (i) 218.1: a degree-2 vertex of a bridge IS a terminal, so terminals occupy EVERY
      internal position of every H-edge; an H-edge of B-length l carries exactly l-1
      CONSECUTIVE terminals.
  (ii) 213.1: two terminals at B-distance delta give an ear of length delta + 2, and
      no-negative-shift forces delta + 2 > |C|/2 >= 6, so delta >= 5.

They were proved six sections apart and never used together. Together they say:

### 224.2 THEOREM: EVERY H-EDGE HAS LENGTH AT MOST 2 (PROVED)

  If l_e >= 3 then e carries terminals at positions 1 and 2, at B-distance 1 < 5,
  contradicting 224.1(ii). Hence l_e <= 2 for EVERY edge of H.

  COROLLARY 1 (MATCHING). If two H-edges e, f share a vertex v and both have l = 2,
  their terminals are at B-distance 2 < 5, again a contradiction. So the edges of
  length 2 - equivalently the terminal-carrying edges - form a MATCHING M of H, and
  s = |M| >= 3.

  COROLLARY 2 (H IS SIMPLE OF GIRTH >= 4). A double edge of H gives a B-cycle of
  length at most 3 + 1 = 4 (at most one of the two can be in M), below girth 5. A
  triangle of H gives a B-cycle of length at most 3 + 1 = 4 likewise, since at most
  one of its three edges lies in the matching M. So H has no multi-edge and no
  triangle.

  THE SURVIVING BRIDGE, COMPLETELY DESCRIBED:

     B is obtained from a SIMPLE CUBIC GRAPH H of girth at least 4 by SUBDIVIDING
     ONCE each edge of a MATCHING M with |M| = s >= 3; the subdivision points are
     exactly the terminals; and they are pairwise at B-distance at least 5.

  Counting: |V(B)| = |V(H)| + s, |E(B)| = |E(H)| + s, mu(B) = mu(H) = |V(H)|/2 + 1.

### 224.3 CORRECTION to 218-221

This voids several statements that assumed long H-edges exist.

  - 221.2 (every even cycle through an H-edge of length l >= 4 has length 0 mod 4) is
    VACUOUS in the surviving case: no edge has length 4. RETRACTED as a tool.
  - 218.3's COROLLARY ("a balanced theta has long H-edges on at most one branch") and
    219.2's corollary about long edges are VACUOUS for the same reason: "long" meant
    l >= 3.
  - The Branch Parity THEOREM 218.3 itself and the Unbalanced Theorem 219.2 SURVIVE,
    because their hypothesis is "the branch carries terminals of BOTH position
    parities", which with l_e <= 2 is still achievable through the pattern of length-1
    and length-2 edges along a branch, not through a single long edge.
  - 223 is unaffected: it concerns the cycle space and uses no edge lengths.

I record this plainly rather than leaving the earlier sections to be read as if still
loaded. Three of the tools built in 218-221 turn out to fire only in a case that
cannot occur.

### 224.4 (SC) restated on H (PROVED)

Let b_e, b_f be the terminals on matching edges e, f. A connecting path leaves b_e to
one end of e, runs through H avoiding the interiors of e and f, and enters b_f. Since
each matching edge traversed contributes 2 to the B-length and each other edge 1,

     |connecting path| = 2 + |P| + |P cap M| ,

where P is an H-path between an endpoint of e and an endpoint of f avoiding e and f.
So (SC) becomes a statement purely about a cubic graph with a distinguished matching:

     FOR EVERY PAIR e, f IN M, ALL H-PATHS P BETWEEN THEIR ENDPOINTS WITH
     |P| + |P cap M| EVEN HAVE |P| + |P cap M| CONSTANT MODULO 4.

Likewise a cycle Z of H gives a B-cycle of length |Z| + |Z cap M|, so

     B-ODD CYCLES  =  cycles Z of H with |Z| + |Z cap M| ODD,

i.e. the odd cycles of B are the NEGATIVE cycles of the SIGNED GRAPH (H, sigma) with
sigma determined by the matching. The gap of 210.4/223.3 - three pairwise disjoint
odd cycles - becomes:

     THREE PAIRWISE DISJOINT CYCLES Z_1, Z_2, Z_3 OF A SIMPLE CUBIC GRAPH H, EACH
     WITH |Z_i| + |Z_i cap M| ODD, WHERE M IS A MATCHING.

This is far more tractable than the general odd-cycle packing problem: three disjoint
CYCLES in a cubic graph are cheap - by the Dirac-Lovasz characterisation the only
cubic graphs without two disjoint cycles are K_4 and K_{3,3} - and the whole
difficulty is now concentrated in the PARITY condition, with a signature that is only
a matching.

### 224.5 What the literature has been missing, and what we were

  THE LITERATURE. The cycles-mod-k community (Bollobas; Thomassen; Dean-Lesniak-Saito;
  Chen-Saito; Lyngsie-Merker; Chu et al.) asks for the EXISTENCE of one cycle in a
  residue class. The Arkin-Papadimitriou-Yannakakis line asks for RIGIDITY - when ALL
  paths between two vertices are congruent mod q - and gives a LINEAR-TIME algorithm,
  which means a structure theorem. Nobody appears to have connected the rigidity
  theory to the existence theory; that connection is what this program is, and the
  rigidity structure theorem has never been imported.

  OUR APPROACH. Two misses. First, we never combined 218.1 with 213.1, which is the
  whole of 224.2. Second, we have always looked for a single global contradiction and
  never for a RECURSION, even though (SC) reproduces itself: deleting the interior of
  a matching edge leaves a graph with mu - 1 in which the two ends are new degree-2
  vertices satisfying the same kind of condition. An induction on mu, with base case
  mu = 1 (a cycle, disposed of by 211.3), is the natural shape and has not been tried.

### 224.6 Status

PROVED here: every H-edge of a surviving bridge has length at most 2; the
terminal-carrying edges form a matching; H is simple of girth at least 4; hence B is a
cubic graph with a matching subdivided once (224.2); the restatement of (SC) and of the
odd cycles as negative cycles of a matching-signed cubic graph (224.4).
CORRECTED: 221.2 and the long-edge corollaries of 218.3 and 219.2 are vacuous (224.3).
NOT PROVED: (INT), hence (H1*), hence the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 224 combines two long-standing facts
to show the surviving bridge is exactly a simple cubic graph of girth at least 4 with a
matching subdivided once, retracts three tools from 218-221 that only fire on
now-impossible long edges, and recasts the remaining gap as finding three disjoint
cycles of prescribed parity in a matching-signed cubic graph.


## 225. EMPIRICS ON THE SURVIVING STRUCTURE: the binding mechanism is NOT odd cycles

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. Using the tight description of 224.2 I ran
three cheap experiments. They overturn the framing the program has carried since 210
and replace it with a sharper and better-supported one.

### 225.1 The experiment

By 224.2 the surviving bridge is a simple cubic graph H of girth at least 4 with a
matching M subdivided once, |M| = s >= 3, terminals pairwise at B-distance at least
5 - which forces the matching edges to be pairwise at H-distance at least 3, and
(since a 4-cycle of H meets M at most once) effectively forces H to have girth 5.
Ball counting gives |V(H)| >= 6s, so |B| >= 7s and, summing over bridges with
sum s_B = |C|, n >= 8|C|. That is a new global bound, better than 191.2's
n > |C|^2/4 for |C| < 32.

I generated cubic H of girth 5 on 18 to 26 vertices, took all matchings of size 3 at
pairwise distance at least 3, built B, and tested.

### 225.2 FINDING 1: nu_odd <= 2 is nowhere near sufficient

     surviving configurations tested                 1860
       with three disjoint negative cycles           1602
       with nu_odd <= 2 (not excluded by 223.3)       258

     of the low-packing configurations, tested for (SC)   149
       (SC) FAILS anyway                                  149
       (SC) HOLDS                                           0

So EVERY configuration that the odd-cycle criterion fails to exclude is excluded by
something else. The condition "three pairwise disjoint odd cycles" - carried since
210.4 and re-derived algebraically at 223.3 - is a genuine NECESSARY consequence of
(SC), but it is far from the binding constraint. Chasing it was chasing the weaker of
two obstructions, and that is why the half-integrality of Reed's theorem kept
blocking: the program was leaning on the wrong one.

### 225.3 FINDING 2: every minimal witness is ONE even cycle of length 2 mod 4

For 25 configurations I extracted a violating terminal pair together with two even
connecting paths P, P' in different classes mod 4, minimising |P xor P'|. The result
is perfectly uniform:

     (#components of P xor P',  |P xor P'| mod 4)  ->  count
                    (1, 2)                        ->   25          (all of them)

     single-cycle witnesses: (|Z| mod 4, segment length mod 2) -> count
                    (2, 0)                                    ->   25          (all)

EVERY minimal witness is a SINGLE CYCLE Z with |Z| = 2 (mod 4), met by the connecting
path in a segment of EVEN length. That is exactly the mechanism of 211.2: the shift is
eps = |Z| - 2 l_1 = 2 - 0 = 2 mod 4. Not three odd cycles - ONE even cycle.

### 225.4 FINDING 3: the cycle of length 2 mod 4 is always there

     cubic graphs of girth >= 5 tested        186 ; without a cycle of length 2 mod 4:  0
     surviving bridges B tested                43 ; without a cycle of length 2 mod 4:  0

  CAVEAT, stated because it affects one line of my output: the enumerator counted only
  INDUCED cycles, so the printed spectra are lower bounds. That makes the positive
  findings above SAFER (a 2-mod-4 cycle was found even among the induced ones) but it
  made the printed line for K_{3,3} wrong - K_{3,3} does have a 6-cycle, so it DOES
  have a cycle of length 2 mod 4. K_4 (cycles 3 and 4 only) and the prism (3,4,5) are
  genuine exceptions, both of girth 3, which is why girth at least 5 is the right
  hypothesis.

### 225.5 THE NEW TARGET

Everything now rests on two statements, both much closer to the existing literature
than odd-cycle packing was:

  (L1) SPECTRUM. Every graph of minimum degree 3 and girth at least 5 contains a cycle
       of length congruent to 2 modulo 4.
       This is the exact companion of DEAN-LESNIAK-SAITO ("every graph of minimum
       degree 3 has a cycle of length 0 mod 4"), and it lives in the same literature -
       BONDY-VINCE (two cycles whose lengths differ by 1 or 2), CHEN-SAITO,
       Lyngsie-Merker. K_4 and the prism show girth 3 is not enough.

  (L2) REALISABILITY. Such a cycle is met by some even connecting path in a segment of
       EVEN length.
       213.3 already proves every even cycle carries attachment pairs at both
       Z-distance parities, and in the structure of 224.2 the attachment points of Z
       are exactly its H-VERTICES - every one of them has a third edge leaving Z,
       since only the subdivision terminals have degree 2. So attachments are as dense
       as they can be, which is the best possible setting for realisability.

Given (L1) and (L2), 212.1's identity |Z| = 2 l_1 (mod 4) gives 2 = 0, and (INT)
follows, hence (H1*), hence the conjecture. Neither is proved here.

### 225.6 Status

PROVED here: nothing new; this section is empirical.
COMPUTED: nu_odd <= 2 fails to exclude 258 of 1860 configurations, yet all 149 of
those tested still fail (SC) (225.2); all 25 minimal witnesses are a single cycle of
length 2 mod 4 met in an even segment (225.3); all 186 cubic girth-5 graphs and all 43
surviving bridges tested contain a cycle of length 2 mod 4 (225.4). New bound
n >= 8|C| (225.1).
NOT PROVED: (L1), (L2), hence (INT), hence the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 225 shows empirically that the
three-disjoint-odd-cycles condition, which the program has treated as the gap since
210, is not the binding obstruction; the binding one is a single cycle of length 2
mod 4 met in an even segment. It restates the endgame as two statements (L1) and (L2),
the first of which is the direct companion of a known theorem of Dean, Lesniak and
Saito.


## 226. (L1) IS THE EXCEPTIONAL RESIDUE - and our class is the opposite of the extremal one

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section reports what the literature says
about (L1), corrects an error in 225.4, and sharpens (L1) to a clean statement.

### 226.1 CORRECTION to 225.4

I listed the PRISM as a cubic graph with no cycle of length 2 mod 4. That is WRONG:
the prism is Hamiltonian on 6 vertices, so it has a 6-cycle and 6 = 2 mod 4. The error
came from the induced-cycle-only enumerator flagged in 225.4; re-running with a full
cycle enumeration gives:

     K_4    girth 3   NO cycle of length 2 mod 4      <- the only failure found
     prism  girth 3   HAS one (the Hamiltonian 6-cycle)
     K_3,3  girth 4   HAS one (6-cycle)
     cube   girth 4   HAS one (6-cycle)

So K_4 is the ONLY cubic graph found without a 2-mod-4 cycle, and the girth-4 examples
I cited as failures are not failures. 225.4's conclusion survives and strengthens; its
supporting list did not.

### 226.2 What the literature says about the residue 2

DEAN'S CONJECTURE: for every k >= 3, every graph of minimum degree at least k contains
a cycle of length divisible by k. Proved for k = 3 (CHEN-SAITO) and k = 4
(DEAN-LESNIAK-SAITO); open for k >= 5.

LUO, MA and ZHAO (arXiv 2601.13552, 2026), Theorem 1.2: for k >= 6, every graph of
minimum degree at least k contains a cycle of length r mod k for EVERY EVEN r, unless
every end-block lies in an exceptional family {K_{k+1}, K_{k,k}} union H_k - and those
exceptional graphs fail ONLY for the residue 2 (mod k). Corollary 1.3 resolves Dean's
conjecture for k >= 6 for every even r not congruent to 2.

Separately, a graph with NO (2 mod 4)-cycle satisfies e(G) <= 5(n-1)/2, with equality
when 4 | (n-1) exactly when every block is K_5.

  READ THIS PLAINLY: our endgame has landed on residue 2 - precisely the one residue
  the modern literature singles out as exceptional. That is bad news for hoping (L1)
  is a known corollary.

  BUT THE EXCEPTIONS ARE DENSE. K_{k+1}, K_{k,k}, H_k and K_5-blocks are all dense,
  girth 3 or 4. The edge bound e <= 5(n-1)/2 never binds on a cubic graph, since
  3n/2 <= 5(n-1)/2 for all n >= 3, so it excludes nothing in our class - and equally,
  none of the extremal examples lives in our class. OUR GRAPHS ARE SUBCUBIC OF GIRTH
  AT LEAST 5, the extreme opposite of every known obstruction to residue 2.

### 226.3 The empirical statement, sharpened

     named cubic cages and symmetric graphs                     9 tested, ALL have a
       Petersen, Heawood, Mobius-Kantor, Pappus, Desargues,     2-mod-4 cycle
       Dodecahedron, McGee, Nauru, Tutte-Coxeter (girth up to 8)
     random cubic graphs of girth >= 5                        376 tested, 0 failures
     surviving bridges B (224.2 structure)                     43 tested, 0 failures

  (L1'')  EVERY CUBIC GRAPH OTHER THAN K_4 CONTAINS A CYCLE OF LENGTH 2 MODULO 4.

  Not a single counterexample beyond K_4 in 389 graphs, including every cage up to
  girth 8. The high-girth cages are the most plausible counterexamples - they have the
  sparsest, most rigid cycle spectra - and they all contain one.

### 226.4 The reduction that (L1'') needs

For the surviving bridge B = H with a matching M subdivided once, a cycle Z of H gives
a B-cycle of length |Z| + |Z cap M|. Since M is a matching whose edges are pairwise at
H-distance at least 3, many cycles of H avoid M entirely, and for those the B-length
is just |Z|. So it suffices to find

     A CYCLE OF H OF LENGTH 2 MOD 4 THAT AVOIDS THE MATCHING M,

i.e. a 2-mod-4 cycle in H - M, a graph of minimum degree 2 obtained from a cubic
girth-5 graph by deleting a sparse matching. Together with (L2) - realisability, for
which 213.3 already supplies attachment pairs of both parities and 224.2 makes EVERY
H-vertex of Z an attachment point - this closes (INT), hence (H1*), hence the
conjecture.

### 226.5 Status

CORRECTED: 225.4's claim that the prism has no 2-mod-4 cycle (226.1).
COMPUTED: 389 cubic graphs tested, K_4 the only one without a cycle of length 2 mod 4;
all nine named cages have one (226.3).
IMPORTED: Dean's conjecture and the Luo-Ma-Zhao theorem, which identify residue 2 mod
k as the sole exceptional residue, with all known exceptional graphs DENSE (226.2).
NOT PROVED: (L1''), (L2), hence (INT), hence the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 226 corrects the prism claim of
225.4, reports that residue 2 mod k is exactly the residue the 2026 literature
singles out as exceptional - while noting every known exceptional graph is dense and
ours are subcubic of girth at least 5 - and sharpens the target to (L1''): every cubic
graph but K_4 has a cycle of length 2 mod 4, verified on 389 graphs including every
cage up to girth 8.


## 227. (L1'') IS THE HARDER PROBLEM - AND IT IS NOT NEEDED

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. (L1'') is harder than (L2): it is an instance
of a PUBLISHED OPEN PROBLEM. This section proves that, and then resolves (L1'') by
showing the argument never required it. The sole remaining item is (L2).

### 227.1 (L1'') is the k = 4 case of the Lyngsie-Merker EVEN-k problem (IMPORTED)

LYNGSIE and MERKER, "Cycle lengths modulo k in large 3-connected cubic graphs"
(arXiv 1904.05076; Advances in Combinatorics 2021:3):

  "We prove that for all natural numbers m and k where k is ODD, there exists a
   natural number N(k) such that any 3-connected cubic graph with at least N(k)
   vertices contains a cycle of length m modulo k."

k = 4 is EVEN, so this does not apply. The authors also show the statement FAILS for
2-connected cubic graphs under certain divisibility conditions - and our H is
guaranteed only 2-connected, not 3-connected. (L1'') is therefore exactly the
m = 2, k = 4 instance of the even-k problem this program identified as a wall several
sessions ago, and independently it is the residue that Luo-Ma-Zhao (226.2) single out
as the exceptional one. It is not a lemma to be proved in passing.

  VERDICT: (L1'') is harder than (L2), and it is open in the literature.

### 227.2 RESOLUTION: the argument never needed (L1'')

Return to what is actually PROVED.

  212.1  For EVERY even cycle Z and EVERY realisable segment l_1,  |Z| = 2 l_1 (mod 4).
         Hence if ONE even cycle is realisable with segments of BOTH parities, 2 l_1
         takes both values 0 and 2 modulo 4 - a contradiction.
  211.3  Every relevant bridge CONTAINS an even cycle.
  213.3  EVERY even cycle carries attachment pairs at BOTH odd and even Z-distance.

That chain needs NO information about |Z| modulo 4. An even cycle with |Z| = 0 works
with an ODD segment; one with |Z| = 2 works with an EVEN segment; either way two
segment parities on a single even cycle is the contradiction. So:

  (L1'') IS NOT REQUIRED. ANY even cycle of B suffices, and 211.3 supplies one.

  WHY 225.3 LOOKED OTHERWISE. The 25 witnesses were MINIMAL ones - obtained by
  minimising |P xor P'| - and the minimal witness naturally has |Z| = 2 mod 4 with an
  even segment, because that is the shortest way to realise a shift of 2. That is a
  fact about which witness is smallest, NOT about which witnesses exist. I read a
  property of the minimiser as a requirement of the argument.

  CORRECTION. 225.5 and 226.4 presented (L1) / (L1'') as one of two statements the
  endgame rests on. That framing is WITHDRAWN. The endgame rests on (L2) alone.

### 227.3 What was proved while attacking (L1'') (PROVED, kept on the record)

Although unnecessary, two facts came out of the attempt and are recorded.

  THETA CLASSIFICATION. Suppose G has no cycle of length 2 mod 4. For any theta
  subgraph with branches p, q, r the three cycle lengths A = p+q, B = p+r, C = q+r
  satisfy A + B + C = 2(p+q+r), which is 0 or 2 mod 4. Enumerating triples from
  {0,1,3} with that sum leaves exactly the multisets

        {0,0,0},  {0,1,1},  {0,1,3},  {0,3,3},

  every one of which CONTAINS A 0. So in a graph with no 2-mod-4 cycle, every theta
  subgraph has a cycle of length divisible by 4. (Multisets {1,1,1}, {1,1,3}, {1,3,3},
  {3,3,3}, {0,0,1}, {0,0,3} are all excluded by the sum condition.)

  EVEN-MEET LEMMA. Suppose every even cycle of G has length 0 mod 4. If two even
  cycles Z_1, Z_2 meet in a single path P, then Z_1 + Z_2 is an even cycle, so
  0 = |Z_1| + |Z_2| - 2|P| = -2|P| (mod 4), giving |P| EVEN. Two even cycles may then
  only meet in an even-length path.

  Also noted: a cubic graph always HAS an even cycle, since a graph all of whose
  cycles are odd is a cactus of odd cycles and a 2-connected cactus is a single cycle
  (211.3). So (L1'') is equivalent to: every cubic graph but K_4 has an even cycle of
  length NOT divisible by 4.

### 227.4 The single remaining item

  (L2) REALISABILITY. Some even cycle Z of B is met by even connecting paths in
       segments of two different parities - equivalently, two attachment pairs of Z at
       Z-distances of opposite parity are both realisable as entry/exit pairs.

  213.3 supplies the attachment pairs. 224.2 makes the setting as favourable as it can
  be: the attachment points of Z are exactly its H-VERTICES, and every one of them has
  a third edge leaving Z, since in B only the subdivision terminals have degree 2. What
  is missing is purely the linkage - routing a connecting path in and out at a
  prescribed pair.

### 227.5 Status

IMPORTED: Lyngsie-Merker covers only ODD k, so (L1'') is open (227.1).
PROVED here: (L1'') is not needed - 212.1, 211.3 and 213.3 already give the
contradiction from any even cycle with two realisable segment parities (227.2); the
theta classification and the Even-Meet Lemma (227.3).
CORRECTED: 225.5 and 226.4 wrongly made (L1) a requirement (227.2).
NOT PROVED: (L2), hence (INT), hence (H1*), hence the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 227 identifies (L1'') as the harder
of the two problems - it is the m=2, k=4 instance of the open even-k Lyngsie-Merker
question - and resolves it by proving it unnecessary: the contradiction needs only an
even cycle realisable with two segment parities, and 211.3 supplies the cycle while
213.3 supplies the parities. The endgame now rests on the single linkage statement
(L2).


## 228. (L2) LOCALISED AT A TERMINAL

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. (L2) asked for realisability somewhere in B -
a global linkage question. This section shows the whole of it happens at a single
TERMINAL, where degree 2 removes all the freedom, and reduces (L2) to a statement
about cycles through one prescribed edge.

### 228.1 THE TERMINAL-CYCLE LEMMA (PROVED)

Let b be a terminal of B, with its two neighbours x, y - by 224.2 these are exactly the
two endpoints of the matching edge e of H that b subdivides.

  Since deg(b) = 2, EVERY cycle through b uses BOTH its edges, so every such cycle is

        Z  =  b x + Q + y b ,     |Z| = |Q| + 2,

  where Q is an x-y path in B - b. There is no choice of how a cycle meets b.

  LEMMA. Suppose some path leaves x, avoids V(Z) - {b, x}, and reaches another
  terminal. Then the connecting path P starting b, x, ... meets Z in EXACTLY the single
  edge bx, so its segment is l_1 = 1, and rerouting P along the other arc of Z gives a
  connecting path P' between the SAME two terminals with

        |P'| - |P|  =  sigma  =  |Z| - 2 .

  Both are simple, because P after x avoids Z and the replacement arc lies inside Z.
  If |Z| is EVEN then sigma is even, so (SC) forces sigma = 0 mod 4, that is

        (SC)  ==>   |Z| = 2  (mod 4)   for every REALISABLE cycle through a terminal.

  Equivalently: (SC) implies NO TERMINAL LIES ON A REALISABLE CYCLE OF LENGTH 0 MOD 4.
  QED

Call a cycle through b REALISABLE if the escape condition of the lemma holds at x or
at y.

### 228.2 (L2) reduces to a statement about one prescribed edge

  (L2*)  SOME TERMINAL OF B LIES ON A REALISABLE CYCLE OF LENGTH 0 MODULO 4.

By 228.1, (L2*) contradicts (SC), so (L2*) gives (INT), hence (H1*), hence the
conjecture. And (L2*) is strictly weaker than (L2) as stated in 227.4: it needs one
cycle at one terminal, not two segment parities on a common cycle.

TRANSLATED TO H. Cycles of B through the terminal b correspond exactly to cycles of H
through the matching edge e, and the B-length of a cycle Z_H is |Z_H| + |Z_H cap M|.
So (L2*) reads:

     FOR SOME e IN M THERE IS A CYCLE Z_H OF H THROUGH e WITH
     |Z_H| + |Z_H cap M| = 0 (mod 4),  satisfying the escape condition.

Three choices of e are available, and every cycle through e is a candidate.

### 228.3 The census

Over surviving configurations built as in 224.2 (cubic H of girth 5 on 18 and 20
vertices, matchings of size 3 at pairwise distance at least 3):

     surviving configurations tested                       207
       with a terminal on a REALISABLE 0-mod-4 cycle       207
       without                                               0

  Distribution of (|Z| mod 4, shift mod 4) over the realisable terminal cycles found:

        (0, 2) -> 207        <- these are the violations of (SC)
        (1, 3) -> 218
        (2, 0) -> 202        <- these are consistent with (SC)
        (3, 1) -> 261

  All four length classes occur among realisable terminal cycles, and the class 0 mod 4
  - the fatal one - occurred in EVERY configuration tested.

### 228.4 Honest assessment

What 228.1 buys is real: (L2) was a global two-disjoint-paths question about an
arbitrary even cycle; it is now a question about cycles through ONE prescribed edge at
a degree-2 vertex, where the cycle has no freedom in how it meets the terminal and the
escape condition is a plain reachability test.

What it does not buy is a proof. (L2*) asks for a cycle of prescribed length modulo 4
through a prescribed edge, and that is once again a cycle-spectrum statement of the
kind 227.1 showed to be open for even moduli. The differences in our favour are that we
may choose among three matching edges, that all cycles through the chosen edge are
candidates, and that the target residue is 0 mod 4 - the residue for which
DEAN-LESNIAK-SAITO is a THEOREM rather than a conjecture, though their theorem gives no
control over which edge the cycle passes through.

### 228.5 Status

PROVED here: the Terminal-Cycle Lemma - every cycle through a terminal is forced, and
(SC) implies no terminal lies on a realisable cycle of length 0 mod 4 (228.1); the
reduction of (L2) to (L2*) and its translation to H (228.2).
COMPUTED: all 207 surviving configurations tested contain a terminal on a realisable
0-mod-4 cycle, so (SC) fails in every one (228.3).
NOT PROVED: (L2*), hence (L2), hence (INT), hence (H1*), hence the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 228 localises (L2) at a terminal,
where degree 2 forces every cycle through it to consist of both its edges plus an x-y
path, and proves that (SC) then forbids any realisable terminal cycle of length 0
modulo 4. The remaining statement (L2*) - that some terminal lies on such a cycle -
held in all 207 configurations tested but is not proved.


## 229. TWO TERMINALS ON ONE CYCLE: a second contradiction mechanism

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section adds two proved lemmas that
between them replace (L2*) by a strictly weaker statement, verified on every
configuration tested.

### 229.1 THE TRIPOD LEMMA: (SC) is never vacuous (PROVED)

  LEMMA. If B has s >= 3 terminals then some PAIR of them is joined by an EVEN
  connecting path.

  Proof. Take a Steiner tree of b_1, b_2, b_3 in B. B is subcubic, so the tree has a
  single branch vertex c, giving a TRIPOD with internally disjoint legs of lengths
  lambda_1, lambda_2, lambda_3 from c to the three terminals. The three connecting
  paths lambda_i + lambda_j are genuine paths of B. Among three integers two share a
  parity, and that pair's sum is EVEN. QED

  This matters because (SC) constrains only EVEN connecting paths: without the lemma,
  a bridge could satisfy (SC) vacuously by having every connecting path odd. The
  tripod rules that out. (It also reproves 219-style facts: all three sums cannot be
  odd, since that would need lambda_1, lambda_2, lambda_3 pairwise of different
  parities, impossible for three numbers.)

### 229.2 THE TWO-TERMINAL EVEN-ARC THEOREM (PROVED)

  THEOREM. Suppose a cycle O of B contains two terminals b_1, b_2 with BOTH arcs
  between them of EVEN length, and suppose some terminal b_3 NOT on O is reachable
  from a neighbour of b_1 by a path avoiding O. Then (SC) FAILS.

  Proof. Write alpha and |O| - alpha for the two arc lengths, both even.
   (a) The two arcs are two EVEN connecting paths between b_1 and b_2, so (SC) forces
       alpha = |O| - alpha (mod 4), i.e. |O| = 2 alpha (mod 4). As alpha is EVEN,
       2 alpha = 0 (mod 4), so  |O| = 0 (mod 4).
   (b) O is a cycle through the terminal b_1, and by hypothesis a connecting path may
       start b_1, x_1 and then escape to b_3 avoiding O. By the Terminal-Cycle Lemma
       228.1 that path meets O in exactly the edge b_1 x_1, so its segment is 1 and
       rerouting gives shift sigma = |O| - 2, which is even; (SC) forces sigma = 0
       (mod 4), i.e.  |O| = 2 (mod 4).
  (a) and (b) give 0 = 2 modulo 4. QED

  Note both halves are needed and neither alone suffices: (a) uses the pair (b_1,b_2),
  (b) uses the pair (b_1,b_3). The theorem is the first mechanism in this program that
  consumes THREE terminals at once, which is exactly the hypothesis s >= 3 that 191.2
  supplies and that has otherwise been used only for counting.

### 229.3 The reduction, and the census

  (L2**)  SOME CYCLE OF B CONTAINS TWO TERMINALS WITH BOTH ARCS EVEN, AND A THIRD
          TERMINAL OFF THAT CYCLE IS REACHABLE FROM A NEIGHBOUR OF ONE OF THEM
          WITHOUT MEETING THE CYCLE.

By 229.2, (L2**) contradicts (SC), hence gives (INT), (H1*) and the conjecture.
(L2**) is weaker than (L2*) of 228.2: it does not ask for a cycle of a prescribed
length modulo 4 at all - the length is FORCED to 0 mod 4 by part (a). That removes the
dependence on a cycle-spectrum statement, which is what 227.1 and 228.4 identified as
the open ingredient.

     surviving configurations tested                          209
       with such a cycle (two terminals, both arcs even,
       third terminal off it and reachable)                   209
       without                                                  0

### 229.4 What is still missing

(L2**) needs a cycle through two terminals whose two arcs are both EVEN. Two-
connectivity gives a cycle through any two terminals, and 229.1 gives an even
connecting path for some pair, but neither forces the two ARCS OF ONE CYCLE to both be
even: a cycle through b_1 and b_2 of even total length has arcs of equal parity, and if
that parity is ODD the theorem does not fire - part (a) needs even arcs, and odd
connecting paths are unconstrained by (SC).

  SO THE RESIDUE IS: rule out the case where every cycle through every pair of
  terminals has ODD arcs. Note that such a bridge still has even connecting paths by
  229.1 - they just are not arcs of a common cycle - so the case is not obviously empty
  and is not settled here.

### 229.5 Status

PROVED here: the Tripod Lemma, so (SC) is never satisfied vacuously (229.1); the
Two-Terminal Even-Arc Theorem, a contradiction mechanism consuming three terminals,
whose cycle length is FORCED rather than assumed (229.2).
COMPUTED: all 209 surviving configurations tested satisfy (L2**) (229.3).
NOT PROVED: (L2**), hence (L2*), (L2), (INT), (H1*), and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 229 proves that some pair of
terminals always has an even connecting path, and proves that a cycle through two
terminals with both arcs even - together with a third terminal reachable off it -
contradicts (SC), with the cycle length forced to 0 mod 4 rather than assumed. This
removes the dependence on an open cycle-spectrum statement. What remains unproved is
that such a cycle exists; it did in all 209 configurations tested.


## 230. (L2**) BECOMES A PARITY-CONSTRAINED MENGER PROBLEM

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. Treating (L2**) as an olympiad problem, the
useful moves turned out to be: LOCAL FORCING at a degree-2 vertex (228), PIGEONHOLE on
parities (229.1), and - decisively here - HUNT FOR THE UNUSED HYPOTHESIS. The unused
hypothesis is non-bipartiteness, available since 195.2 and never applied at this end
of the argument.

### 230.1 THE BOTH-PARITIES THEOREM (PROVED)

  CLASSICAL FACT (195.2). In a 2-connected NON-BIPARTITE graph, any two vertices are
  joined by paths of BOTH parities.

  THEOREM. In the surviving bridge B, EVERY pair of terminals is joined by connecting
  paths of both parities.
  Proof. B is 2-connected (205.1 end-block descent). If B were bipartite it would be
  excluded outright by 205.2 and 208.2. So B is 2-connected and non-bipartite, and the
  classical fact applies to any two of its vertices, in particular to any two
  terminals. QED

  This SUPERSEDES the Tripod Lemma 229.1, which produced one even connecting path for
  one pair; the theorem gives an even one and an odd one for EVERY pair. I record that
  plainly: 229.1 is now redundant, though its proof is independent of
  non-bipartiteness and so survives as a fallback.

  CONSEQUENCE. (SC) is never vacuous at any pair, and the even class it constrains is
  always non-empty.

### 230.2 THE ARC-CONGRUENCE LEMMA (PROVED)

  LEMMA. Let O be a cycle through terminals b_1, b_2 whose two arcs alpha, beta are
  both ODD, and suppose O is realisable at b_1 in the sense of 228.1. Then

        |O| = 2 (mod 4)     and     alpha = beta (mod 4).

  Proof. |O| = alpha + beta is even, so 228.1 applies and forces |O| = 2 (mod 4). With
  alpha, beta both odd and alpha + beta = 2 (mod 4), either both are 1 or both are 3
  modulo 4, since 1 + 3 = 0. QED

  So the both-odd case is not free either - it pins the two arcs to a common class -
  but it is not contradictory, which is why 229.2 needed even arcs.

### 230.3 (L2**) RESTATED AS A DISJOINT-PATHS PROBLEM (PROVED EQUIVALENT)

Two internally disjoint b_1-b_2 paths form a cycle through b_1 and b_2 whose two arcs
are exactly those paths. Hence

  (L2**)  IS EXACTLY:  SOME PAIR OF TERMINALS IS JOINED BY TWO INTERNALLY DISJOINT
          EVEN CONNECTING PATHS (with a third terminal reachable off their union).

This is a PARITY-CONSTRAINED MENGER problem: not "are there two disjoint paths", which
2-connectivity answers yes, but "are there two disjoint paths OF PRESCRIBED PARITY".
230.1 supplies one even path for free; what is missing is a second one disjoint from
it.

  WHY THIS IS PROGRESS. Every earlier form of the gap - three disjoint odd cycles
  (210.4), a cycle of length 2 mod 4 (225.5), a 0-mod-4 cycle through a prescribed edge
  (228.2) - was a CYCLE SPECTRUM statement, and 227.1 showed those are open for even
  moduli. (L2**) in this form is not a spectrum statement at all: no residue mod 4
  appears in it. The mod-4 content has been fully absorbed into 229.2, which derives
  |O| = 0 mod 4 rather than assuming it. What remains is a disjoint-paths question with
  a parity side condition, which is the subject of a developed literature
  (Kawarabayashi-Reed and successors on parity-constrained linkages).

### 230.4 The residue

  RULE OUT: a 2-connected non-bipartite subcubic B, girth at least 5, with s >= 3
  terminals pairwise at distance at least 5, in which NO pair of terminals is joined by
  two internally disjoint EVEN paths - even though 230.1 guarantees each pair is joined
  by at least one even path and at least one odd path.

  Two remarks on how tight this is. First, by 230.2 any cycle through two terminals in
  such a B has arcs that are both odd and congruent mod 4, or of mixed parity. Second,
  the census of 229.3 found the required configuration in all 209 cases tested, so if
  the residue is non-empty its members are rare.

### 230.5 Status

PROVED here: every pair of terminals has connecting paths of both parities, so (SC) is
never vacuous (230.1); the Arc-Congruence Lemma for the both-odd case (230.2); the
equivalence of (L2**) with a parity-constrained disjoint-paths statement (230.3).
SUPERSEDED: the Tripod Lemma 229.1.
NOT PROVED: (L2**), hence (L2*), (L2), (INT), (H1*), and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 230 applies the unused hypothesis of
non-bipartiteness to prove that every pair of terminals has connecting paths of both
parities, and restates (L2**) as the existence of TWO INTERNALLY DISJOINT EVEN
connecting paths between some pair of terminals. This removes every trace of a cycle
spectrum condition from the remaining gap, leaving a parity-constrained Menger
problem, which is not proved here.


## 231. THE PARITY-CONSTRAINED MENGER PROBLEM IS A 2-LINKAGE

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section converts (L2**) into a
2-linkage with a prescribed PAIRING, identifies exactly which pairing is needed, and
imports the Seymour-Shiloach-Thomassen characterisation. It also records honestly why
that characterisation does not close the case.

### 231.1 (L2**) is a linkage with a prescribed pairing (PROVED)

Both terminals have degree 2, so a cycle through b_1 and b_2 uses all four edges
b_1x_1, b_1y_1, b_2x_2, b_2y_2, and consists of those plus TWO VERTEX-DISJOINT PATHS in
B - {b_1,b_2} joining {x_1,y_1} to {x_2,y_2}. The two arcs have B-lengths

        1 + (path from y_1) + 1     and     1 + (path from x_1) + 1,

so BOTH ARCS ARE EVEN exactly when BOTH LINKING PATHS HAVE EVEN LENGTH. Hence

  (L2**)  =  find two disjoint paths from {x_1,y_1} to {x_2,y_2}, BOTH OF EVEN LENGTH.

Two-connectivity gives two disjoint paths (Menger), realising ONE of the two possible
pairings, with no control on parity. The whole difficulty is that we need a particular
pairing.

### 231.2 Which pairing, when H is bipartite (PROVED)

Suppose H is bipartite with classes V_0, V_1; each matching edge e_i = x_i y_i has one
end in each, say x_i in V_0 and y_i in V_1. Write h_1, h_2 for the H-lengths of the two
linking paths and m_1, m_2 for the number of OTHER matching edges each contains. Then

        arc B-length = 2 + h_i + m_i .

With s = 3 there is exactly one other matching edge e_3, lying on at most one arc, so
(m_1,m_2) is (0,0), (1,0) or (0,1). Since H is bipartite the cycle's H-length
2 + h_1 + h_2 is even, so h_1 = h_2 (mod 2). Therefore:

     (1,0) and (0,1) are IMPOSSIBLE: they need h_1, h_2 of opposite parity.
     (0,0) works exactly when h_1 and h_2 are both EVEN, i.e. when the linkage pairs
           x_1 with x_2 and y_1 with y_2 - the SAME-CLASS pairing.

  CONCLUSION. For bipartite H, (L2**) is exactly: a cycle through e_1 and e_2 AVOIDING
  e_3 that pairs the two V_0-ends together and the two V_1-ends together.

  So the third matching edge cannot act as a parity switch - a mechanism I looked for
  and had to discard.

### 231.3 The literature tool (IMPORTED)

  SEYMOUR (1980), SHILOACH (1980), THOMASSEN (1980) independently characterised
  2-linked graphs. For terminals s_1, t_1, s_2, t_2 there are NO disjoint s_1-t_1 and
  s_2-t_2 paths if and only if the graph reduces - by repeatedly splitting along cuts
  of size at most 3 - to a PLANAR graph embedded with the four terminals on one face in
  the crossing cyclic order s_1, s_2, t_1, t_2.

  This is exactly the shape of obstruction our problem has: the pairing we need is the
  NON-crossing one relative to the class structure, and it fails only in the planar,
  terminals-on-a-face configuration.

  ALIGNMENT WORTH NOTING. By 155's Mac Lane dichotomy, PLANARITY is precisely the case
  where the mod-4 layer of the degree filtration is linear - the case the program
  already understands, since a planar graph has a 2-basis and the cubic defect vanishes.
  So the obstruction to (L2**) and the case the mod-4 machinery handles cleanly are the
  same case. That is a genuine structural alignment and the natural place to push.

### 231.4 Why this does NOT close the case, stated plainly

The clean form of the two-paths theorem is usually quoted for 4-CONNECTED graphs. Our
B is SUBCUBIC, so it is at most 3-connected and is riddled with 3-cuts - at every
vertex. The theorem therefore applies to us only through its reduction form, and the
reduction along 3-cuts is not a formality here: it is the entire content. I have not
carried it out, and I am not going to present the alignment of 231.3 as if it were the
argument.

What would finish it: show that the reduced graph of B relative to the four terminals
x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2 is either non-planar, or planar with those terminals NOT in the
crossing order - using girth at least 5, s >= 3 terminals pairwise at distance at least
5, and the freedom to choose which PAIR of the three terminals to work with.

### 231.5 Status

PROVED here: (L2**) is exactly a two-disjoint-paths problem with both paths of even
length (231.1); for bipartite H it is exactly the same-class pairing on a cycle
avoiding the third matching edge, and the third matching edge cannot serve as a parity
switch (231.2).
IMPORTED: the Seymour-Shiloach-Thomassen characterisation of 2-linked graphs, whose
obstruction is planar-with-four-terminals-on-a-face (231.3).
NOT PROVED: that our B avoids that obstruction; hence (L2**), (L2*), (L2), (INT),
(H1*), and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 231 shows the remaining gap is a
2-linkage with a prescribed pairing - two disjoint EVEN paths between the neighbour
pairs of two terminals - determines that for bipartite H the required pairing is the
same-class one on a cycle avoiding the third matching edge, and imports the
Seymour-Shiloach-Thomassen theorem, whose only obstruction is the planar
terminals-on-a-face configuration. Ruling that configuration out for subcubic B, where
3-cuts are everywhere, is not done here.


## 232. CARRYING OUT THE PLANARITY ANALYSIS

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section does what 231.4 said would
finish the argument. The result is NEGATIVE for the route I proposed, and I record the
correction before anything else.

### 232.1 CORRECTION to 231.3 (the alignment is not a route)

231.3 suggested that because Mac Lane makes planarity the case where the mod-4 layer is
linear, planarity might be the lever that rules out the Seymour-Shiloach-Thomassen
obstruction. IT DOES NOT. Work out the insertion:

The obstruction for the pairing (s_1,t_1) = (x_1,x_2), (s_2,t_2) = (y_1,y_2) is a face
carrying the four terminals in the order s_1, s_2, t_1, t_2, that is

        x_1 ,  y_1 ,  x_2 ,  y_2      (cyclically).

In that cyclic order x_1 and y_1 are CONSECUTIVE, and so are x_2 and y_2. Re-inserting
b_1, adjacent to exactly x_1 and y_1, and b_2, adjacent to exactly x_2 and y_2, places
each inside the face between its two neighbours, with NO CROSSING. So the obstruction
is entirely COMPATIBLE with B being planar. My suggestion in 231.3 that this was "the
natural place to push" was wrong, and I withdraw it.

### 232.2 THE FACE-ORDER LEMMA (PROVED)

What the insertion argument does give, run in the other direction:

  LEMMA. If the required linkage fails for the pair (b_1,b_2), then the reduced graph
  of B is planar and carries b_1 and b_2 on a COMMON FACE, in the cyclic order

        x_1 ,  b_1 ,  y_1 ,  x_2 ,  b_2 ,  y_2 .

  Proof. By Seymour-Shiloach-Thomassen the reduced graph is planar with x_1,y_1,x_2,y_2
  on a face in the order above; b_1 and b_2 have degree 2 with exactly those neighbours,
  so each embeds in that face between its two neighbours. QED

So the residue is not merely "some linkage fails" - it is a fully planar configuration
with the two terminals cofacial in a prescribed order. If the linkage fails for ALL
THREE pairs of terminals, the same face order is forced for each pair, which is
consistent with all three terminals lying on ONE face in the order
x_1,b_1,y_1,x_2,b_2,y_2,x_3,b_3,y_3 - a very rigid picture, but I could not derive a
contradiction from it.

### 232.3 The planar case is non-empty (COMPUTED)

By the ball-packing bound of 225.1, three matching edges pairwise at H-distance at
least 3 need |N[e]| = 6 vertices each, so |V(H)| >= 18; the DODECAHEDRON on 20 vertices
is the smallest planar cubic girth-5 host. Testing it:

     Dodecahedron, n = 20, girth 5, 30 edges
     matchings of 3 edges pairwise at distance >= 3   :  20
     configurations where (SC) FAILS                  :  20
     configurations where (SC) HOLDS                  :   0

So the planar surviving structure EXISTS - 20 of them on the Dodecahedron alone - and
(SC) fails in every one. The planar case is therefore neither vacuous nor a source of
counterexamples, and it is not disposed of by any argument given here.

### 232.4 What the literature does give us about planarity (IMPORTED)

  HECKMAN and KRAKOVSKI, "Erdos-Gyarfas Conjecture for Cubic Planar Graphs",
  Electron. J. Combin. 20(2) (2013) #P7: the conjecture HOLDS for 3-CONNECTED CUBIC
  PLANAR GRAPHS. Their proof uses the discharging method and is computer-assisted in
  parts.

  So in the reduction to 3-connected cubic G we may assume G is NON-PLANAR. That is a
  genuine simplification of the ambient problem.

  BUT IT DOES NOT CLOSE 232.2, and I will not pretend otherwise: the Face-Order Lemma
  concludes that the BRIDGE B is planar, and a non-planar G may perfectly well have
  planar bridges - indeed most bridges of a non-planar cubic graph are planar. The
  obstruction lives in B, the theorem applies to G, and there is no implication between
  them.

### 232.5 Status

CORRECTED: 231.3's suggestion that planarity rules out the SST obstruction - it is
compatible with it (232.1).
PROVED here: the Face-Order Lemma - failure of the linkage forces the reduced B to be
planar with b_1, b_2 cofacial in the order x_1,b_1,y_1,x_2,b_2,y_2 (232.2).
COMPUTED: the Dodecahedron carries 20 valid surviving structures and (SC) fails in all
20 (232.3).
IMPORTED: Heckman-Krakovski, so the ambient G may be assumed non-planar - which does
NOT transfer to the bridge (232.4).
NOT PROVED: that B avoids the SST obstruction; hence (L2**), (L2*), (L2), (INT),
(H1*), and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 232 carries out the planarity analysis
proposed in 231.4 and finds it does not finish the argument: the SST obstruction is
compatible with a planar bridge, so the Mac Lane alignment suggested in 231.3 is
withdrawn. What is proved is the Face-Order Lemma, pinning the residue to a planar
bridge with the two terminals cofacial in a prescribed order; the planar structure is
shown to exist on the Dodecahedron, where (SC) nonetheless fails in all 20 cases; and
Heckman-Krakovski lets the ambient graph be assumed non-planar without settling the
bridge.


## 233. THE EMPIRICS SAY: A SINGLE-PAIR ARGUMENT CANNOT WORK

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section asks the empirics the one
question that determines the SHAPE of any proof of (L2**), and gets a clean answer.

### 233.1 The question

(L2**) needs ONE pair of terminals carrying a both-arcs-even cycle with an escape.
There are three pairs available, since s >= 3 (191.2). Either

   (A) every pair works, and a single-pair argument suffices; or
   (B) individual pairs can fail, and the proof MUST use the freedom to switch pairs.

232 showed the failure mode is the Seymour-Shiloach-Thomassen planar obstruction, so
this is really asking whether that obstruction can hit one pair, and whether it can hit
all three at once.

### 233.2 The answer (COMPUTED)

Over 174 surviving configurations (cubic H of girth 5 on 18 and 20 vertices, matchings
of size 3 at pairwise distance at least 3), counting how many of the three terminal
pairs admit a cycle through both with BOTH ARCS EVEN:

     3 pairs work  ->  171 configurations
     1 pair works  ->    3 configurations
     0 pairs work  ->    0 configurations

  and additionally requiring the third-terminal ESCAPE of 229.2:

     3 pairs work  ->  163 configurations
     2 pairs work  ->    8 configurations
     1 pair works  ->    3 configurations
     0 pairs work  ->    0 configurations

  CONCLUSION. Alternative (B) holds. The obstruction DOES hit individual pairs - in 3
  configurations two of the three pairs fail outright, and in 8 more the escape fails
  for one pair - but it NEVER hit all three. Every one of 174 configurations had at
  least one working pair, as did all 209 of 229.3.

  SO: NO SINGLE-PAIR ARGUMENT CAN PROVE (L2**). Any proof must use s >= 3 and the
  freedom to change which pair of terminals it works with. That is a sharp constraint
  on the shape of the argument, and it explains why every attempt in 228-232, all of
  which fixed a pair, stalled.

  It also shows both conditions of 229.2 genuinely bind: the linkage fails in 3 cases,
  the escape fails in 8 further cases. Neither is a formality.

### 233.3 What the all-three-obstructed configuration would look like (PROVED)

By the Face-Order Lemma 232.2, obstruction at the pair (b_i,b_j) forces the reduced B
to be planar with b_i and b_j on a common face, in the order x_i,b_i,y_i,x_j,b_j,y_j.
If all three pairs were obstructed, the three terminals would be PAIRWISE COFACIAL in
those prescribed orders inside one planar graph.

  A note on why that is a natural stopping point rather than an accident. If all three
  terminals lie on ONE face, then - B being 2-connected and planar - that face boundary
  is a CYCLE containing all three. Any cycle through two of them then has NO terminal
  off it, so the escape condition of 229.2 fails for every pair simultaneously. The
  three configurations where only one pair worked are of exactly this flavour: the
  escape, not the linkage, is what the geometry attacks.

### 233.4 The statement to prove

  (L2***)  IN A SURVIVING BRIDGE, AT LEAST ONE OF THE THREE TERMINAL PAIRS ADMITS A
           CYCLE THROUGH BOTH TERMINALS WITH BOTH ARCS EVEN AND THE THIRD TERMINAL
           REACHABLE OFF IT.

  Verified: 174 of 174 here, 209 of 209 in 229.3. By 229.2 it contradicts (SC), giving
  (INT), (H1*) and the conjecture.

  WHAT A PROOF WOULD HAVE TO DO, now precisely: rule out a planar bridge in which all
  three terminals are pairwise cofacial in the Face-Order arrangement. Equivalently -
  and this is the form I would attack next - show that three terminals pairwise at
  distance at least 5 in a subcubic planar graph of girth at least 5 cannot all lie on
  one face boundary while every cycle through two of them has odd arcs.

### 233.5 Status

COMPUTED: the obstruction hits individual terminal pairs but never all three; 174 of
174 configurations have a working pair, with the linkage failing in 3 and the escape
failing in 8 more (233.2).
PROVED: the all-three-obstructed configuration forces the three terminals to be
pairwise cofacial, and if they share one face its boundary cycle defeats the escape
condition for every pair at once (233.3).
NOT PROVED: (L2***), hence (L2**), (L2*), (L2), (INT), (H1*), and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 233 establishes empirically that the
planar obstruction can defeat individual terminal pairs but never all three, so no
single-pair argument can succeed and any proof must use s >= 3 to switch pairs. It
records the precise remaining statement (L2***) and identifies the configuration a
proof must exclude: three terminals pairwise cofacial in a planar bridge.


## 234. THE THREE-TERMINAL GAP LEMMA, and why the escape is the real enemy

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. Three new proved facts, one of them negative,
which together say exactly where (L2***) can and cannot come from.

### 234.1 THE GAP LEMMA (PROVED)

Let O be a cycle containing ALL THREE terminals, and write g_1, g_2, g_3 for the three
gaps: g_1 from b_1 to b_2, g_2 from b_2 to b_3, g_3 from b_3 to b_1, so
|O| = g_1 + g_2 + g_3. The two arcs for the pair (b_1,b_2) are g_1 and |O| - g_1, and
similarly for the other pairs. Hence

     BOTH ARCS EVEN FOR THE PAIR OPPOSITE g_i   <==>   |O| EVEN AND g_i EVEN.

  LEMMA. If |O| is ODD, NO pair has both arcs even, since |O| - g_i always has the
  opposite parity to g_i. If |O| is EVEN, the number of odd gaps is even, so the number
  of EVEN gaps is 3 or 1 - in either case AT LEAST ONE. Therefore:

     EVERY EVEN CYCLE THROUGH ALL THREE TERMINALS YIELDS A PAIR WITH BOTH ARCS EVEN,
     and if all three gaps are even it yields all three pairs at once.

  QED

### 234.2 THE NEGATIVE FACT: such a cycle can never give the contradiction (PROVED)

This looks like it finishes (L2***), and it does not. On a cycle through ALL THREE
terminals there is NO terminal off O, so the escape condition of 228.1/229.2 fails for
every pair simultaneously. And part (a) of 229.2 alone is not contradictory: it is just
the identity 212.1, |O| = 2 l_1 (mod 4), applied with l_1 = g_i. Indeed with all three
gaps even, the three pairs give |O| = 2g_1 = 2g_2 = 2g_3 = 0 (mod 4), and the long arcs
give |O| = 2(g_i + g_j) = 0 as well: every instance agrees, and nothing is violated.

  CONCLUSION. The contradiction can ONLY come from a cycle through EXACTLY TWO
  terminals. The Gap Lemma is therefore not a shortcut - it is a warning that the
  three-terminal cycle is a dead end, and it explains 233.2's three configurations
  where only one pair worked.

### 234.3 THE EVEN BYPASS EXISTS (PROVED)

To get from a three-terminal cycle to a two-terminal one, b_3 must be bypassed. Since
b_3 has degree 2, O uses both its edges, so bypassing means replacing the sub-path
x_3, b_3, y_3 (length 2) by some x_3-y_3 path R avoiding b_3. Then

        |O'| = |O| - 2 + |R| ,

and the arc of the pair (b_1,b_2) not containing b_3 is unchanged, while the other
changes by |R| - 2. So BOTH ARCS OF O' ARE EVEN exactly when both arcs of O were and
|R| is EVEN.

  LEMMA. An even such R always EXISTS. B is 2-connected and non-bipartite - bipartite
  bridges are excluded by 205.2/208.2 - so by the classical fact of 195.2, quoted at
  230.1, ANY two vertices of B are joined by paths of both parities. Apply this to x_3
  and y_3 inside B - b_3, or equivalently note that b_3 lies on some EVEN cycle of B,
  whose complement at b_3 is an even x_3-y_3 path. QED

### 234.4 What is left, stated exactly

  (L2***) now needs only: an even x_3-y_3 bypass R that is DISJOINT from the rest of O.

234.3 gives the bypass; what is unproved is that one can be chosen internally disjoint
from O - {x_3, b_3, y_3}. This is once more a disjointness condition, but it is far more
local than anything before it: a single path between two ADJACENT-in-H vertices,
required to avoid one arc of one cycle, with the parity already guaranteed by 234.3 and
a whole parity class of candidates to choose from.

  THE CHAIN, FOR THE RECORD. even cycle through all three terminals (exists whenever
  the terminals are cofacial, 233.3) -> a pair with both arcs even (234.1) -> bypass
  b_3 by an even R (234.3) -> a cycle through exactly two terminals with both arcs even
  and the third off it -> 229.2 -> (SC) fails -> (INT) -> (H1*) -> the conjecture.
  Every arrow is proved except the disjointness of R.

### 234.5 Status

PROVED here: the Gap Lemma - every even cycle through all three terminals yields a pair
with both arcs even (234.1); the negative fact that such a cycle can never produce the
contradiction, because the escape fails and part (a) alone is consistent (234.2); and
the existence of an even bypass of b_3, from non-bipartiteness (234.3).
NOT PROVED: that the bypass can be chosen disjoint from O; hence (L2***), (L2**),
(L2*), (L2), (INT), (H1*), and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 234 proves that any even cycle through
all three terminals yields a pair with both arcs even, proves that such a cycle can
nevertheless never yield the contradiction because no terminal is left to escape to,
and proves that an even bypass of the third terminal always exists. The single
remaining step is to choose that bypass disjoint from the rest of the cycle.


## 235. CORRECTION: the bypass defeats its own escape condition

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. Before working on the disjointness of R I
checked what the bypass construction of 234.3 actually delivers. It does not satisfy
the hypotheses of 229.2. The error is mine and is recorded here in full.

### 235.1 THE ERROR

234.4 proposed: bypass b_3 by an even x_3-y_3 path R, obtaining a cycle O' through
b_1 and b_2 but not b_3, with both arcs even, and then apply 229.2.

229.2 requires a terminal NOT on O' that is REACHABLE from a neighbour of b_1 by a path
AVOIDING O'. The only terminal off O' is b_3. But b_3 has degree 2, and its two
neighbours are exactly x_3 and y_3 - and the bypass R runs FROM x_3 TO y_3, so BOTH of
them lie on O'. Any path to b_3 must arrive through x_3 or y_3, hence must meet O'.

     THE ESCAPE CONDITION FAILS FOR O' BY CONSTRUCTION.

So the gap in 234.4 was not merely the disjointness of R. Even a perfectly disjoint R
produces a cycle that 229.2 cannot be applied to. The chain of 234.4 is BROKEN, not
incomplete, and I withdraw it.

  WHAT SURVIVES. 234.1, the Gap Lemma, is unaffected: every even cycle through all
  three terminals yields a pair with both arcs even. 234.2 is unaffected and is in fact
  reinforced - it said the three-terminal cycle is a dead end because no terminal is
  left to escape to, and 235.1 shows the obvious repair inherits exactly that defect.
  234.3's existence claim (an even x_3-y_3 path exists) is true but useless here.

### 235.2 THE CORRECTED TARGET

Reading 228.1 and 229.2 carefully, what is needed of the cycle O through b_1 and b_2 is:

     (i)   both arcs between b_1 and b_2 are EVEN;
     (ii)  b_3 is not on O;
     (iii) at least ONE of x_3, y_3 is NOT on O - otherwise b_3 is walled off as above;
     (iv)  that vertex is reachable from x_1 or y_1 by a path avoiding O.

Condition (iii) is the one 234 missed. It says the cycle must not merely avoid b_3 but
must stay off at least one side of its NEIGHBOURHOOD.

  IMPORTANT: THE CENSUSES ARE UNAFFECTED. The escape test used in 229.3 and 233.2 is a
  breadth-first search from x_1 (or y_1) that avoids V(O) entirely and looks for a
  terminal; it therefore enforces (ii), (iii) and (iv) automatically. So the counts
  209 of 209 and 174 of 174 remain valid evidence for the corrected target. The defect
  was in 234's proposed ROUTE, not in the statement being tested.

### 235.3 Where a proof can still go

Translate to H. The bridge is H with a matching M subdivided (224.2), and x_3, y_3 are
the ends of the matching edge e_3. Conditions (i)-(iv) ask for

     A CYCLE OF H THROUGH e_1 AND e_2, AVOIDING e_3 AND AVOIDING AT LEAST ONE OF ITS
     ENDS, WHOSE TWO ARCS BOTH HAVE EVEN B-LENGTH.

  A CONDITIONAL STEP (PROVED). If H is 3-CONNECTED then H - x_3 is 2-connected, and in a
  2-connected graph any two edges lie on a common cycle; so a cycle through e_1 and e_2
  avoiding x_3 - hence avoiding e_3 - EXISTS. What that argument does not control is the
  PARITY of the two arcs, which is the whole of condition (i).

  H need not be 3-connected: B is only a 2-connected end block, and a 2-cut of B may be
  resolved in G by the cycle C rather than inside B. So even the conditional step is not
  available unconditionally.

### 235.4 Status

CORRECTED: 234.3 and 234.4 - the bypass construction cannot satisfy 229.2, because it
places both neighbours of b_3 on the new cycle (235.1). The chain proposed there is
withdrawn.
UNAFFECTED: the Gap Lemma 234.1; the negative fact 234.2; the censuses of 229.3 and
233.2, whose escape test already enforced the corrected conditions (235.2).
PROVED here: the corrected list of conditions (i)-(iv) (235.2); and, conditionally on H
being 3-connected, the existence of a cycle through e_1 and e_2 avoiding x_3, though
with no control on arc parity (235.3).
NOT PROVED: (L2***), hence everything above it, hence the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 235 retracts the bypass route of 234:
replacing b_3 by an x_3-y_3 path puts both neighbours of b_3 on the resulting cycle, so
b_3 becomes unreachable and the escape condition fails by construction. The corrected
requirement is that the cycle avoid at least one neighbour of b_3, which the earlier
censuses already tested; what remains unproved is the existence of such a cycle with
both arcs even.


## 236. THE CORRECTED TARGET: what is provable, and where every route converges

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. Working on the corrected conditions (i)-(iv)
of 235.2, this section proves three lemmas and then states plainly the single obstacle
that every remaining route runs into.

### 236.1 Translation, and why only condition (i) is arithmetic (PROVED)

With B = H plus a subdivided matching (224.2), let O be a cycle of H through e_1 and
e_2 avoiding e_3. Since no other matching edge lies on it, each arc of the
corresponding B-cycle between b_1 and b_2 has B-length 2 + h, where h is the H-length
of the corresponding H-path. Hence

     BOTH ARCS EVEN  <==>  BOTH CONNECTING H-PATHS HAVE EVEN LENGTH.

Conditions (ii),(iii),(iv) of 235.2 are pure reachability - they ask the cycle to avoid
e_3 and one of its ends and leave b_3 reachable - and involve no arithmetic. All the
arithmetic sits in (i).

### 236.2 THE PARITY FLIP LEMMA (PROVED)

  LEMMA. Let O be a cycle through b_1 and b_2 with one arc EVEN and one arc ODD, and
  let W be an ODD cycle of B meeting the odd arc in a single segment and disjoint from
  the even arc. Rerouting the odd arc along W yields a cycle through b_1 and b_2 with
  BOTH ARCS EVEN.
  Proof. Rerouting a segment of length l along W changes that arc's length by
  |W| - 2l, which is ODD since |W| is odd; so the odd arc becomes even. The even arc is
  untouched because W is disjoint from it. QED

  This is the cheapest route to condition (i): it needs only a MIXED-parity cycle plus
  one suitably placed odd cycle, rather than two even paths built from scratch.

### 236.3 AN ODD CYCLE THROUGH b_3 ALWAYS EXISTS (PROVED)

  LEMMA. b_3 lies on an odd cycle of B, and also on an even one.
  Proof. b_3 has degree 2, so every cycle through it is b_3 together with an x_3-y_3
  path. B is 2-connected and non-bipartite - bipartite bridges are excluded by
  205.2/208.2 - so by the classical fact of 195.2 there are x_3-y_3 paths of BOTH
  parities. Adding b_3 gives cycles of both parities through b_3. QED

  Combined with 234.3 this says the neighbourhood of the third terminal is a reliable
  source of odd cycles for the flip of 236.2 - which is the natural supply, since
  conditions (ii)-(iv) already force the cycle O to stay away from b_3.

### 236.4 THE SINGLE OBSTACLE

Every route now assembled runs into the same thing:

  - 229.2 needs two disjoint EVEN connecting paths (231.1);
  - 234's bypass needed R disjoint from O, and was withdrawn anyway at 235.1;
  - 236.2 needs W disjoint from the even arc and meeting the odd arc in a segment;
  - 235.3's conditional step gives a cycle avoiding x_3 but with no parity control.

In every case the existence of the OBJECT is proved - even paths exist (230.1), odd
cycles through b_3 exist (236.3), cycles through two prescribed edges exist (235.3) -
and what is missing is always that two of them can be chosen DISJOINT with prescribed
PARITIES. That is the parity-constrained linkage problem named at 230.3, and I have not
solved it, nor found a theorem in the literature that applies at connectivity 2 with
subcubic degrees.

  I want to state this without dressing it up: 228 through 236 have sharpened the
  target repeatedly - from a cycle-spectrum statement to a linkage, from a global
  linkage to a local one at a terminal, from arbitrary cycles to ones avoiding a
  prescribed neighbourhood - and every sharpening has left the same residue. The
  sharpenings are real and are all proved. The residue has not moved.

### 236.5 Status

PROVED here: both arcs even is equivalent to both connecting H-paths being even, so
only condition (i) carries arithmetic (236.1); the Parity Flip Lemma (236.2); the
existence of odd and even cycles through b_3 (236.3).
NOT PROVED: any of the disjointness statements; hence (L2***), (L2**), (L2*), (L2),
(INT), (H1*), and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 236 proves that in the corrected
target only the arc-parity condition is arithmetic, proves a Parity Flip Lemma turning
a mixed-parity cycle into a both-arcs-even one given a suitably placed odd cycle, and
proves that odd and even cycles through the third terminal always exist. It then states
plainly that every remaining route reduces to choosing two objects DISJOINT with
prescribed parities - the parity-constrained linkage problem - which is not solved here.


## 237. EMPIRICS ON THE LINKAGE: no parity invariant, but mixed cycles are universal

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. Three readings, one negative and one that
identifies the statement worth proving.

### 237.1 The survey

Over 219 terminal pairs from surviving configurations (cubic H of girth 5 on 18 and 20
vertices, matchings of size 3 at pairwise distance at least 3), counting for each pair
all cycles through both terminals, classified by the parities of the two arcs:

     pairs with ZERO both-arcs-even cycles          :  10  of 219
     pairs possessing a MIXED-parity cycle          : 219  of 219
     number of both-arcs-even cycles per pair       : min 0, median 62, max 151

     parity of that count:   even -> 107 pairs ,  odd -> 112 pairs
     parity of the count that also escapes: even -> 113 , odd -> 106

### 237.2 READING 1 (NEGATIVE): there is no parity invariant

The parity of the number of both-arcs-even cycles is 107 against 112 - indistinguishable
from a coin flip - and the same for the escaping ones, 113 against 106. So there is NO
Smith-type theorem here.

  This matters because it rules out an entire proof strategy. SMITH's theorem (every
  edge of a cubic graph lies on an EVEN number of Hamiltonian cycles) and THOMASON's
  lollipop generalisation make counting-mod-2 the natural weapon in cubic graphs, and
  "the number of good cycles is odd, hence non-zero" would have been the cleanest
  possible proof of (L2***). The data says that route does not exist.

### 237.3 READING 2: the target is ABUNDANT, not delicate

Where both-arcs-even cycles exist at all there are typically dozens - median 62, up to
151. So (L2***) is not a knife-edge statement needing a delicate construction; it fails
only in the 10 of 219 pairs where the count collapses to exactly zero. A proof should be
robust rather than constructive, and should concentrate entirely on why the count cannot
be zero for all three pairs at once.

### 237.4 READING 3 (THE USEFUL ONE): mixed-parity cycles are universal

EVERY one of the 219 pairs possessed a cycle through both terminals with one arc even
and one odd - equivalently, an ODD-LENGTH cycle through both terminals, since the arcs
have different parities exactly when the cycle is odd.

That is exactly the input the Parity Flip Lemma 236.2 needs. So the route

     odd cycle through b_1 and b_2   +   an odd cycle placed on its odd arc
                                     ->  both arcs even

has its first ingredient available universally in the data, and the remaining question
is only the placement of the second.

### 237.5 What the literature gives, and a counterexample at connectivity 2 (PROVED)

  KNOWN: in a 3-CONNECTED non-bipartite graph, ANY PAIR OF VERTICES lies on an odd
  cycle; indeed every 3-connected non-bipartite graph on n vertices has at least n odd
  cycles.

  Our B is 2-connected and, having degree-2 terminals, is never 3-connected. And the
  2-connected version is FALSE. Counterexample: the theta graph with branch lengths
  1, 2, 2 between s and t - that is, the edge st together with paths s-u-t and s-v-t.
  It is 2-connected and non-bipartite, its cycles being s-u-t-s and s-v-t-s of length 3
  and s-u-t-v-s of length 4. The only cycle containing BOTH degree-2 vertices u and v is
  the 4-cycle, which is EVEN. So u and v lie on no odd cycle.

  Note what saves us: that example has GIRTH 3. Our bridges have girth at least 5 and
  their terminals are pairwise at distance at least 5. So the statement to prove is

  (ODD-PAIR)  In a 2-connected non-bipartite subcubic graph of girth at least 5, any two
              degree-2 vertices at distance at least 5 lie on a common ODD cycle.

  verified on all 219 pairs, false without the girth hypothesis by the example above.

### 237.6 Status

COMPUTED: no parity invariant governs the count of both-arcs-even cycles (237.2); the
target is abundant where it holds, median 62 per pair, and collapses to zero in only 10
of 219 pairs (237.3); every one of the 219 pairs has a mixed-parity, i.e. odd, cycle
through both terminals (237.4).
PROVED: the 2-connected analogue of the 3-connected odd-cycle-through-a-pair theorem is
FALSE, by the theta graph with branches 1,2,2 (237.5).
IMPORTED: any pair of vertices of a 3-connected non-bipartite graph lies on an odd cycle.
NOT PROVED: (ODD-PAIR), the placement of the flipping cycle, hence (L2***) and the
conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 237 rules out counting-mod-2 as a
proof strategy - the parity of the number of good cycles is not invariant - shows the
target is abundant rather than delicate, and identifies that every terminal pair carries
an odd cycle through both terminals, which is exactly what the Parity Flip Lemma needs.
The corresponding statement (ODD-PAIR) is known at connectivity 3, is false at
connectivity 2 without a girth hypothesis, and is unproved in our setting.


## 238. THE ODD-CYCLE ATTACHMENT LEMMA, and the 2-cut obstruction

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section proves (ODD-PAIR) except for one
precisely identified obstruction, and shows that obstruction is exactly what the
pair-switching of 233.2 is for.

### 238.1 (ODD-PAIR) is a linkage of DIFFERENT parities (PROVED)

b_1 and b_2 have degree 2, so a cycle through both consists of the paths x_1 b_1 y_1 and
x_2 b_2 y_2 together with two disjoint paths joining {x_1,y_1} to {x_2,y_2}, of lengths
p and q. Then |O| = 4 + p + q, so

     |O| IS ODD  <==>  p and q have DIFFERENT parities.

Compare 231.1, where both arcs even meant both p and q EVEN. (ODD-PAIR) is the weaker
requirement that they merely DIFFER.

### 238.2 THE ATTACHMENT LEMMA (PROVED)

  LEMMA. Let O be a cycle through b_1 and b_2, and W an ODD cycle of B disjoint from O.
  By 2-connectivity there are two vertex-disjoint paths R_1, R_2 from O to W, internally
  disjoint from both; say R_i runs from o_i on O to w_i on W. If o_1 and o_2 do NOT
  separate b_1 from b_2 on O, then some cycle through b_1 and b_2 is ODD.

  Proof. Both b_1 and b_2 lie on one arc A of O between o_1 and o_2. Let W_a, W_b be the
  two w_1-w_2 arcs of W. Then

        C_a = A + R_1 + W_a + R_2      and      C_b = A + R_1 + W_b + R_2

  are both cycles containing b_1 and b_2, and
        |C_a| - |C_b| = |W_a| - |W_b| ,   while  |W_a| + |W_b| = |W| is ODD,
  so |W_a| and |W_b| have different parities and hence so do |C_a| and |C_b|. One of the
  two is ODD. QED

  The lemma needs NO parity control on the attachment paths R_1, R_2 and no control on
  where W sits - only that o_1, o_2 do not separate b_1 from b_2. That is why it is
  cheaper than everything attempted in 229-236.

### 238.3 THE OBSTRUCTION IS A SEPARATING 2-CUT (PROVED)

By 238.2, (ODD-PAIR) can fail only if for EVERY odd cycle W and every attachment, the
landing pair {o_1,o_2} SEPARATES b_1 from b_2 - in particular {o_1,o_2} is a 2-cut of B
with b_1, b_2 and W in three different components.

  SUBCUBIC BOUND (PROVED). In a subcubic graph a 2-cut {o_1,o_2} yields at most THREE
  components. Each component must send at least one edge to each of o_1 and o_2, since
  otherwise a single vertex would separate it, contradicting 2-connectivity. Three
  components therefore consume 3 edges at o_1 and 3 at o_2, so both cut vertices have
  degree exactly 3 and each component attaches by exactly ONE edge to each.

  So the obstructing configuration is completely rigid: a 2-cut of two degree-3
  vertices, splitting B into exactly three pieces, one holding b_1, one holding b_2, and
  one holding every odd cycle of B - so that B minus that piece is BIPARTITE.

### 238.4 WHY THIS IS WHERE PAIR-SWITCHING ENTERS

233.2 established empirically that no single-pair argument can work and that the proof
must use s >= 3. 238.3 shows exactly why, and hands us the pigeonhole:

  THREE terminals, at most THREE components. If b_3 lies in the SAME component as b_1
  or as b_2, then for that pair the cut {o_1,o_2} does NOT separate them, and 238.2
  applies to give an odd cycle through that pair. If instead b_3 lies in the third
  component - the one holding the odd cycles - then W and b_3 are on the same side, and
  again the cut fails to separate them.

  EITHER WAY THIS PARTICULAR CUT CANNOT OBSTRUCT ALL THREE PAIRS.

  WHAT IS MISSING, stated plainly: a different odd cycle may be hidden behind a
  DIFFERENT 2-cut, chosen to obstruct the pair that this one failed to obstruct. To
  finish, one must show that a single family of 2-cuts cannot simultaneously separate
  all three terminal pairs from all odd cycles. That is a statement about the SPQR
  decomposition of B, and I have not proved it.

### 238.5 Status

PROVED here: (ODD-PAIR) is a linkage of different parities (238.1); the Attachment
Lemma, giving an odd cycle through b_1 and b_2 from any odd cycle whose attachment does
not separate them (238.2); that the only obstruction is a separating 2-cut, which in a
subcubic graph is rigid - two degree-3 vertices, exactly three components, one edge from
each component to each cut vertex (238.3); and that any ONE such cut fails to obstruct
at least one of the three terminal pairs (238.4).
