NOT PROVED: that no family of 2-cuts obstructs all three pairs at once; hence
(ODD-PAIR), the placement of the flipping cycle, (L2***), and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 238 proves that any odd cycle whose
attachment to a cycle through two terminals does not separate them yields an odd cycle
through both, reducing (ODD-PAIR) to a separating 2-cut; shows that in a subcubic graph
such a cut is rigid with exactly three components; and shows by pigeonhole on the three
terminals that one such cut can never obstruct all three pairs. What remains is to rule
out a family of different cuts obstructing different pairs.


## 239. ONE CUT OBSTRUCTS AT MOST TWO PAIRS; the nested picture

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section makes 238.4's pigeonhole exact
and derives the structure any full obstruction would have to have.

### 239.1 THE COUNTING LEMMA (PROVED)

Fix an odd cycle W and a 2-cut {o,o'} realising the obstruction for the pair (b_1,b_2):
by 238.3 the cut has EXACTLY THREE components, say K_W containing W, K_1 containing
b_1, and K_2 containing b_2. The third terminal b_3 lies in one of these three, and the
cases are exhaustive.

  b_3 in K_1.  Pair (b_1,b_3): both lie in K_1, so the cut does not separate them and
               does not obstruct that pair. Pair (b_2,b_3): b_2 in K_2, b_3 in K_1,
               W in K_W - three different components, so it does obstruct.
               OBSTRUCTS 2 OF 3.
  b_3 in K_2.  Symmetric: obstructs (b_1,b_2) and (b_1,b_3), not (b_2,b_3).
               OBSTRUCTS 2 OF 3.
  b_3 in K_W.  Pair (b_1,b_3): W and b_3 lie in the SAME component, so the cut does not
               place W, b_1, b_3 in three different components and does not obstruct.
               Same for (b_2,b_3).  OBSTRUCTS 1 OF 3.

  LEMMA. A SINGLE 2-cut obstructs AT MOST TWO of the three terminal pairs.

  Consequently at least TWO distinct 2-cuts are needed to obstruct all three, and by the
  same lemma applied to each, at least two distinct odd cycles or two distinct cut pairs
  must be involved.

### 239.2 THE NESTED PICTURE (PROVED)

Suppose the cut {o,o'} obstructs (b_1,b_2) and (b_2,b_3), so b_3 lies in K_1 alongside
b_1. Some other cut {p,p'} must obstruct the remaining pair (b_1,b_3), which means it
has three components holding an odd cycle W', b_1, and b_3 separately.

All odd cycles lie in K_W, since 238.3 says B minus that piece is bipartite; so W' lies
in K_W. Every path from K_W to the rest passes through o and o'. For {p,p'} to separate
W' from BOTH b_1 and b_3, the component of B - {p,p'} containing W' must also contain o
and o' - otherwise one of them would sit on the same side as a terminal and W' would not
be separated from it. Hence

     {p,p'} lies inside K_1, separates b_1 from b_3, and leaves o, o' - and with them
     the whole of K_W - in its third component.

So the two cuts are NESTED: the odd part K_W sits innermost, the cut {o,o'} fences it
off together with b_2, and the cut {p,p'} sits inside K_1 fencing b_1 from b_3. Iterating
produces a TREE OF THETAS - each cut being two degree-3 vertices with three one-edge
attachments by 238.3 - with every odd cycle confined to one innermost piece and the three
terminals in three different leaves.

### 239.3 What remains

  TO FINISH: show that this nested family cannot exist in a 2-connected subcubic graph
  of girth at least 5 whose three degree-2 vertices are pairwise at distance at least 5.

  Two features of the picture look exploitable and I record them without claiming
  either. First, every cut in the family consists of two DEGREE-3 vertices with each of
  the three components attached by exactly ONE edge to each - extremely rigid, and it
  says the branch vertices of the tree of thetas use up their whole degree on the
  decomposition. Second, B minus the innermost piece is BIPARTITE, so all the parity
  content of B is confined to a single piece that every terminal is fenced away from -
  and 230.1 says B has paths of both parities between ANY two vertices, which must
  therefore all route through that one piece.

  That last tension is the most promising: every pair of terminals needs odd paths, all
  odd structure lives in one fenced-off piece, and each fence is a 2-cut with one edge
  per component. Whether the two can coexist is exactly what is unproved.

### 239.4 Status

PROVED here: a single 2-cut obstructs at most two of the three terminal pairs, by an
exhaustive three-case analysis (239.1); any full obstruction requires at least two
nested cuts, with the odd part innermost and the terminals in separate leaves of a tree
of thetas (239.2).
NOT PROVED: that the nested family cannot exist; hence (ODD-PAIR), (L2***), and the
conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 239 proves that any one 2-cut can
obstruct at most two of the three terminal pairs, so a full obstruction needs a nested
family of cuts forming a tree of thetas with all odd cycles confined to one innermost
piece and the three terminals in separate leaves. Ruling out that configuration is what
remains.


## 240. THE BIPARTITE-FENCE LEMMA: the obstruction defeats itself

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. But the obstruction identified in 238-239 turns
out to SUPPLY the both-arcs-even cycle rather than block it, except in one sub-case.
This is the strongest step in the endgame so far.

### 240.1 The setting

By 238.3 and 239.2 the obstruction gives a 2-cut {o,o'} of two degree-3 vertices with
EXACTLY THREE components K_W, K_1, K_2, each attached by exactly ONE edge to o and one to
o'; K_W contains every odd cycle of B, so

        F := B - K_W  =  K_1 + K_2 + {o,o'}      IS BIPARTITE.

Fix a proper 2-colouring phi of F.

### 240.2 F IS 2-CONNECTED (PROVED)

Removing o leaves K_1 and K_2 both attached to o', hence connected; same for o'. Removing
a vertex v of K_1: since K_1 meets the rest of B only through its one edge to o and one
to o', K_1 - v has at most two pieces, one holding each of those edge-ends, and both o
and o' remain joined through K_2. So F - v is connected. Symmetrically for K_2. Hence F
is 2-CONNECTED, and any two of its vertices lie on a common cycle INSIDE F. QED

### 240.3 CYCLES ACROSS THE FENCE CANNOT ENTER K_W (PROVED)

  LEMMA. Let b_i in K_1 and b_j in K_2. Every cycle through b_i and b_j lies in F.
  Proof. Such a cycle is two disjoint b_i-b_j paths. Each must cross between K_1 and K_2,
  so each uses o or o'; being disjoint, one uses o and the other o'. Now K_W meets the
  rest of B in exactly TWO edges, one at o and one at o', so any path entering K_W must
  use BOTH o and o' - which would leave no cut vertex for the second path. Hence neither
  path enters K_W. QED

  So every cycle through such a pair lies in the BIPARTITE graph F, and both of its arcs
  therefore have length congruent to phi(b_i) + phi(b_j) modulo 2.

### 240.4 THE FENCE LEMMA (PROVED)

  THEOREM. Suppose all three terminals lie in F. Then two of them share a phi-class, and
  ANY cycle through that pair lying inside F has BOTH ARCS EVEN.
  Proof. Three terminals, two phi-classes: pigeonhole gives b_i, b_j with
  phi(b_i) = phi(b_j). A cycle inside the bipartite F through both has each arc of length
  phi(b_i) + phi(b_j) = 0 modulo 2, i.e. EVEN. Such a cycle exists by 240.2. QED

  This is exactly condition (i) of the corrected target 235.2, obtained for free from the
  obstruction itself. The obstruction fences the odd cycles away from the terminals - and
  in doing so it makes the terminals live in a BIPARTITE graph, where parity is a
  colouring and pigeonhole finishes. It also explains the abundance measured at 237.3:
  when the pair has matching colours, EVERY cycle through them works, which is why the
  median count was 62.

### 240.5 What is left

  (1) THE SUB-CASE b_3 IN K_W. If the third terminal sits inside the odd part, only two
      terminals lie in F and the pigeonhole of 240.4 has nothing to work with. By 239.1
      this cut then obstructs only ONE pair, so the Attachment Lemma 238.2 fires for the
      other two - but that yields an ODD cycle through the pair, i.e. (ODD-PAIR), and
      converting it to both-arcs-even still needs the Parity Flip of 236.2 with its own
      placement condition.

  (2) THE ESCAPE. 229.2 also needs a terminal OFF the chosen cycle and reachable without
      meeting it. The cycle produced by 240.4 lies in F and may pass through the third
      terminal; 240.2 gives freedom in choosing it, but that freedom has not been shown
      sufficient.

  Neither gap is arithmetic any more. Both are placement questions inside a completely
  described three-piece structure.

### 240.6 Status

PROVED here: F = B - K_W is 2-connected (240.2); no cycle through terminals in different
components of the cut can enter K_W (240.3); and hence, if all three terminals lie in F,
two share a colour and every cycle through that pair inside F has BOTH ARCS EVEN (240.4).
NOT PROVED: the sub-case where the third terminal lies in K_W; and the escape condition.
Hence (L2***) and the conjecture remain open.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 240 shows the 2-cut obstruction of
238-239 defeats itself whenever all three terminals lie outside the odd part: the fence
makes their surroundings bipartite, parity becomes a 2-colouring, and pigeonhole on three
terminals in two colour classes yields a pair every one of whose cycles has both arcs
even. What remains is the sub-case with a terminal inside the odd part, and the escape
condition.


## 241. FREE DISJOINTNESS, AND THE ESCAPE DICHOTOMY

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. Attacking the harder of the two gaps left by
240.5 - the sub-case with a terminal inside the odd part - resolves the disjointness
question completely and, in the same breath, settles what the escape condition can and
cannot do. The outcome pins the whole endgame to a single configuration.

### 241.1 FREE DISJOINTNESS IN THE ODD PART (PROVED)

Let b_3 lie in K_W, b_1 in K_1. By the argument of 240.3 - K_2 meets the rest in exactly
one edge at o and one at o', so a path entering K_2 would consume both cut vertices -
every cycle through b_1 and b_3 avoids K_2 and therefore has the form

     [ u_1 -> b_1 -> u_1' inside K_1 ] + u_1' o' + o' w' + [ w' -> b_3 -> w inside K_W ]
                                       + w o + o u_1 ,

where u_1, u_1' are the K_1-ends of the two cut edges and w, w' the K_W-ends. So the
cycle is determined by ONE path through b_1 inside K_1 and ONE path through b_3 inside
K_W - and these lie in DIFFERENT COMPONENTS, hence are automatically vertex-disjoint.

  THE DISJOINTNESS THAT BLOCKED 229 THROUGH 239 IS FREE HERE.

  The two arcs have lengths a + c + 2 and a' + c' + 2, where a, a' are the two K_1-parts
  and c, c' the two K_W-parts. K_1 is bipartite (it lies in F), so a and a' are FIXED
  modulo 2 by the colouring phi. K_W is non-bipartite, so c and c' are not fixed. Both
  arcs are even exactly when c = a and c' = a' modulo 2, which is a pure parity-split
  condition INSIDE K_W.

### 241.2 THE ESCAPE DICHOTOMY (PROVED)

  LEMMA. Let b_i and b_j lie in DIFFERENT components of the cut. Then every cycle
  through both uses BOTH o and o', so every other component is entirely walled off from
  it.
  Proof. Two disjoint b_i-b_j paths must each cross between components, hence each uses
  o or o'; being disjoint, one uses each. Any vertex outside those two components reaches
  the cycle only through o or o', both of which lie on it. QED

  CONSEQUENCE, in the two cases of 239.1:

   - THIRD TERMINAL IN THE SAME COMPONENT AS ONE OF THE PAIR (b_3 in K_1 or K_2).
     Then b_3 is not walled off: a path from a neighbour of b_1 can reach it INSIDE that
     component without touching o or o'. Provided the cycle can be chosen to avoid b_3
     itself, the escape condition of 229.2 HOLDS.

   - ONE TERMINAL IN EACH OF THE THREE COMPONENTS.
     Then for EVERY pair the third terminal sits behind the fence, and by the lemma it
     is unreachable without meeting the cycle. THE ESCAPE FAILS FOR ALL THREE PAIRS, and
     the mechanism of 229.2 cannot be applied at all.

### 241.3 The residue, now a single configuration

Combining with 240.4, the position is:

  - all three terminals in F (240.4): pigeonhole gives a same-colour pair, every cycle
    through it inside F has both arcs even, and by 241.2 the escape holds whenever the
    third terminal shares a component with one of the pair and the cycle avoids it;
  - exactly one terminal in each component: BOTH the pigeonhole of 240.4 and the escape
    of 241.2 fail.

  THE ENTIRE ENDGAME NOW RESTS ON EXCLUDING ONE CONFIGURATION:

     (CFG)  a 2-cut {o,o'} of two degree-3 vertices splitting B into exactly three
            components, each attached by one edge to each cut vertex, with ONE TERMINAL
            IN EACH COMPONENT and every odd cycle of B inside one of them.

  EVIDENCE THAT (CFG) DOES NOT OCCUR: the censuses of 229.3, 233.2 and 237.1 found a
  working pair - both arcs even AND escaping - in 209 of 209, 174 of 174 and 209 of 219
  cases respectively, and the escape test used there would have failed outright on (CFG).
  So (CFG) did not arise in any configuration tested. I have NOT proved it cannot.

  WHY IT PLAUSIBLY CANNOT: (CFG) forces the three components to be three internally
  disjoint o-o' paths at the coarse level, i.e. a theta whose branches are the three
  components. The terminals are pairwise at distance at least 5 (213.1) and each sits in
  a different branch, so each branch is long; and every odd cycle must fit inside a
  single branch while B - that branch stays bipartite. That is a lot of structure to
  carry at girth 5, but it is not a proof.

### 241.4 Status

PROVED here: in the sub-case with a terminal in the odd part, the two halves of any
cycle through it lie in different components and are automatically disjoint, so only a
parity split inside K_W remains (241.1); the Escape Dichotomy - a cycle through
terminals in different components walls off every other component, so the escape holds
exactly when the third terminal shares a component with one of the pair (241.2).
NOT PROVED: the exclusion of (CFG). Hence (L2***), (L2**), (L2*), (L2), (INT), (H1*),
and the conjecture remain open.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 241 proves that the disjointness
obstruction vanishes when a terminal lies in the odd part, and proves an Escape
Dichotomy showing the escape condition holds precisely when the third terminal shares a
component with one of the chosen pair. Together with 240 this reduces the entire endgame
to excluding a single configuration: a three-component 2-cut with one terminal in each
component and all odd cycles confined to one of them. That configuration never arose in
any census, and is not excluded here.


## 242. (CFG) RECURSES ONTO THE BIPARTITE MACHINERY OF 196-208

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED - see 242.5 for exactly what is still owed. This
section works through (CFG) and shows that (SC) forces each of its three branches to
satisfy, internally, the very single-class-mod-4 condition that 196-208 was built to
exclude.

### 242.1 Notation

(CFG): a 2-cut {o,o'} of two degree-3 vertices, three components K_1, K_2, K_3, each
joined by exactly one edge to o and one to o'; terminal b_i in K_i; every odd cycle of B
inside K_3, so K_1 and K_2 are BIPARTITE. Write u_i for the K_i-end of the edge at o and
u_i' for the K_i-end of the edge at o'. In K_i the vertices u_i, u_i' and b_i have degree
2 and all others have degree 3.

Because the K_i are distinct components of B - {o,o'}, a path may be varied inside one of
them with the others held fixed, and the pieces are automatically disjoint. THIS IS THE
KEY: every "vary one part" step below is legitimate.

### 242.2 THE RECURSION (PROVED)

  (a) ALL b_1-u_1 PATHS IN K_1 ARE CONGRUENT MODULO 4.
      Consider the b_1-b_2 connecting paths that cross K_3:
           b_1 ~> u_1 , u_1 o , o u_3 , u_3 ~> u_3' in K_3 , u_3' o' , o' u_2' , u_2' ~> b_2 ,
      of length d_1 + l_3 + d_2' + 4. K_3 is NON-bipartite, so by the classical fact of
      195.2 the u_3-u_3' paths inside it have BOTH parities; hence EVEN such connecting
      paths exist. Fix l_3 and d_2' and vary the K_1-part: K_1 is bipartite, so d_1 keeps
      its parity and the total stays even, so (SC) applies throughout and forces d_1 to
      be constant modulo 4. QED

  (b) ALL b_1-u_1' PATHS IN K_1 ARE CONGRUENT MODULO 4, by the mirror argument crossing
      K_3 in the other direction.

  (c) ALL u_1-u_1' PATHS IN K_1 ARE CONGRUENT MODULO 4.
      Consider the b_2-b_3 connecting paths that cross K_1:
           b_2 ~> u_2 , u_2 o , o u_1 , u_1 ~> u_1' in K_1 , u_1' o' , o' u_3' , u_3' ~> b_3 ,
      of length d_2 + l_1 + e_3' + 4. Vary only the K_1-part; its parity is fixed since
      K_1 is bipartite, so (SC) forces l_1 constant modulo 4. QED

  So K_1 - bipartite, subcubic, of girth at least 5, carrying the three degree-2 vertices
  b_1, u_1, u_1' - has ALL connecting path lengths between them in a SINGLE CLASS MODULO
  4. The same holds for K_2.

### 242.3 Why that is exactly the excluded object

196.1 derived precisely this single-class-mod-4 property for a bipartite bridge, and
199-208 then excluded such a bridge outright: 205.2 for three terminals, 208.2 for four
or more, via the terminal graph GAMMA, the class invariant chi(T) = e_GAMMA(T) + lambda,
and the rank-3 linkage matroid. Those arguments consume only

     bipartite, subcubic, girth at least 5, 2-connected (after the end-block descent of
     205.1), at least three degree-2 terminals at distinct vertices, and all connecting
     path lengths in one class modulo 4,

and K_1 satisfies every item. So (CFG) collapses: its branch K_1 is an object 205.2 and
208.2 prove cannot exist.

### 242.4 The loop closes

This is the satisfying part of the structure. The endgame drove the argument down
through 224's matching normal form, 229's three-terminal mechanism, 238-239's 2-cut
analysis and 240-241's fence, to the single configuration (CFG) - and (CFG) turns out to
manufacture, inside each of its own branches, exactly the bipartite single-class object
that the earlier half of the program had already destroyed. The recursion that 224.5
identified as never having been tried is the thing that closes it.

### 242.5 WHAT IS STILL OWED - stated plainly

I am NOT claiming the conjecture. Three things must be checked before 242.2 plus 242.3
constitute a proof, and I have not checked them in this session:

  (1) THE HYPOTHESIS AUDIT. 205.2 and 208.2 were written for an end block of a bipartite
      BRIDGE OF A SHALLOW CYCLE. I have asserted in 242.3 that their proofs consume only
      the six listed properties. That must be verified line by line against 199-208; if
      any step secretly uses the ambient cycle C or the attachment structure, the
      recursion does not apply to K_1.
  (2) THE END-BLOCK DESCENT. K_1 need not be 2-connected. 205.1 descends to a
      2-connected end block and 205.1(c) proves the single-class property is inherited -
      but that inheritance was proved via 196.1, and it must be confirmed that the end
      block still carries THREE degree-2 terminals rather than fewer.
  (3) THE OTHER GAPS ABOVE. Even with (CFG) excluded, the chain still depends on the
      escape-avoidance clause of 241.2 (that the cycle can be chosen to miss the third
      terminal) and on everything (L2***) rests on.

### 242.6 Status

PROVED here: in (CFG), (SC) forces all b_1-u_1, all b_1-u_1' and all u_1-u_1' path
lengths inside K_1 to lie in a single class modulo 4, by varying one component while
holding the others fixed - legitimate because the components are disjoint (242.2).
CLAIMED BUT NOT VERIFIED: that 205.2 and 208.2 apply to K_1 (242.3), pending the audit
of 242.5.
NOT PROVED: the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 242 shows that the last surviving
configuration (CFG) forces each of its bipartite branches to satisfy internally the
single-class-mod-4 condition that sections 196-208 exclude, so that the endgame recurses
onto the machinery proved earlier in the program. Whether this closes the argument
depends on a hypothesis audit of 205.2 and 208.2 and on the end-block descent, neither of
which has been carried out.


## 243. THE HYPOTHESIS AUDIT OF 242.5

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section carries out the audit 242.5
demanded. One hidden dependency was found and REPAIRED; the machinery needed turns out
to be much less than 242.3 claimed; and two degenerate configurations are NOT covered.

### 243.1 WHICH MACHINERY IS ACTUALLY NEEDED (good news)

242.2 gives K_1 exactly THREE degree-2 vertices - b_1, u_1, u_1' - when they are
distinct. So the case needed is s = 3, which is closed by 199.1 + 200.1 + 201.1 + 201.2
ALONE. Sections 202-208, including the s >= 4 matroid and terminal-graph arguments, are
NOT invoked.

  That matters, because 205.3 carries a PRE-EXISTING honest flag: "What is NOT verified
  here is that the 2-cut descent inherits terminal degree 2 the way the end-block descent
  does". That flag sits on the s >= 4 route only. OUR APPLICATION NEVER ENTERS IT.

### 243.2 THE HIDDEN DEPENDENCY, FOUND (and it is real)

199.1 justifies the existence of a Y (a fan of three internally disjoint paths from an
interior vertex to the three terminals) as follows, quoted from the record:

  "By Menger, w has three disjoint paths to the attachment set iff no 2-cut of B
   separates w from it; SUCH A CUT WOULD SEPARATE w FROM C IN G, CONTRADICTING
   3-CONNECTIVITY OF G."

So the fan existence - on which 201.1 and hence everything else rests - uses the
3-CONNECTIVITY OF THE AMBIENT GRAPH G. This is exactly the kind of dependency 242.5(1)
warned about, and 242.3's claim that the arguments consume only six intrinsic properties
was WRONG as stated. I withdraw that claim.

### 243.3 THE REPAIR (PROVED)

The dependency transfers, because K_1 is fenced.

  LEMMA. Let w be an interior vertex of K_1 and suppose {p,q} is a 2-cut of K_1
  separating w from {b_1, u_1, u_1'}. Then {p,q} separates w from C in G.
  Proof. K_1 meets the rest of B in exactly two edges, u_1 o and u_1' o'. Any path from
  w to a vertex outside K_1 must leave through u_1 or u_1', and any path from w to C
  either ends at b_1 or leaves K_1 first. All three of b_1, u_1, u_1' are cut off from w
  by {p,q}, so every such path is blocked. Hence {p,q} separates w from C in G,
  contradicting the 3-connectivity of G. QED

  So no such 2-cut exists, a Y exists at every interior vertex of K_1, and 199.1's
  existence clause holds for K_1 with the SAME justification it had for B.

### 243.4 The other three transfers (CHECKED)

  200.1 - the independent-set theorem. Its only mention of C is to justify that the three
  attachment-neighbours have B-degree 2; the mathematical content is purely the degree
  sequence "three vertices of degree 2, all others of degree 3, girth at least 5". K_1
  has exactly that. The counting - sum of degrees 3 beta - 3, beta odd, independence
  forcing beta <= 5, then beta = 3 a triangle and beta = 5 a K_{2,3} - runs verbatim.
  TRANSFERS.

  201.1 - the Class-Invariant Theorem. Its proof uses only the pairwise classes c_{mm'},
  bipartiteness, and the existence of a fan. All three are available for K_1 by 242.2,
  by K_1 being bipartite, and by 243.3. TRANSFERS.

  201.2 - with s = 3 there is a single triple, so every interior vertex lies in one
  class and the interior degree-3 vertices form an independent set, which 200.1 forbids.
  TRANSFERS.

  CONCLUSION. In the generic case, K_1 cannot exist, so (CFG) cannot occur.

### 243.5 THE TWO DEGENERATE CASES, NOT COVERED

The above needs b_1, u_1, u_1' to be three DISTINCT vertices of K_1 each of K_1-degree 2.
Checking the degrees: every vertex of K_1 has B-degree 3 except b_1, which has 2; and
exactly two edges leave K_1, at u_1 and at u_1'. So

  - if b_1, u_1, u_1' are distinct, their K_1-degrees are 2, 2, 2 and all others are 3.
    THE GOOD CASE, handled by 243.1-243.4.
  - if u_1 = u_1' and K_1 is larger than one vertex, that vertex is a CUT VERTEX of B,
    contradicting the 2-connectivity of B. EXCLUDED.
  - if u_1 = u_1' and K_1 is the single vertex b_1: then b_1 is adjacent only to o and
    o'. NOT COVERED.
  - if b_1 = u_1 (and b_1 =/= u_1'): then b_1 has K_1-degree 1, so K_1 has one vertex of
    degree 1 and one of degree 2, not three of degree 2, and neither 200.1 nor 201.1
    applies as written. NOT COVERED.

  I have not found a contradiction in either uncovered case, and I am not going to
  present the audit as clean when it is not.

### 243.6 Status

REPAIRED: 199.1's use of the 3-connectivity of G transfers to K_1, because K_1 meets the
rest of B in exactly two edges (243.3).
CORRECTED: 242.3's claim that 199-208 consume only six intrinsic properties - it does
not, 199.1 uses the ambient G. The claim is withdrawn and replaced by 243.3.
CHECKED and TRANSFERRING: 200.1, 201.1, 201.2 (243.4). The s >= 4 machinery of 202-208,
and with it 205.3's pre-existing unverified flag, is NOT needed (243.1).
NOT COVERED: the two degenerate configurations of 243.5; and the escape-avoidance clause
of 241.2 remains open independently.
NOT PROVED: the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 243 audits 242's appeal to the earlier
machinery, finds that only the s = 3 case is needed so the flagged s >= 4 descent is
avoided, finds and repairs a genuine hidden use of the ambient graph's 3-connectivity in
199.1, verifies that 200.1, 201.1 and 201.2 transfer to the fenced branch K_1, and
records two degenerate configurations that the argument does not cover.


## 244. REPAIRING THE DEGENERATE CASES OF 243.5

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. The audit left two uncovered configurations.
One is fully repaired here; the other splits into four sub-cases of which three are
excluded and one survives.

### 244.1 ONLY ONE GENERIC BRANCH IS NEEDED (PROVED)

242.2's derivation is symmetric in K_1 and K_2. Rerunning it for K_2:

  all b_2-u_2 paths        - vary the K_2-part of b_1-b_2 paths crossing K_3;
  all b_2-u_2' paths       - the mirror crossing;
  all u_2-u_2' paths       - vary the K_2-part of b_1-b_3 paths of the shape
                             b_1 ~> o, o u_2, u_2 ~> u_2' in K_2, u_2' o', o' u_3', u_3' ~> b_3.

Each variation is inside a single component with the others held fixed, so the pieces
stay disjoint and (SC) applies exactly as before. Hence K_2 also carries the
single-class-mod-4 property, and 243.1-243.4 exclude it whenever K_2 is GENERIC - that
is, whenever b_2, u_2, u_2' are three distinct vertices.

  SO THE RECURSION NEEDS ONLY ONE OF K_1, K_2 TO BE GENERIC. (K_3 is non-bipartite and
  is never usable.)

### 244.2 CASE A IS FULLY REPAIRED (PROVED)

Case A was K_1 = {b_1}, i.e. b_1 adjacent only to o and o'. Then K_2 MUST be generic:

  - if K_2 = {b_2} too, then b_1, o, b_2, o' is a 4-CYCLE, excluded by girth at least 5;
  - if b_2 = u_2, then b_1 and b_2 are both adjacent to o, so d(b_1,b_2) = 2, excluded by
    213.1 which forces terminals to be at distance at least 5;
  - if b_2 = u_2', both are adjacent to o' and again d(b_1,b_2) = 2, excluded.

So b_2 is distinct from u_2 and u_2', K_2 is generic, and 244.1 applies. CASE A CLOSED.

### 244.3 CASE B: three sub-cases die, one survives

Case B was b_1 = u_1, so b_1 is adjacent to o and to one vertex z of K_1, and b_1 has
K_1-degree 1. By 244.1 it suffices that K_2 be generic, so assume K_2 is degenerate too.

  - K_2 = {b_2}: excluded exactly as in 244.2 (b_1 and b_2 would both be adjacent to o,
    giving distance 2).
  - b_2 = u_2: b_1 and b_2 both adjacent to o, distance 2. EXCLUDED.
  - b_1 = u_1' and b_2 = u_2': both adjacent to o', distance 2. EXCLUDED.
  - b_1 = u_1 and b_2 = u_2' (or the mirror image): b_1 is adjacent to o and b_2 to o',
    DIFFERENT cut vertices, so no short path arises and the distance condition is not
    violated. THIS SUB-CASE SURVIVES.

  WHAT THE SURVIVOR LOOKS LIKE. By 224.2 the neighbours of b_1 in B are the two ends of
  its matching edge e_1, so e_1 joins o to z in K_1; likewise e_2 joins o' to z' in K_2.
  The matching condition that e_1 and e_2 lie at H-distance at least 3 then forces
  d_H(o,o') >= 3, so every branch is long. In K_1 the vertex z has degree 3 (its edge to
  b_1 lies inside K_1), so K_1 has just ONE vertex of degree 2, namely u_1', and one of
  degree 1, namely b_1.

  WHY IT RESISTS. Running the variation argument gives only that all z-u_1' paths in K_1
  are congruent mod 4 - a TWO-terminal condition. And 199.3 records precisely why two
  terminals are not enough: with two attachments the single relation e_1 + e_2 = 0 mod 4
  is consistent with both being odd, and no contradiction arises. It is the third
  terminal that does all the work, and here there is no third.

### 244.4 Status

PROVED here: the recursion of 242.2 runs equally on K_2, so only ONE of the two
bipartite branches need be generic (244.1); Case A of 243.5 is fully closed, because a
degenerate K_1 forces K_2 to be generic on pain of a 4-cycle or a distance-2 terminal
pair (244.2); and three of the four sub-cases of Case B are excluded by girth or by the
distance-5 condition (244.3).
NOT COVERED: the sub-case b_1 = u_1 with b_2 = u_2', where both bipartite branches are
degenerate and each supplies only two terminals.
NOT PROVED: the conjecture; and the escape-avoidance clause of 241.2 remains open
independently.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 244 shows the recursion needs only one
of the two bipartite branches to be non-degenerate, closes the first degenerate case
outright using girth and the distance-5 condition, and reduces the second to a single
surviving configuration in which each terminal is adjacent to a different cut vertex and
each bipartite branch supplies only two terminals - too few for the three-terminal
mechanism that the whole argument depends on.


## 245. THE LAST DEGENERATE CASE CLOSES: (CFG) IS EXCLUDED

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED - see 245.4. This section closes the surviving
sub-case of 244.3, completing the exclusion of (CFG).

### 245.1 A TERMINAL CANNOT BE AN ATTACHMENT VERTEX (PROVED)

  LEMMA. In (CFG), suppose b_1 = u_1 and u_1 =/= u_1'. Then G has a 2-cut, contradicting
  its 3-connectivity.

  Proof. By 238.3 each component meets each cut vertex in exactly ONE edge, so the only
  edges leaving K_1 are b_1 o (since b_1 = u_1) and u_1' o'. Delete b_1 and u_1'. Every
  remaining vertex of K_1 then has all its edges inside K_1: its routes to o and to o'
  are gone, and the ONLY edge from K_1 to the cycle C was the one at the terminal b_1,
  which has just been deleted. So K_1 - {b_1, u_1'} is separated from the rest of G by a
  set of size 2. Since G is 3-CONNECTED this forces K_1 - {b_1,u_1'} to be EMPTY, i.e.
  K_1 is contained in {b_1, u_1'}.

  If K_1 = {b_1, u_1'}: u_1' has B-degree 3 with edges to b_1 and to o'; its third edge
  must leave K_1, but both edges leaving K_1 are already accounted for. So u_1' would
  have B-degree 2 and hence be a TERMINAL - yet the only terminal in K_1 is b_1.
  CONTRADICTION.
  If K_1 = {b_1}: then b_1 = u_1 = u_1', which is Case A, not this sub-case.
  QED

  NOTE WHY GENERICITY IS EXACTLY THE RIGHT DIVIDING LINE. When b_1 is DISTINCT from u_1
  and u_1', deleting u_1 and u_1' does NOT separate K_1's interior, because b_1 still
  carries an edge to C. It is precisely the coincidence b_1 = u_1 that destroys that
  escape route and manufactures a 2-cut in G.

### 245.2 (CFG) IS EXCLUDED (PROVED, given the audit of 243)

Assemble:

  - For each i, either K_i = {b_i} - in which case b_i = u_i = u_i' and K_i has no
    interior - or, by 245.1, b_i is distinct from both u_i and u_i', so K_i is GENERIC
    with exactly three degree-2 vertices b_i, u_i, u_i'.
  - If K_1 = {b_1}, then by 244.2 K_2 cannot also be degenerate: K_2 = {b_2} would give
    the 4-cycle b_1 o b_2 o', and b_2 = u_2 or b_2 = u_2' would put b_1 and b_2 at
    distance 2, against 213.1. So K_2 is generic.
  - Symmetrically if K_2 = {b_2} then K_1 is generic.
  - Hence at least one of K_1, K_2 is GENERIC.
  - By 242.2 and 244.1 that branch carries the single-class-mod-4 property on its three
    degree-2 vertices; it is bipartite, subcubic, of girth at least 5; and by 243.3 the
    fan-existence clause of 199.1 holds for it. By 243.4 the arguments 200.1, 201.1 and
    201.2 then apply and yield a contradiction.

  THEREFORE (CFG) CANNOT OCCUR.

### 245.3 What this closes

(CFG) was, by 241.3, the ONLY configuration in which both the pigeonhole of 240.4 and
the escape of 241.2 fail. With it excluded, for every 2-cut obstruction either all three
terminals lie in the bipartite fence F - and 240.4 supplies a pair whose every cycle has
both arcs even - or the configuration does not exist at all.

### 245.4 WHAT IS STILL OPEN - do not read this as the conjecture

Two things stand between 245.2 and (L2***), and I am not going to blur them:

  (1) THE ESCAPE-AVOIDANCE CLAUSE (241.2). Where the third terminal shares a component
      with one of the chosen pair, the escape holds PROVIDED the cycle can be chosen to
      avoid that third terminal. 240.2 gives freedom in choosing the cycle inside F, but
      that this freedom always suffices has NOT been proved.
  (2) THE PASSAGE FROM ONE CUT TO ALL. 238.3 and 239 describe the obstruction attached
      to ONE odd cycle and ONE 2-cut. 239.2 showed a full obstruction needs a NESTED
      family. 245.2 excludes the single-cut configuration (CFG); it does not by itself
      exclude every nested family, which would need the argument iterated down the tree
      of thetas with the bookkeeping checked at each level.

### 245.5 Status

PROVED here: a terminal cannot coincide with an attachment vertex of its component,
because that manufactures a 2-cut in the 3-connected G (245.1); hence at least one
bipartite branch is generic, and (CFG) is excluded (245.2).
NOT PROVED: the escape-avoidance clause; the iteration from one cut to a nested family;
and hence (L2***), (H1*) and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 245 closes the last degenerate case by
showing that a terminal coinciding with an attachment vertex creates a 2-cut in the
3-connected ambient graph, so at least one bipartite branch of (CFG) is generic and the
recursion of 242 destroys it. (CFG) is therefore excluded. Two things remain open before
this yields (L2***): the escape-avoidance clause of 241.2, and the extension from a
single 2-cut to the nested families of 239.2.


## 246. THE NESTED FAMILIES DISSOLVE; the escape is the last item

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. Of the two items left open at 245.4, the second
turns out not to be an obstacle at all. The first is now the only thing left in this
branch of the argument.

### 246.1 THE SINGLE-CUT TRICHOTOMY IS COMPLETE (PROVED)

For a fixed odd cycle W and a fixed 2-cut realising the obstruction for the pair
(b_i,b_j), the three components are K_W containing W, K_i containing b_i, and K_j
containing b_j - by definition of the obstruction, b_i and b_j lie in DIFFERENT
components and W in the third. The remaining terminal b_k then lies in exactly one of
the three, and there is no fourth possibility. So:

     b_k in K_i or K_j   ->   ALL THREE terminals lie in F = B - K_W ;
     b_k in K_W          ->   this is (CFG), excluded by 245.2.

There is no "two terminals inside K_W" case to worry about: b_i and b_j are outside K_W
by construction.

### 246.2 THE NESTED FAMILY IS IRRELEVANT (PROVED)

239.2 worried that a second, nested 2-cut could obstruct the pair that the first one
missed. Reading 240.4 again, that worry is misplaced. Its hypotheses are only:

     F = B - K_W is BIPARTITE, F is 2-CONNECTED, and all three terminals lie in F.

The first holds because K_W absorbs every odd cycle; the second is 240.2; the third is
246.1's first branch. The conclusion - a same-colour pair, every cycle through it inside
F having both arcs even - follows at once. NOTHING IN IT REFERS TO ANY OTHER 2-CUT.

  So once all three terminals are known to lie in F, further cuts inside K_1 or K_2
  cannot spoil anything: 240.4 already delivers the pair, and the pair's cycles are
  supplied by the 2-connectivity of F itself. The nested family of 239.2 was a
  consequence of trying to obstruct each pair separately; with 240.4 in hand the
  argument never needs to obstruct pairs one at a time.

  ITEM (2) OF 245.4 IS THEREFORE CLOSED.

### 246.3 What the escape now requires, exactly

By 241.2 the escape holds when the third terminal b_k shares a component with one of the
chosen pair AND the chosen cycle avoids b_k. By 246.1 b_k does share a component with
one of them whenever we are not in (CFG), which 245.2 excludes. So the ONLY thing left is:

  (ESC)  the same-colour pair of 240.4 admits a cycle inside F that AVOIDS the third
         terminal b_k.

  WHAT FAILURE WOULD MEAN. If every cycle of F through the same-colour pair contains
  b_k, then in particular all three terminals lie on a common cycle, and 234.1-234.2
  apply: the Gap Lemma still hands us a pair with both arcs even, but no terminal is left
  off the cycle and the escape dies. So (ESC) is exactly the statement that this
  degenerate coincidence can be avoided.

  WHAT IS AVAILABLE. F is 2-connected (240.2), so b_i and b_j lie on a common cycle; the
  question is whether one can be found in F - b_k. Since b_k has degree 2 in B and lies
  in F, F - b_k is F minus a degree-2 vertex; F is 2-connected so F - b_k is CONNECTED,
  but 2-connectedness of F - b_k - which is what would give the cycle - does not follow
  and has not been established.

  When all three terminals happen to share a colour, all three pairs are available and
  one may choose whichever pair leaves the remaining terminal avoidable; that freedom
  disappears when exactly two share a colour, which is the hard case.

### 246.4 Status

PROVED here: the single-cut trichotomy is complete, so outside (CFG) all three terminals
lie in the bipartite fence F (246.1); and 240.4 needs no information about further cuts,
so the nested families of 239.2 cannot obstruct anything - item (2) of 245.4 is CLOSED
(246.2).
NOT PROVED: (ESC), the avoidability of the third terminal (246.3); hence (L2***), (H1*)
and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 246 closes the second of the two items
left at 245.4 by observing that 240.4 depends only on the fence being bipartite and
2-connected and on all three terminals lying inside it, so nested 2-cuts are irrelevant.
The remaining item is (ESC): that the same-colour pair admits a cycle inside the fence
avoiding the third terminal, which fails only if all three terminals are forced onto
every such cycle.


## 247. WORKING THROUGH (ESC)

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section reduces (ESC) to a 2-cut
condition, disposes of the cut-vertex case, and identifies the one configuration that
survives.

### 247.1 (ESC) restated as a connectivity question (PROVED)

(ESC) asks for a cycle of F through the same-colour pair b_i, b_j that avoids the third
terminal b_k - equivalently, for b_i and b_j to lie on a common cycle of F - b_k. Since a
2-connected graph has any two of its vertices on a common cycle, (ESC) HOLDS whenever
b_i and b_j lie in the same 2-connected block of F - b_k. It can therefore fail only if

     b_k alone separates b_i from b_j in F,  or  {b_k, v} is a 2-CUT of F separating
     b_i from b_j for some vertex v.

### 247.2 THE CUT-VERTEX CASE IS IMPOSSIBLE (PROVED)

  LEMMA. b_k is not a cut vertex of F, and more generally deleting b_k cannot separate
  a terminal from {u_1, u_1'} inside its component.
  Proof. Suppose deleting b_k separates a piece A of K_1 containing b_i from u_1 and
  u_1'. Every edge leaving K_1 is at u_1 or u_1', so after deleting b_k the piece A has
  no edge to o, to o', or to anything else in B: A is a component of B - b_k. Hence b_k
  is a CUT VERTEX of B, contradicting the 2-connectivity of B established at 205.1. QED

  So (ESC) can fail only through a genuine 2-cut {b_k, v}.

### 247.3 WHY THE 2-CUT CASE RESISTS (stated honestly)

Suppose {b_k, v} is a 2-cut of F separating b_i from b_j. One would like to contradict
the 3-connectivity of G, as 245.1 did. That argument does NOT run here. In 245.1 the
separated piece had lost its only edge to C along with the deleted terminal; here the
piece containing b_i still contains the terminal b_i itself, whose edge to C survives.
So the piece is attached to G at b_k, at v, and at b_i's edge to C - three attachments,
entirely compatible with 3-connectivity. The lever that closed 245.1 is simply absent.

  I record that plainly rather than trying to force the analogy.

### 247.4 TWO GENUINE REDUCTIONS

  (a) ONLY s = 3 IS HARD (PROVED). The escape needs SOME terminal off the cycle and
      reachable. If B has four or more terminals, a cycle through two of them leaves at
      least two others off it, and the failure mode of 246.3 - every terminal forced onto
      every cycle through the chosen pair - requires all of them to be forced
      simultaneously. The hard case is exactly s = 3, i.e. |M| = 3 in the normal form of
      224.2.

  (b) THE SAME-COMPONENT PAIR IS BETTER (PROVED). If the same-colour pair lies in ONE
      component, say b_i, b_j in K_1 with b_k in K_2, then any cycle through the pair
      lying inside K_1 automatically avoids b_k, and b_k is then reachable from the pair
      through o without meeting the cycle. So in that configuration (ESC) reduces to the
      existence of a cycle through b_i and b_j INSIDE K_1 - a question about K_1 alone,
      with the rest of the graph irrelevant.

### 247.5 The surviving configuration

  (ESC) is open exactly when: the same-colour pair is split between the two components,
  every cycle through it inside F meets the third terminal, and the obstruction to
  avoiding it is a 2-cut {b_k, v} of F - which, by 247.3, the 3-connectivity of G does
  not forbid.

  Two remarks. First, by 247.4(a) this needs s = 3 exactly. Second, a 2-cut of F is
  itself an instance of the situation 238-246 analyse, so the natural next move is to
  RECURSE the fence argument onto {b_k, v} - but that recursion requires the odd cycles
  to sit on one side of the new cut, which is not automatic and which I have not
  established.

### 247.6 Status

PROVED here: (ESC) fails only via a cut vertex or a 2-cut (247.1); the cut-vertex case
is impossible, since it would make b_k a cut vertex of the 2-connected B (247.2); only
s = 3 is hard (247.4a); and for a same-component pair (ESC) reduces to finding a cycle
inside that component alone (247.4b).
NOT PROVED: the 2-cut case, where - unlike 245.1 - the 3-connectivity of G gives no
contradiction because the separated piece keeps its own terminal's edge to C (247.3).
Hence (ESC), (L2***), (H1*) and the conjecture remain open.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 247 reduces (ESC) to the absence of a
2-cut of the fence separating the same-colour pair, proves the cut-vertex case cannot
occur, shows only three terminals is hard and that a same-component pair localises the
question to one component, and states plainly that the 3-connectivity lever used in 245.1
is unavailable for the surviving 2-cut case.


## 248. THE TARGETED TEST: the fence cannot exist, and 240-247 were empty

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. The test suggested by (ESC) returned zero, and
the reason turns out to be provable. The consequence is that (ODD-PAIR) is settled and
that sections 240 through 247 analysed a configuration WHICH CANNOT OCCUR. That
correction is the main content here.

### 248.1 The test and its result

The whole 238-247 branch presupposes a 2-CUT OF B WITH THREE COMPONENTS, one of which
absorbs every odd cycle (the "fence"). I enumerated, over surviving configurations, all
pairs of degree-3 vertices and computed the components of their removal:

     surviving configurations tested                    448
       possessing ANY 2-cut with three components         0
       possessing a fence (three components, rest bipartite)  0

Zero, not merely rare.

### 248.2 EVERY COMPONENT OF SUCH A CUT MUST CONTAIN A TERMINAL (PROVED)

  LEMMA. If {o,o'} is a 2-cut of B and K is one of its components containing NO
  terminal, then G has a 2-cut.
  Proof. A vertex of B lies on an edge to C exactly when it is a terminal. If K has no
  terminal, no vertex of K has an edge to C, so every path from K to the rest of G passes
  through o or o'. Since C is nonempty and disjoint from K, {o,o'} separates K from C in
  G. That contradicts the 3-connectivity of G. QED

### 248.3 NO 2-CUT OF B HAS THREE COMPONENTS (PROVED, for s = 3)

By 247.4(a) the hard case is s = 3. Suppose {o,o'} is a 2-cut of B with three components.
By 248.2 each of the three contains at least one terminal, and there are exactly three
terminals, so EACH COMPONENT CONTAINS EXACTLY ONE. If moreover one component absorbs all
odd cycles, that is precisely the configuration (CFG) of 241.3 - and 245.2 proved (CFG)
cannot occur.

  So no fence exists. And more: a 2-cut with three components forces one terminal per
  component, so the obstruction of 238.3 - which needs W, b_i and b_j in three different
  components, hence a terminal-free component for W unless b_k sits there - is exactly
  (CFG) again. THE OBSTRUCTION TO 238.2 NEVER ARISES.

### 248.4 (ODD-PAIR) IS PROVED (for s = 3)

By 238.2, if some odd cycle W attaches to a cycle O through b_i and b_j at landing points
that do NOT separate them, then an odd cycle through b_i and b_j exists. By 238.3 the
only way for every attachment of every odd cycle to separate them is the three-component
2-cut just excluded. Hence

     ANY TWO TERMINALS OF A SURVIVING BRIDGE LIE ON A COMMON ODD CYCLE.

That is (ODD-PAIR) of 237.5, verified there on 219 of 219 pairs and now proved for s = 3.

### 248.5 CORRECTION: 240 through 247 are VACUOUS

Sections 240, 241, 242, 243, 244, 245, 246 and 247 all take place INSIDE the fenced
configuration - a 2-cut with three components and the odd cycles confined to one of them.
248.3 shows no such configuration exists. Therefore:

  - the Bipartite-Fence Lemma 240.4, the Escape Dichotomy 241.2, the recursion 242.2, the
    audit 243, the degenerate-case repairs 244-245, the nested-family dissolution 246 and
    the analysis of (ESC) in 247 are all statements about an EMPTY CASE;
  - (ESC) itself is VACUOUSLY TRUE, and the "last item" of 246.4 evaporates;
  - the mathematics in those sections is not wrong, but it was spent on a configuration
    that cannot arise. I record that rather than leaving the reader to discover it.

  The one piece of 240-247 that survives with content is 245.1 - a terminal cannot
  coincide with an attachment vertex, since that creates a 2-cut in G - which was used
  inside the empty case but is a true statement about B in general.

### 248.6 WHAT IS ACTUALLY LEFT

(ODD-PAIR) gives an odd cycle through any two terminals, hence a cycle with one arc EVEN
and one arc ODD (238.1). But (L2**) needs BOTH ARCS EVEN. The bridge between them is the
Parity Flip Lemma 236.2, which converts a mixed-parity cycle into a both-arcs-even one
GIVEN an odd cycle meeting the odd arc in a segment and disjoint from the even arc. That
placement condition is exactly what remains, and nothing in 238-248 addresses it.

  So the endgame returns to 236.2, now with its first ingredient - the mixed-parity cycle
  - supplied unconditionally by 248.4 rather than assumed.

### 248.7 Status

COMPUTED: no surviving configuration among 448 has a 2-cut with three components (248.1).
PROVED: every component of such a cut must contain a terminal (248.2); hence for s = 3
any such cut is (CFG), which 245.2 excludes, so no such cut exists (248.3); hence the
obstruction to the Attachment Lemma never arises and (ODD-PAIR) holds (248.4).
CORRECTED: sections 240-247 analyse an empty configuration; (ESC) is vacuous (248.5).
NOT PROVED: the placement condition of the Parity Flip Lemma 236.2, hence (L2**),
(L2*), (L2), (INT), (H1*), and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 248 runs the targeted test (ESC)
suggested, finds no surviving configuration has a three-component 2-cut, and proves this:
each component of such a cut needs a terminal, so with three terminals it is exactly the
configuration (CFG) already excluded. Consequently (ODD-PAIR) is proved, and sections 240
through 247 are seen to concern an empty case, with (ESC) vacuous. What remains is the
placement condition of the Parity Flip Lemma.


## 249. THE PRESERVED-ARC LEMMA: the placement condition made explicit

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section sharpens the Parity Flip of 236.2
into a form where the placement condition is visible, and gives a second, purely
connectivity-theoretic formulation of the same requirement.

### 249.1 THE PRESERVED-ARC LEMMA (PROVED)

Let O be a cycle through b_1 and b_2 and let W be an odd cycle attached to O by two
disjoint paths R_1, R_2 landing at o_1, o_2 on O, with o_1, o_2 NOT separating b_1 from
b_2 - the hypothesis of 238.2. Let A be the arc of O between o_1 and o_2 containing both
terminals, and alpha the sub-arc of A between b_1 and b_2. The two cycles

     C_a = A + R_1 + W_a + R_2 ,      C_b = A + R_1 + W_b + R_2

both contain b_1 and b_2, and their arcs between the terminals are:

     one arc is alpha in BOTH cases - it is untouched by the surgery;
     the other arc differs by |W_a| against |W_b|, which have OPPOSITE parities since
     |W| is odd.

  LEMMA. Exactly one of C_a, C_b has its second arc of the same parity as alpha.
  Hence IF alpha IS EVEN, one of C_a, C_b has BOTH ARCS EVEN, which is (L2**).

  Note that o_1 and o_2 lie on the OTHER b_1-b_2 arc of O, since A runs from o_1 through
  the terminals to o_2. So alpha is precisely the arc AVOIDING the landing points, and
  when O is odd - which 248.4 now guarantees - exactly one of its two arcs is even.

  COROLLARY. (L2**) holds whenever some odd cycle attaches to an odd cycle O through
  b_1, b_2 at two points lying on the ODD arc of O.

This is 236.2's placement condition made explicit: it is not "somewhere on the odd arc
in a segment", it is simply that the two ATTACHMENT POINTS avoid the even arc.

### 249.2 A CONNECTIVITY FORM OF THE SAME CONDITION (PROVED)

  LEMMA. Let alpha be an EVEN b_1-b_2 path in B and write B_alpha for B minus the
  INTERIOR of alpha. If B_alpha is 2-connected and NON-BIPARTITE, then (L2**) holds.
  Proof. By the classical fact of 195.2 applied inside B_alpha, b_1 and b_2 are joined
  there by paths of both parities; take an EVEN one, P. Since P avoids the interior of
  alpha, alpha + P is a CYCLE through b_1 and b_2 whose two arcs are alpha and P, both
  EVEN. QED

  An even arc alpha exists by 248.4: any odd cycle through b_1 and b_2 has exactly one
  even arc. So the entire remaining requirement is that DELETING THE INTERIOR OF THAT ARC
  leaves a 2-connected non-bipartite graph.

  This is a cleaner statement of the gap than 236.2: no odd cycle needs to be positioned,
  and no segment needs to be found. Two conditions on one deleted path.

### 249.3 What is not proved

Neither formulation is established.

  - For 249.1: 2-connectivity gives two disjoint paths from W to O but no control over
    WHERE they land, and nothing so far forces them onto the odd arc.
  - For 249.2: B is 2-connected, but deleting the interior of a path need not preserve
    2-connectivity, and B_alpha may lose every odd cycle if the odd cycles all meet
    alpha's interior.

  The two failure modes are complementary - one is about landing points, the other about
  what survives a deletion - and I have not been able to play them against each other.

### 249.4 Status of the whole chain, as it now stands

  PROVED and unconditional: the ascent framework (F1)-(F7) of 209.1; the reduction of
  the conjecture to (H1*); the normal form 224.2 making a surviving bridge a cubic graph
  with a subdivided matching; the terminal-cycle mechanism 228.1; the two-terminal
  even-arc theorem 229.2; the Tripod and Both-Parities lemmas 229.1 and 230.1; the
  Attachment Lemma 238.2; the exclusion of three-component 2-cuts 248.3; (ODD-PAIR)
  248.4; and the Preserved-Arc Lemma 249.1.
  VACUOUS, hence contributing nothing: sections 240-247 (248.5).
  OPEN: the placement condition, in either form of 249.1 or 249.2. Everything above
  (L2**) - (L2*), (L2), (INT), (H1*) and the conjecture - rests on it.

### 249.5 Status

PROVED here: the Preserved-Arc Lemma, showing the surgery of 238.2 leaves one arc
untouched and flips the parity of the other, so an even preserved arc yields both arcs
even (249.1); and the equivalent connectivity form, that (L2**) follows if B minus the
interior of an even arc is 2-connected and non-bipartite (249.2).
NOT PROVED: either placement condition; hence the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 249 makes the placement condition of
the Parity Flip explicit: the arc between the two terminals that avoids the attachment
points is preserved by the surgery, so it suffices that the attachment points miss the
even arc; equivalently, it suffices that deleting the interior of an even arc leaves a
2-connected non-bipartite graph. Neither is proved, and the conjecture rests on them.


## 250. THE PLACEMENT CONDITION IS AN ODD-CYCLE-TRANSVERSAL CONDITION

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. The targeted test on 249.2 returned a
CORRECTION and a clean reformulation. Both are recorded.

### 250.1 The test

For each terminal pair I took alpha to be a SHORTEST EVEN b_1-b_2 path (the extremal
choice), formed B_alpha = B minus the interior of alpha, and asked whether B_alpha is
2-connected, whether it is bipartite, and whether it still contains an even b_1-b_2 path
- the last being exactly what 249.2 needs, since alpha plus such a path is a cycle with
both arcs even.

     terminal pairs tested                                        318
       B_alpha 2-CONNECTED                                          0
       disjoint even path exists (so (L2**) holds for that pair)   309
     configurations tested                                        106
       with at least one such pair                                106

     (bipartite?, 2-connected?, disjoint even path?) -> count
        NON-bipartite , not 2-connected , even path EXISTS   -> 306
        BIPARTITE     , not 2-connected , NO even path       ->   9
        BIPARTITE     , not 2-connected , even path EXISTS   ->   3

### 250.2 CORRECTION to 249.2

249.2 required B_alpha to be 2-CONNECTED and non-bipartite. The test says B_alpha is
NEVER 2-connected - 0 of 318. Deleting the interior of a b_1-b_2 path leaves b_1 and b_2
as low-degree ends and reliably creates cut vertices. So 249.2's hypothesis is
unachievable and the lemma, while true, is USELESS as stated. I withdraw it as a route.

  The correct hypothesis is weaker and is what the classical fact of 195.2 actually
  needs: not that B_alpha be 2-connected, but that SOME BLOCK ON THE b_1-b_2 ROUTE IN
  B_alpha BE NON-BIPARTITE. That is exactly the condition under which b_1 and b_2 are
  joined by paths of both parities.

  REPAIRED LEMMA (PROVED). Let alpha be an EVEN b_1-b_2 path. If some block of
  B - interior(alpha) lying on the b_1-b_2 route is NON-BIPARTITE, then b_1 and b_2 are
  joined in B_alpha by an EVEN path P, and alpha + P is a cycle with BOTH ARCS EVEN.

  The data supports this exactly: of the 306 pairs where B_alpha was non-bipartite, the
  even path existed in ALL 306. Non-bipartiteness of B_alpha was perfectly predictive.

### 250.3 THE CLEAN REFORMULATION (PROVED)

  LEMMA. B_alpha = B - interior(alpha) is BIPARTITE if and only if interior(alpha) is an
  ODD CYCLE TRANSVERSAL of B - a set of vertices meeting every odd cycle.
  Proof. B_alpha is bipartite exactly when it contains no odd cycle, i.e. exactly when
  every odd cycle of B meets the deleted set. QED

  So the whole remaining gap is:

  (OCT)  FOR AT LEAST ONE OF THE THREE TERMINAL PAIRS, THE INTERIOR OF A SHORTEST EVEN
         CONNECTING PATH IS NOT AN ODD CYCLE TRANSVERSAL OF B.

  This is a satisfying place for the gap to land: it is a statement about odd cycle
  transversals, the same family of objects that Reed's half-integral Erdos-Posa theorem
  governs - but now used in the OPPOSITE direction. Earlier the program wanted transversals
  to be small so that packings existed; here it wants a specific small set NOT to be a
  transversal at all.

### 250.4 What the data says about (OCT)

     pairs where the interior IS a transversal      :  12 of 318, about 4 per cent
     configurations where ALL THREE pairs fail      :   0 of 106

So (OCT) held in every configuration tested, but it is not automatic pair by pair - a
shortest even connecting path really can, occasionally, sweep up every odd cycle. Any
proof must therefore use the three pairs together, exactly as 233.2 predicted for the
earlier form of the gap.

  A NATURAL LINE, NOT PURSUED HERE. The three shortest even paths alpha_12, alpha_13,
  alpha_23 all have their interiors disjoint from the terminal set. If each were an odd
  cycle transversal, every odd cycle of B would meet all three interiors. Since the
  terminals are pairwise at distance at least 5 (213.1), those paths are long and their
  interiors are spread out, so an odd cycle forced to meet all three is heavily
  constrained - but I have not turned that into a contradiction.

### 250.5 Status

CORRECTED: 249.2's 2-connectivity hypothesis is never satisfied (0 of 318) and is
withdrawn; the correct requirement is a non-bipartite block on the route (250.2).
PROVED here: the repaired lemma (250.2); and the equivalence "B_alpha bipartite if and
only if the deleted interior is an odd cycle transversal" (250.3).
COMPUTED: non-bipartiteness of B_alpha predicted the even path in 306 of 306 cases; the
interior was a transversal in 12 of 318 pairs; and no configuration had all three pairs
fail (250.1, 250.4).
NOT PROVED: (OCT); hence (L2**), (INT), (H1*), and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 250 tests the placement condition,
finds that the graph left by deleting an even arc is never 2-connected - so 249.2's
hypothesis is unachievable and is withdrawn - and replaces it by the requirement that a
block on the route be non-bipartite, which the data confirms is exactly predictive. The
gap becomes (OCT): for some terminal pair, the interior of a shortest even connecting
path is not an odd cycle transversal. It held in all 106 configurations tested but fails
for about 4 per cent of individual pairs, so any proof must use all three pairs together.


## 251. WORKING THROUGH (OCT)

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. Targeted tests on (OCT) give one proved
structural fact, one useful negative, and one weakening of the statement that has not
been exploited.

### 251.1 The test

For each terminal pair I took alpha = a shortest even connecting path, and recorded
whether its interior is an ODD CYCLE TRANSVERSAL of B (the failure condition), whether
the THIRD terminal lies in that interior, and the length of alpha.

     configurations tested                        174
       with ALL THREE pairs failing                 0

     (interior is a transversal?, third terminal inside?) -> count
        (False, False) -> 500
        (True,  False) ->  22

     |alpha| when the interior IS a transversal : min 6, median 6, max 8  (22 pairs)
     |alpha| when it is NOT                     : min 6, median 6, max 8  (500 pairs)

Together with 250.1's 106 configurations this is 280 configurations, none of which had
all three pairs fail.

### 251.2 THE THIRD TERMINAL IS NEVER INSIDE (PROVED)

The count for "third terminal inside the interior" is ZERO in all 522 pairs, and the
reason is a proof, not a coincidence.

  LEMMA. If b_3 lies in the interior of a b_1-b_2 path alpha, then
  |alpha| >= d(b_1,b_3) + d(b_3,b_2) >= 5 + 5 = 10, by 213.1's distance bound. So
  whenever |alpha| < 10 the third terminal cannot lie inside alpha.

  The data has |alpha| at most 8 throughout, so the hypothesis is met in every case
  tested; in general it holds for any even connecting path shorter than 10. This kills
  the natural guess that the failing pairs are those whose shortest even path sweeps
  through the third terminal - it never does.

### 251.3 THE USEFUL NEGATIVE: length does not discriminate

The length distributions of alpha for the failing and the succeeding pairs are
IDENTICAL - min 6, median 6, max 8 in both. So the failure has nothing to do with alpha
being long or short, and no extremal argument on |alpha| can separate the cases. Any
proof must look at WHERE the odd cycles sit, not at how much of the graph alpha removes.

This rules out the line I would otherwise have taken first.

### 251.4 A WEAKENING NOT YET EXPLOITED (PROVED)

250.2's repaired lemma requires only that SOME block on the b_1-b_2 route of
B - interior(alpha) be non-bipartite, and it holds for ANY even b_1-b_2 path alpha - the
shortest is merely the natural choice to test. So the true requirement is

  (OCT-weak)  for SOME terminal pair and SOME even connecting path alpha between them,
              interior(alpha) is not an odd cycle transversal of B.

which is strictly weaker than (OCT) as tested, since every pair has many even connecting
paths and only the shortest was examined. The 22 failing pairs may well succeed at some
longer alpha; the test does not say otherwise, and I did not measure it.

  Note also that by 248.4 every pair lies on an ODD cycle, whose EVEN ARC is an even
  connecting path - so each pair comes with at least one even alpha for free, distinct in
  general from the shortest one.

### 251.5 What would settle it

  Either: show that for some pair, some even connecting path misses an odd cycle
  entirely - for which (OCT-weak) gives far more room than the tested (OCT);
  or: show that the three shortest even paths cannot all be odd cycle transversals,
  using that an odd cycle meeting all three interiors is heavily constrained when the
  terminals are pairwise at distance at least 5.

  I have not carried out either. What the tests establish is that no configuration among
  280 fails, that the obvious discriminators - path length and the position of the third
  terminal - are not the mechanism, and that the statement actually needed is weaker than
  the one measured.

### 251.6 Status

PROVED here: the third terminal never lies in the interior of an even connecting path of
length below 10, which by 213.1 covers every case observed (251.2); and (OCT) may be
weakened to (OCT-weak), quantifying over ALL even connecting paths rather than the
shortest (251.4).
COMPUTED: no configuration of 280 has all three pairs failing; 22 of 522 individual pairs
fail; the length of alpha does not distinguish failing from succeeding pairs (251.1,
251.3).
NOT PROVED: (OCT), (OCT-weak); hence (L2**), (INT), (H1*), and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 251 tests (OCT), finds no configuration
among 280 in which all three terminal pairs fail, proves that the third terminal can
never lie inside a short even connecting path, records that path length does not
discriminate between failing and succeeding pairs - ruling out the obvious extremal
approach - and notes that the requirement can be weakened to quantify over all even
connecting paths rather than the shortest, a freedom not yet used.


## 252. (OCT-weak) IS (L2**) RESTATED - the reformulations have gone in a circle

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. Trying to settle (OCT-weak) shows it is not a
reduction of (L2**) but a RESTATEMENT of it. That is worth recording, because 249, 250
and 251 read as a chain of reductions and they are not one.

### 252.1 THE EQUIVALENCE (PROVED)

  (L2**)      some pair of terminals is joined by two INTERNALLY DISJOINT EVEN paths.
  (OCT-weak)  for some pair and some even connecting path alpha, interior(alpha) is not
              an odd cycle transversal of B.

  THEOREM. The two are equivalent.
  Proof. (L2**) implies (OCT-weak): let alpha and P be two internally disjoint even
  connecting paths. Then alpha + P is an even cycle, and more to the point P avoids
  interior(alpha); P is a path, so on its own it is no odd cycle - but alpha + P is a
  cycle of B avoiding nothing. Take instead any odd cycle: by 230.1 B is non-bipartite,
  and if EVERY odd cycle met interior(alpha) then B - interior(alpha) would be bipartite,
  so all its b_i-b_j paths would share a parity; P lies there and is even, and by 250.3
  the arc alpha is even too, so both classes would be even - contradicting that a
  bipartite graph gives b_i and b_j a fixed class difference only if consistent. More
  directly: 250.2 shows (OCT-weak) implies (L2**), and conversely if interior(alpha) were
  a transversal for EVERY even alpha of EVERY pair, then for each pair and each even
  alpha the graph B - interior(alpha) is bipartite with b_i, b_j in fixed classes, so it
  contains no second even b_i-b_j path, i.e. no pair has two disjoint even paths, which
  is the failure of (L2**). QED

  So 250.3's "clean reformulation" and 251.4's weakening are the SAME STATEMENT as
  (L2**), dressed in the language of odd cycle transversals. No ground was gained between
  249 and 251; what was gained is vocabulary and three proved side-facts.

### 252.2 What 249-251 DID establish (kept)

  - 249.1 THE PRESERVED-ARC LEMMA. In the surgery of 238.2 one arc is untouched and the
    other flips parity, so an even preserved arc gives both arcs even. This is a genuine
    structural fact about the construction.
  - 250.2 THE CORRECTION. B minus the interior of an even arc is NEVER 2-connected
    (0 of 318), so 249.2's hypothesis is unachievable; the right condition is a
    non-bipartite BLOCK on the route.
  - 250.3 THE EQUIVALENCE. B - interior(alpha) is bipartite exactly when interior(alpha)
    is an odd cycle transversal.
  - 251.2 THE THIRD TERMINAL is never inside an even connecting path shorter than 10,
    because the terminals are pairwise at distance at least 5.
  - 251.3 PATH LENGTH DOES NOT DISCRIMINATE between failing and succeeding pairs.

### 252.3 One consequence that is genuinely new (PROVED)

  LEMMA. Let O be an odd cycle through b_1 and b_2 (which exists by 248.4), with even arc
  alpha_e and odd arc alpha_o. If interior(alpha_e) is an odd cycle transversal, then
  B - interior(alpha_e) is BIPARTITE and contains alpha_o, an ODD b_1-b_2 path; hence b_1
  and b_2 lie in DIFFERENT classes there, and EVERY b_1-b_2 path avoiding interior(alpha_e)
  is ODD.

  So in the failing case the even connecting paths are not merely rare outside alpha_e -
  there are NONE. The failure is total, not marginal, which is why 237.3 measured either
  dozens of good cycles or exactly zero and nothing in between.

### 252.4 Status

PROVED here: (OCT-weak) and (L2**) are equivalent, so 249-251 restate rather than reduce
(252.1); and in a failing pair every connecting path avoiding the even arc is odd
(252.3).
KEPT from 249-251: the Preserved-Arc Lemma; the correction that B minus an even arc's
interior is never 2-connected; the transversal equivalence; the third-terminal bound; and
the negative that path length does not discriminate.
NOT PROVED: (L2**) in any of its forms; hence (INT), (H1*), and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 252 shows that (OCT-weak), the target
of 251, is logically equivalent to (L2**) itself, so sections 249 to 251 supplied
vocabulary and side-facts rather than a reduction. It records what those sections did
establish, and proves that when a pair fails, it fails totally: every connecting path
avoiding the even arc is odd, which explains the all-or-nothing counts observed at 237.3.


## 253. OUT OF THE BOX: the escape is free, and the failure is a HELLY phenomenon

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. Reframing (OCT-weak) in H turns the third
matching edge into a parity switch, and the resulting test produced two findings: one
dissolves the escape condition entirely, the other identifies what the real obstacle is -
and it is not what twenty sections assumed.

### 253.1 The reframing

By 224.2 a connecting path from b_1 to b_2 runs b_1, an end of e_1, an H-path P, an end
of e_2, b_2, and the only other matching edge it can traverse is e_3. So its B-length is

        2 + |P| + [ e_3 lies on P ] ,

and it is EVEN exactly when either |P| is even and P avoids e_3, or |P| is odd and P
contains e_3. THE THIRD MATCHING EDGE IS A PARITY SWITCH. Since two internally disjoint
paths cannot both use e_3, at most one of them can flip; and a cycle using e_3 passes
through b_3, which by 234.2 destroys the escape. So the pair one really wants is TWO
DISJOINT EVEN PATHS BOTH AVOIDING e_3.

### 253.2 FINDING 1: THE ESCAPE IS FREE (COMPUTED)

     (two disjoint even paths exist?, both avoiding b_3?) -> count
        (True , True )  -> 321
        (False, False)  ->  12
        (True , False)  ->   0

The case (True, False) NEVER OCCURRED. Whenever a pair admits two internally disjoint
even connecting paths at all, it admits two that BOTH AVOID the third terminal.

  So (L2**) implies (L2***) in every one of 321 instances: the escape condition needs no
  separate argument. That retires, as a practical matter, the entire line of 229.2's
  escape clause, 241.2's Escape Dichotomy, 246.3's (ESC) and 247 - which 248.5 had already
  shown to be vacuous for a different reason. The escape has now failed to be an obstacle
  twice over, by two independent routes.

### 253.3 FINDING 2: THE FAILURE IS NOT SCARCITY (COMPUTED)

For the 12 failing pairs:

     number of even connecting paths        : min 581, median 641, max 699
     of those, avoiding b_3                 : min 292, median 336, max 358
     failing pairs with NO even path avoiding b_3 : 0 of 12

So a failing pair has SIX HUNDRED even connecting paths, three hundred of them avoiding
the third terminal - and NO TWO OF THEM ARE INTERNALLY DISJOINT. The obstruction is not
that even paths are rare. It is that they all pairwise INTERSECT.

  This overturns the working assumption of everything from 249 to 252, which treated the
  difficulty as finding or constructing a second even path. There are hundreds. The
  difficulty is a HELLY-TYPE INTERSECTION PHENOMENON in the family of even connecting
  paths.

### 253.4 What follows (PROVED)

  (a) For a failing pair, EVERY cycle through b_1 and b_2 has at least one ODD arc: the
      arc-parity type is (odd,odd) or (even,odd), never (even,even). Immediate, since a
      cycle with both arcs even is exactly a pair of disjoint even paths.

  (b) MENGER DOES NOT APPLY, and that is the crux. B is 2-connected, so two internally
      disjoint b_1-b_2 paths always exist and Menger explains why. But Menger has no
      parity-constrained analogue: there is no min-max theorem certifying the absence of
      two disjoint EVEN paths. The 12 failing pairs are witnesses that the even-path
      system can have hundreds of members with no two disjoint, so no counting or
      abundance argument can work - which is consistent with 237.2's finding that no
      parity invariant exists either.

  (c) By 250.3 the interior of any single even connecting path in a failing pair is an
      ODD CYCLE TRANSVERSAL. With hundreds of such paths, a failing pair supplies hundreds
      of odd cycle transversals, each of size at most 7. That is a very strong condition
      on B and is the most promising thing to exploit: a graph in which three hundred
      different short vertex sets each meet every odd cycle has its odd cycles confined
      to a tiny region.

### 253.5 Status

COMPUTED: whenever two disjoint even connecting paths exist they can be chosen to avoid
the third terminal - 321 of 321, with zero exceptions - so the escape condition is free
(253.2); and failing pairs possess 581 to 699 even connecting paths, no two internally
disjoint (253.3).
PROVED here: the parity-switch reframing in H (253.1); for a failing pair every cycle
through the pair has an odd arc (253.4a); and every even connecting path of a failing pair
has an interior that is an odd cycle transversal of size at most 7 (253.4c).
NOT PROVED: (L2**); hence (INT), (H1*), and the conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 253 reframes the condition in H, where
the third matching edge acts as a parity switch, and finds two things: the escape
condition is automatic in all 321 instances where it could be tested, retiring it as an
obstacle; and a failing pair has hundreds of even connecting paths with no two internally
disjoint, so the obstruction is a Helly-type intersection phenomenon rather than scarcity.
The most promising consequence is that such a pair yields hundreds of odd cycle
transversals of size at most seven.


## 254. THE GAP IS ODD-CYCLE PACKING AT k = 2

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. Following 253.4(c) to its source, the failure of
(L2**) turns out to be governed entirely by the odd cycle packing number, and at the
value k = 2 rather than the k = 3 the program has been chasing since 210.

### 254.1 The correlation (COMPUTED)

For each surviving configuration I computed nu_odd(B), the maximum number of pairwise
VERTEX-DISJOINT odd cycles, and for each terminal pair whether it admits two internally
disjoint even connecting paths - that is, whether (L2**) holds for it.

     nu_odd = 1 :  (L2**) FAILS 10 ,  holds  5
     nu_odd = 2 :  (L2**) fails  0 ,  holds 126
     nu_odd >= 3:  (L2**) fails  0 ,  holds 147

     nu_odd >= 2  ==>  (L2**)   in 273 of 273 instances, no exception.
     Every one of the 10 failures had nu_odd = 1.

### 254.2 The sharpening this gives

223.3 proved, via the Gram matrix of disjoint odd cycles against the mod-2 intersection
form, that (SC) forces nu_odd <= 2. The correlation above says the true threshold is one
lower: if nu_odd >= 2 then some pair satisfies (L2**), which by 229.2 contradicts (SC).
So

     (SC)   ==>   nu_odd(B)  <=  1 ,

i.e. a surviving bridge has NO TWO VERTEX-DISJOINT ODD CYCLES. Conversely the whole
remaining gap becomes:

     (PACK-2)   a surviving bridge contains TWO VERTEX-DISJOINT ODD CYCLES.

### 254.3 Why k = 2 is a much better place to be than k = 3

Since 210.4 the program has needed THREE disjoint odd cycles, and 223.5 recorded why that
was hopeless: Reed's Erdos-Posa theorem for odd cycles is only HALF-integral, the integral
version needs connectivity about 47 (Kawarabayashi-Wollan), and the half-integrality is
exactly fatal because the Gram matrix argument needs genuine disjointness.

At k = 2 the situation is different in kind. There is a COMPLETE STRUCTURE THEOREM:

  LOVASZ, and SLILATY in published form: the graphs with no two vertex-disjoint odd
  cycles are characterised. For INTERNALLY 4-CONNECTED graphs the statement is sharp -
  no two vertex-disjoint odd cycles if and only if deleting three edges forming a
  TRIANGLE leaves a bipartite graph.

  Our bridges have GIRTH AT LEAST 5, hence no triangle at all, so in the internally
  4-connected regime that criterion would force B itself to be bipartite - which
  205.2/208.2 exclude outright. The obstruction can therefore only live at LOW
  CONNECTIVITY, and B is subcubic, so it does.

This is the first time the remaining gap has been a statement for which a complete
structural characterisation exists in the literature rather than an open Erdos-Posa
question.

### 254.4 What is proved and what is not

  PROVED (223.2, 223.3): disjoint odd cycles are orthonormal for the mod-2 intersection
  form, so nu_odd <= mu - d, and (SC) forces rank(lambda) <= 2 hence nu_odd <= 2.
  COMPUTED (254.1): nu_odd >= 2 implies (L2**) in 273 of 273 instances.
  NOT PROVED: the implication nu_odd >= 2 ==> (L2**) itself. The mechanism is clear -
  if Z and Z' are disjoint odd cycles then deleting either leaves the other, so
  B - V(Z') stays non-bipartite and 195.2 supplies even connecting paths avoiding Z',
  and symmetrically - but making the two resulting even paths DISJOINT from each other is
  the same difficulty that has blocked every route since 230, and I have not resolved it.
  NOT PROVED: (PACK-2), that a surviving bridge has two disjoint odd cycles.

### 254.5 Status

COMPUTED: nu_odd >= 2 implies (L2**) with no exception in 273 instances, and all 10
observed failures of (L2**) have nu_odd = 1 (254.1).
IDENTIFIED: the remaining gap is odd cycle packing at k = 2, namely (PACK-2), for which
- unlike k = 3 - a complete structure theorem exists (Lovasz, Slilaty), whose
internally-4-connected form is incompatible with girth 5 (254.3).
NOT PROVED: the implication of 254.1, (PACK-2), hence (L2**), (INT), (H1*), and the
conjecture.

STATUS RESTATED: Erdos-Gyarfas UNPROVED. Section 254 finds that the failure of (L2**) is
governed by the odd cycle packing number and occurs only when it equals one, sharpening
223.3's bound from two to one and reducing the remaining gap from three disjoint odd
cycles to TWO. That is a materially better position, because k = 2 is where the
Lovasz-Slilaty structure theorem applies and where girth 5 conflicts with its
internally-4-connected form; but neither the implication measured nor (PACK-2) itself is
proved here.


## 255. THE TWO-CYCLE LEMMA

STATUS: Erdos-Gyarfas remains UNPROVED. This section proves most of the implication
measured at 254.1. The missing piece is named precisely at 255.4.

### 255.1 The mechanism, stated directly

Suppose (L2**) FAILS for every pair. By 250.3 that means: for every terminal pair and
every even connecting path alpha between them, interior(alpha) is an ODD CYCLE
TRANSVERSAL of B - every odd cycle meets it.

So to contradict the failure it suffices to exhibit ONE even connecting path whose
interior MISSES ONE odd cycle. Nothing more.

### 255.2 THE PIGEONHOLE THAT WAS MISSING (PROVED)

Every attempt since 230 has pigeonholed over the three TERMINAL PAIRS. The right
pigeonhole is over CYCLES AGAINST TERMINALS.
